cambridge-econ.name: Economics, BA (Hons) (Economics Tripos)
cambridge-econ.applies: Undergraduate course page for October 2027 entry (or deferred 2028); Faculty paper-outline list and Programme Specification 2025-26; topic detail from the Economics Tripos supplementary regulations in Statutes and Ordinances 2017 (latest version that could be read in full)
cambridge-econ.rules: Part I: five compulsory papers, no options. Part IIA: three compulsory papers (Microeconomics, Macroeconomics, Theory and Practice of Econometrics I) plus one optional paper; a second option is allowed but rare, and the weaker of the two counts only if it helps. Part IIB: two compulsory papers (Microeconomic Principles and Problems, Macroeconomic Principles and Problems), a compulsory dissertation counting as one paper (6,000-7,500 words on a Faculty-approved economics topic), and two optional papers; a third option may be taken, with the weakest counting only if it helps. Some options are borrowed from Human, Social and Political Sciences (HSPS) and from the other Part. The Faculty does not guarantee that every option runs every year. Students may switch Tripos (e.g. into HSPS or Management Studies) with College approval.
cambridge-econ.teaching: The Economics Tripos runs over three years: Part I, Part IIA and Part IIB, each examined at the end of its year and given its own class. The Faculty provides lectures, with about 10-15 a week in first year, plus practical classes in some technical subjects. Colleges arrange small-group supervisions in liaison with the Faculty. Assessment is mainly by two- or three-hour written exams at the end of each year. There is also an essay in Year 1, a project in Year 2 and a compulsory 6,000-7,500-word dissertation in Year 3. The final degree is weighted 0% Part I, 30% Part IIA and 70% Part IIB.

profile.body: The Faculty of Economics organises lectures, and each paper is made up of several lecture courses. In first year that usually means 10 to 15 lectures a week. Some subjects add practical classes. Supervisions are arranged by your College in liaison with the Faculty, and organised by your Director of Studies. The University describes these as groups of usually one to three students with a supervisor, lasting about an hour. You get spoken and written feedback on the work you hand in for them. Lecturers publish course outlines so supervisors and students can choose supervision topics and reading. Teaching is concentrated in the eight-week Michaelmas and Lent terms. The University expects at least 35 hours of work a week, counting both contact time and independent study.

Each Part is examined at the end of its year, normally through a two- or three-hour written exam for each paper. Alongside the exams there is an essay in Year 1 and a project in Year 2. Year 3 has a compulsory dissertation of 6,000-7,500 words, which counts as one paper. The course page says other formats such as in-class tests, presentations and posters may be used, and that each year's methods are confirmed by the end of Michaelmas Term. You usually cannot resit. Each Part is classed First, 2:1, 2:2 or Third on the average of its paper marks. The overall degree weights Part I at 0%, Part IIA at 30% and Part IIB at 70%.

Part I (Year 1) has five compulsory papers: Microeconomics, Macroeconomics, Quantitative Methods, an applied social science paper on the political and social side of economics, and Economic History. Part IIA (Year 2) has three compulsory papers (Microeconomics, Macroeconomics and Theory and Practice of Econometrics I) plus one option. Part IIB (Year 3) has two compulsory papers (Microeconomic Principles and Problems, and Macroeconomic Principles and Problems), two options and the dissertation. According to the programme specification, you have to pass Part I to move on to Part IIA and pass Part IIA to move on to Part IIB. Completing all three Parts earns the BA (Hons). Because Part I counts for nothing in the final class, the second and especially the third year decide the outcome.

In Part IIA the options include International Trade and Development, Labour, Mathematics and Statistics for Economists, and History and Philosophy of Economics. Three papers are borrowed from HSPS: The Modern State and its Alternatives, Modern Societies, and International Conflict, Order and Justice. Part IIB options include Economic Theory and Analysis, Political Economics, Banking and Finance, Public Economics, Economics of Developing Countries, Industry, Econometrics II and Global Capitalism. Some papers can be borrowed from the other Part. You can take an extra option in either year, although few students do in IIA. The Faculty does not guarantee that every option runs every year, so talk to your Director of Studies first. Moving to HSPS or Management Studies means switching Tripos and needs College approval.

The degree deliberately pairs mathematical and statistical economics with history, politics and sociology. The compulsory first year includes economic history and an applied social science paper, and HSPS papers can be borrowed later. Every student writes a dissertation on an economics topic approved by the Faculty. The first year does not count towards the final class, and 70% of the result comes from Year 3. A-level Mathematics is required and all applicants sit the TMUA. Most entrants have also taken Further Maths: the Faculty reports 93% before the pandemic. Resources include the Marshall Library of Economics, statistical databases and software. The Complete University Guide 2026 ranks the course first in the UK.

cambridge-eng.name: Engineering (Engineering Tripos), BA (Hons) and MEng
cambridge-eng.applies: Course page describes October 2027 entry; Department teaching pages and module/set lists describe academic year 2026-27. The BA is awarded after Year 3 (Part IIA) and the MEng after Year 4 (Part IIB).
cambridge-eng.rules: Part IA: all courses and coursework compulsory; four 3-hour papers; coursework credited under a standard-credit scheme. Part IB: Papers 1-7 compulsory; Paper 8 has a compulsory section (The Engineer in Business) plus questions from two of seven elective topic sections (one section if offering a foreign language; Civil is coursework-only). Part IIA: offer 10 modules for examination, five in Michaelmas and five in Lent, at most one per set; at least six from one Engineering Area to qualify in that area (otherwise General Engineering); one Extension Activity (20 marks); two Easter projects (80 marks each); exams 600 marks, coursework 240. Part IIB: offer 8 modules (usually 4 Michaelmas and 4 Lent), normally one per set, at most three from the 4E/4I1/4M1-4/4M23/4M28/4M29 group, no module repeated from IIA; at least two management modules across IIA and IIB; a dissertation may replace one module; the individual project is 50% of credit. MEng progression needs at least a 2.ii in Year 2 or Year 3. At least six weeks of industrial experience are required by June of Year 3. BA class is 30% IB and 70% IIA; MEng is unclassed with Merit/Distinction.
cambridge-eng.teaching: The course mixes Department lectures, lab experiments, coursework and design projects with small-group College supervisions based on examples papers. First-years have about 22 hours of teaching a week. Each year has three terms, Michaelmas, Lent and Easter: two have eight weeks of formal teaching and one has seven. Each Part combines written exams with coursework. Part IA and IB exams come at the end of Easter Term, while Part IIA and IIB exams come at the start of Easter Term, followed by projects. The years are called Part IA and Part IB (together Part I), then Part IIA (BA) and Part IIB (MEng).

profile.body: Teaching combines Department lectures, lab practicals, projects and small-group supervisions arranged by your College. First-years have about 22 hours of teaching a week. The Department expects roughly 36-45 hours of study a week in term, around 1,200 hours a year. In Part IA, examples papers come out about every four lectures and are worked through in supervisions. There are also about two 2-hour lab experiments a week, plus drawing, CAD and computing. Part IIA modules have 16 lectures each, with labs and coursework. Part IIB modules have 12-16 timetabled slots and use examples classes rather than supervisions.

Every year combines written exams with coursework. Part IA has four 3-hour papers with no choice of questions, and experimental work is about one-ninth of the credit. Part IB has eight papers (mostly 2 hours), with about 15% from experimental work. In IA and IB, coursework earns 'standard credit' once you reach the qualifying level. Part IIA has a 1.5-hour exam per module at the start of Easter Term (600 marks) plus 240 coursework marks, including two Easter projects. In Part IIB the individual project is 50% of credit, and modules are assessed by exam, coursework, or both. The BA class is 30% Part IB and 70% Part IIA. The MEng is unclassed but awarded with Merit or Distinction.

Part I (IA and IB) is general engineering for everyone. You cover mechanics, structures, materials, thermofluids, electrical and information engineering and maths, with almost no choice for the first five terms. A small Easter-term choice comes in Part IB's Paper 8. Part II is where you specialise. In Part IIA (Year 3) you take ten modules and two projects, and earn your BA. Part IIB (Year 4) leads to the MEng, which needs at least a 2.ii in Year 2 or Year 3. You must complete at least six weeks of industrial experience by June of Year 3. A few students spend Year 3 on exchange in Paris or Singapore. You can also switch to Manufacturing Engineering or Management Studies.

Choices start in Part IB's Paper 8. Everyone takes The Engineer in Business, then answers on two of seven Easter-term discipline topics, or takes a language. In Part IIA you choose ten modules from about 45, five each in Michaelmas and Lent, with only one module per timetable set. To qualify in an Engineering Area, at least six must come from one of nine areas, such as Aerospace, Civil, Bioengineering or Information and Computer Engineering. Otherwise you can take General Engineering. You also pick one Extension Activity and rank project preferences. In Part IIB you pick eight modules from about 75, again one per set, with limits on management and language modules. Selections go through the COMET system.

Cambridge runs a single Engineering course rather than separate degrees for each branch. Everyone studies broad general engineering for two years and only specialises in Part II, choosing from nine Engineering Areas or staying general. Hands-on work is built in from the start, including a Lego Mindstorms exercise in week one and a robot-vehicle Integrated Design Project in Year 2. A Design Challenge is run with Engineers Without Borders. Part IIB centres on a year-long individual project that often links to Department research. The four-year MEng is accredited by the Engineering Council and major institutions, and the Manufacturing Engineering route runs through the Institute for Manufacturing.

cambridge-hsps.name: Human, Social, and Political Sciences, BA (Hons) (HSPS Tripos), Politics and International Relations track
cambridge-hsps.applies: Course page for October 2027 entry. HSPS Part I and Part IIA paper lists for 2026-27 (Part IIA options booklet dated 28-04-26). Provisional Part IIB list for 2027-28. POLIS paper pages for 2025-26.
cambridge-hsps.rules: Part I: four papers. Three come from POL1, POL2, SAN1 and SOC1, and must include POL1 or POL2. The fourth is another of those or one of SAN2, A1, A3, B1 and PBS02. Politics students normally take both POL1 and POL2. Part IIA (single-track Politics and IR): POL3 and POL4, one of POL7 or POL8, and one further paper from POL5, POL6 or an approved paper outside POLIS. Part IIB: POL9 is compulsory. Students then take two Politics papers from POL10-POL23, or one Politics paper plus a 10,000-word Politics dissertation, plus one further paper that may come from outside POLIS. Four papers are taken in each year, and at least three must be assessed wholly or partly by written exam. Only one of POL19, POL23 and a dissertation can be chosen. POL10 is barred if POL8 was taken in IIA, POL13 needs POL3 or POL4 in IIA, and POL6 and SOC5 cannot both be taken. Papers already sat in Part I (A1, A3, B1, PBS02, SAN2) cannot be taken again. Option lists change each year, and paper choices are submitted online in Easter term.
cambridge-hsps.teaching: HSPS is a three-year Tripos: a broad Part I, then Part IIA and Part IIB on a chosen track, here single-subject Politics and International Relations, run by the POLIS department. Faculty departments give lectures and seminars, and Colleges arrange small-group supervisions, so first-years can expect about 8 hours of lectures and one or two supervisions a week. From 2026-27, all HSPS exams are unseen, in-person papers of two or three hours, and some papers are assessed by long essays or projects instead. In Year 3 you can replace one paper with a Politics dissertation of up to 10,000 words. Your degree class depends entirely on Part IIB.

profile.body: Faculty departments run lectures and seminars, which students from all Colleges attend together. Your College, through your Director of Studies, arranges supervisions, which the University describes as usually one to three students with a supervisor for about an hour. In first year you typically have about 8 hours of lectures and one or two supervisions a week. In Michaelmas and Lent you attend lectures and supervisions and write selected essays. Easter term is given over to revision lectures, revision supervisions and exam preparation. From the second year, the POLIS department runs the Politics track, and its paper guides and supervision guidance are on Moodle. If you write a dissertation, you get six supervisions: three in Michaelmas and three in Lent. Your Director of Studies approves your supervisor, who cannot be a graduate student.

From 2026-27, every HSPS exam is an unseen, invigilated, in-person paper lasting two or three hours. Dissertations, long essays and projects are not affected by this change. In each of Parts IIA and IIB you take four papers, and at least three of them must be examined at least partly by written exam. For example, the POL6 statistics paper is half exam and half a 5,000-word report. The optional Politics dissertation must be between 6,000 and 10,000 words, with penalties outside that range. Titles are due in mid-October, and the 2025-26 submission deadline was noon on 30 April. Main exams fall in May and June. Each year you get its own class, but for students who started from 2020 the degree is weighted 0% Part I, 0% Part IIA and 100% Part IIB. You usually cannot resit.

Part I (Year 1) is four papers. Three come from POL1 (The Modern State and its Alternatives) or POL2 (International Conflict, Order and Justice), SAN1 and SOC1. The fourth can be the other POL paper or an archaeology, biological anthropology or psychology option. Near the end of Year 1 you choose a track. You cannot switch tracks later, except from a joint track to one of its two subjects. The single Politics and IR track sets Part IIA (Year 2) as POL3 International Organisation, POL4 Comparative Politics, POL7 or POL8 History of Political Thought, and one approved further paper. In Part IIB (Year 3) you take POL9, the compulsory conceptual-issues paper, two Politics papers (or one plus a dissertation) and one further paper.

You choose papers for the next year in Easter term using an online form, which opened on 7 May in 2026. Restrictions and prerequisites apply. You cannot take POL10 if you took POL8 in IIA. POL13 requires POL3 or POL4. POL6 and SOC5 cannot be combined. You can choose only one of POL19, POL23 or a dissertation. You also cannot retake papers already sat in Part I. Your further paper in IIA can come from Archaeology, Biological Anthropology, History and Philosophy of Science, Psychology, Social Anthropology or Sociology. In IIB it can come from several of these, or from History or Asian and Middle Eastern Studies. Option lists change every year and timetable clashes happen, so check the draft timetable before choosing. Supervisors, tutors and your Director of Studies can advise.

In first year you study politics alongside sociology and social anthropology before narrowing down, and you can still borrow papers from neighbouring subjects later. Everything rides on Part IIB: first- and second-year marks do not count towards the final class. Part IIA's Comparative Politics paper is taught through country-pair modules, such as Burma/Myanmar and Siam/Thailand, Jordan and Saudi Arabia, or Sierra Leone and Liberia. Third year centres on POL9, a paper on conceptual issues and texts in politics and IR. The department awards the John Dunn Prize each year for the best Politics dissertation. Facilities include two faculty libraries and the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology. The Guardian University Guide 2026 ranks Politics second in the UK.

cambridge-law.name: Law (BA Hons) - Law Tripos
cambridge-law.applies: Prospectus page shows October 2027 entry; paper list from the Faculty's BA Tripos site; half-paper and seminar lists published for 2025-26 (latest found); Paper 47 withdrawal effective 2026-27
cambridge-law.rules: Part IA: four compulsory papers (Civil Law in Context, Constitutional Law, Criminal Law, Law of Tort), after an online pre-arrival Legal Skills and Methodology programme. Part IB: five papers chosen from Group II (Contract, Land Law) and Group III; almost all students take Contract and Land Law. Part II: five papers chosen from Groups III and IV (and Criminal Law if not taken in Part IA); two Paper 49 half-papers count as one paper, and one paper may be replaced by a Paper 50 seminar course with a dissertation of up to 12,000 words. No paper may be taken twice, and Advanced Civil Law requires Civil Law in Context. The seven foundation subjects for a qualifying law degree (Criminal, Tort, Constitutional, Land, Contract, Equity, EU Law) are not strictly compulsory for the BA but nearly everyone takes them.
cambridge-law.teaching: The Law Tripos is a three-year BA split into Part IA, Part IB and Part II, with an optional year abroad after Part IB that makes it four years. The Faculty of Law gives one-hour lectures (roughly 10-12 per paper, up to about 200 students), while your College arranges supervisions in groups of two to four, about one per paper every fortnight. Supervision essays and problem answers are for feedback only and do not count. Almost all assessment is by written exams at the end of each year, with three hours per full paper and two per half-paper. The one exception is an optional 12,000-word seminar dissertation in Part II. Teaching runs in the eight-week Michaelmas and Lent terms, and Easter term is for revision and exams.

profile.body: Teaching is split between the Faculty and your College. The Faculty runs lectures for students from every College together. Each lecture lasts an hour and can have up to around 200 students, and a paper usually has 10-12 of them. Your College, through your Director of Studies, arranges supervisions: hour-long sessions where an expert in the subject meets two to four students. You can expect one supervision per paper every two weeks, which works out at about two or three a week. Before each one you read and answer set questions, and across the year you hand in about five pieces of written work per subject. That work is for feedback only. Before you arrive you complete an online Legal Skills and Methodology course. The University expects at least 35 hours of study a week across its three eight-week terms.

You are assessed at the end of each year in written exams: three hours for each full paper and two hours for each Paper 49 half-paper. Supervision work does not count, although many Colleges set mock exams in January. The one non-exam option is a Paper 50 seminar course, available in Part II. You write a dissertation of up to 12,000 words, including footnotes, in place of one of your five papers. It is due by the seventh day of Full Easter Term, and you may be called for a viva. You usually cannot resit exams. Each Part has its own class list. University data gives the overall degree weighting as 0:50:50, so Part IA does not count and Parts IB and II count equally. Prizes are awarded for outstanding exam performance.

Part IA (Year 1) is four fixed papers: Civil Law in Context, Constitutional Law, Criminal Law and Law of Tort. In Part IB (Year 2) you take five papers. Almost everyone takes Contract and Land Law, plus three options. Part II (Year 3) is another five papers, and students usually include Equity and EU Law. Under the regulations, you need honours in Part IB before you can take Part II. The optional year abroad comes after Part IB. You apply at the start of your second year to one of six partners: Regensburg, Poitiers, Utrecht, Auckland, the National University of Singapore or Pompeu Fabra. Selection includes an interview, and the Germany and Spain places also involve a language test. You then come back for a fourth year to complete Part II. Turing Scheme grants may help with costs.

Papers are organised in numbered groups. Part IB options include Administrative, Family, Human Rights and International Law, Jurisprudence and Legal History. Part II draws on Groups III and IV, including Commercial, Company, Competition and Labour Law, Intellectual Property, and Conflict of Laws. You can count two Paper 49 half-papers as one paper, or replace one paper with a Paper 50 seminar course and dissertation. You cannot take the same paper twice. The seven foundation subjects that the Bar requires for the academic stage are not compulsory for the BA, but nearly everyone takes them. Half-papers and seminar topics change every year. Paper 47 (Advanced Obligations) is withdrawn from October 2026. The Faculty holds an annual subject forum where course organisers present their papers.

The Faculty describes a normal term-time week as 8-12 one-hour lectures plus two or three one-hour supervisions. In first year, with four papers each supervised every other week, that usually means two supervisions a week. Before each supervision you work through the reading and answer a set of questions or an essay, and your supervisor then discusses it with you and the two or three others in your group. Weekly formal teaching therefore comes to roughly 10-15 hours, and the rest of the week goes on reading and preparing written work.

First year opens with Civil Law in Context, which is Roman law and the only subject taught at Cambridge since the Law Faculty began. Feedback comes mainly from College supervisions of two to four students rather than large seminars, while assessment rests almost entirely on end-of-year exams. The course links law with philosophy, economics, ethics, criminology, social policy and history. The University does not frame it as a qualifying law degree, but it prepares you for the SQE route to becoming a solicitor. It also covers the Bar's academic stage if you take the seven foundation subjects. Facilities include a moot court and the Squire Law Library, and the Faculty and the student Law Society run careers events and mooting. The Complete University Guide 2026 ranks it first in the UK.

cambridge-maths.name: Mathematics (Mathematical Tripos), BA (Hons) and MMath
cambridge-maths.applies: Course page describes October 2027 entry; Faculty schedules, Part II guide and lecture lists describe academic year 2026-27 (Part II structure changes to modular exams from 2027-28). Year 4 (Part III) is optional; the BA is a 3-year degree.
cambridge-maths.rules: Part IA: option (a) Pure and Applied Mathematics takes Papers 1-4; option (b) Mathematics with Physics takes Papers 1-3 plus the Natural Sciences Physics paper and practical notebooks (Numbers and Sets and Dynamics and Relativity are dropped). Part IA credit: all Section I questions and up to five Section II questions, with no more than three from one course. Part IB: 16 lecture courses plus Computational Projects with no fixed number to take; credit for up to four Section I and six Section II questions per paper; Computational Projects worth up to 160 marks. Part II: choose freely from 10 C and 27 D courses (typically 8-10); Computational Projects worth up to 150 marks; four cross-sectional papers in 2026-27, with modular papers from 2027-28. Part III: up to 16 units from exam papers (courses worth 2 or 3 units, typically 5-6 courses) plus an optional 3-unit essay; progression depends on Part II performance (Faculty guideline: a first or strong evidence of first-class potential).
cambridge-maths.teaching: Students attend Faculty lectures (about 12 a week in Year 1, Monday to Saturday mornings) and College supervisions, usually in pairs, averaging two a week, where they go over example sheets. Michaelmas and Lent each have eight weeks of lectures. Easter has about four weeks of lectures, which finish shortly before the exams. Part IA, IB and II are each examined by four written papers at the end of the year, with optional Computational Projects submitted beforehand in the second and third years. The years are called Part IA, Part IB and Part II (the BA), plus Part III, an optional fourth year leading to the MMath. Part III is examined by end-of-year papers and an optional essay.

profile.body: Teaching is built around Faculty lectures and College supervisions. In the first year you normally have about 12 lectures and two supervisions a week, with lectures lasting roughly 50 minutes and running on weekday and Saturday mornings. Supervisions are usually with one other student and a supervisor arranged by your College: you work through example sheets set for each course and then go over your solutions together. Lecture attendance is not compulsory, but the Faculty says few students manage without it. From the second year onward the number of lectures and supervisions depends on which courses you pick. Computational Projects add independent computing work in the second and third years.

Assessment is almost entirely by written exams at the end of each year in Easter Term. Parts IA, IB and II each have four papers. Every paper has a short-question Section I and a long-question Section II, and in Part IA you can earn credit on at most three long questions from any one course. Calculators and formula booklets are not allowed. The optional Computational Projects are submitted before the exams (up to 160 marks in IB and 150 in II) and added to your paper marks. Resits are not normally possible. Your Part II class is your overall BA class. From 2027-28, Part II exams will become modular. Part III is examined by papers in late May and June, plus an optional essay.

The Mathematical Tripos runs over three years: Part IA (Year 1), Part IB (Year 2) and Part II (Year 3). You must pass each Part to move on, and you graduate with a BA (Hons). Part IA is fixed: either Pure and Applied Mathematics, or Mathematics with Physics for students heading to Physics. Part IB goes deeper into first-year topics and adds new ones. In Part II you specialise. The optional fourth year, Part III, is a nine-month Masters leading to the MMath. Whether you can continue depends on your Part II results; the Faculty's guideline is a first or strong evidence of first-class potential. About a third of students stay on. You can also transfer to Management Studies, usually in Year 2 or 3.

In Part IA you choose only between option (a) and option (b), Mathematics with Physics. You state this when you apply but can change it when you arrive, and option (b) students can still continue in Mathematics. Part IB offers 16 lecture courses plus Computational Projects. There is no required number of courses, and the Faculty recommends studying fewer courses well rather than skimming all of them. Part II offers 10 C courses (more accessible) and 27 D courses (more advanced), with no restriction on mix. Most students take around 8 to 10, and those aiming for Part III are steered towards D courses. In Part III you usually choose 6 to 8 of roughly 75 to 80 courses, worth up to 16 units from exams, and can add a 3-unit essay.

At Cambridge, Maths is a single, broad Tripos covering pure maths, applied maths, theoretical physics and statistics. Up to Part II it is non-modular: exams cover the whole year's material and there is no pass threshold for individual courses. Small-group College supervisions sit alongside very fast-paced Faculty lectures. Part III is one of the best-known taught Masters in mathematics, with over 250 students, more than 70 courses and an essay chosen from a long list of research-level titles; Cambridge students who take it receive the MMath. The Faculty has close links with the Isaac Newton Institute. A Mathematics with Physics route gives first-years a way into Physics.

m.d: First course in abstract algebra, building group theory from concrete examples up to actions and quotients.
w: Small groups, quaternions and the Fermat–Euler theorem
Normal subgroups, quotient groups and the isomorphism theorem
Permutations, sign and the simplicity of A₅

m.d: Covers complex numbers, vector algebra and matrix methods, finishing with eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

m.g: Option (a) only; replaced in Mathematics with Physics
m.d: Introduces rigorous proof through logic, sets and functions, number theory and the construction of the reals.
w: The integers: induction and the Binomial Theorem
Primes, highest common factors and Euclid's algorithm
Modular arithmetic, Chinese Remainder Theorem, Fermat-Euler, Wilson and RSA

m.d: Develops calculus techniques and methods for solving first-order, nonlinear and higher-order ODEs, with multivariable applications.
w: Higher-order linear ODEs: general theory, impulses and series solutions
Multivariate functions: gradient, Taylor series and stationary points
Coupled systems, phase portraits and simple PDEs

m.d: Short non-examinable bridging course on particle and rigid-body mechanics for students without much prior mechanics.
w: Dynamics of particles, including projectiles with air resistance
Springs, strings and simple harmonic motion

m.d: Rigorous treatment of limits, continuity, differentiation, power series and the Riemann integral.
w: Differentiability and the mean value theorem
Power series and radius of convergence
The fundamental theorem of calculus and improper integrals

m.d: Builds probability from basic counting to an axiomatic setup, covering discrete and continuous random variables and limit theorems.
w: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' formula
Discrete random variables: distributions, expectation and variance
Generating functions, conditional expectation and branching processes

m.d: Calculus of curves, surfaces and volumes in three dimensions, the integral theorems, Laplace's equation and Cartesian tensors.
w: Curves in R³: arc length, curvature and torsion
Surface and volume integrals; change of variables
Vector operators: grad, div, curl and identities
Integration theorems: divergence, Green's and Stokes's

m.g: Option (a) only; replaced in Mathematics with Physics
m.d: Newtonian dynamics of particles, systems and rigid bodies, followed by an introduction to special relativity.
w: Basic concepts: frames, Newton's laws, dimensions and forces
Particle dynamics: polar coordinates, work and potential energy
Angular momentum, orbits and Rutherford scattering
Rotating frames: centrifugal and Coriolis forces
Systems of particles, the two-body problem and rockets
Rigid bodies: moments of inertia and rolling

m.d: Introductory lectures on algorithms and programming that prepare students for the Computational Projects assessed in Part IB.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Applied techniques for ODEs and PDEs: Sturm-Liouville theory, separation of variables, Green's functions and Fourier transforms.

m.d: Introduces wave mechanics via the Schrodinger equation, observables and the hydrogen atom.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Pure treatment of analytic functions, Cauchy's theorem and residues; shares an either/or exam question with Complex Methods.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Applied view of complex variable theory, using residues and integral transforms to solve problems.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Maxwell's theory from static fields to electrodynamics and its relativistic formulation.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Kinematics and dynamics of fluids, covering inviscid, viscous, potential and rotating geophysical flows.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Polynomial approximation, numerical ODE solvers and methods for linear systems and least squares.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Foundations of statistical inference: estimation, hypothesis testing and linear models.

m.g: Part IB courses (lectured but not examined in 2026-27)
m.d: Spherical, Riemannian and hyperbolic geometry; may be taken in Easter of the first or second year.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Calculus of variations: Euler-Lagrange equations, least action, Noether's theorem and second variation.

m.g: Part IB courses (free choice, no fixed number)
m.d: Convex optimisation, Lagrangian duality and linear programming with applications.

Classical elementary and analytic number theory, from congruences and reciprocity to primality testing.
A selection of attractive results from analysis, including fixed point theorems, approximation and transcendence.
w: Irrationality and transcendence of e, pi

m.d: Information theory, error-correcting codes and the mathematics of classical and public-key cryptography.
Theory of computation: computability, regular and context-free languages and the machines that recognise them.
Practical regression modelling in R, from normal linear models to generalised linear models and classification.
Deterministic, stochastic and spatial models of biological systems.
Advanced complex-variable techniques including analytic continuation, special functions and ODE solutions.
Lagrangian and Hamiltonian reformulations of mechanics, with rigid bodies and conserved quantities.
w: Rigid bodies and the symmetric top

m.d: Mathematical description of the expanding universe, its contents and the growth of structure.
Finite-dimensional quantum mechanics applied to qubits, quantum communication and quantum algorithms.
Propositional and predicate logic, completeness, ordinals and cardinals and axiomatic set theory.
Structural and extremal graph theory including connectivity, matchings, colouring and Ramsey theory.
Field extensions and Galois correspondence, culminating in the insolubility of the quintic.
Linear representations and character theory of finite groups, with a look at compact groups.
Algebraic invariants of spaces such as the fundamental group and simplicial homology.
Functional analysis of normed spaces, spaces of continuous functions and Hilbert spaces.
Modern analysis tools: Lebesgue and Sobolev spaces, Fourier transforms and weak derivatives applied to PDEs.
Geometry of solution sets of polynomial equations, from varieties to elliptic curves.
Smooth manifolds in Euclidean space, curvature, geodesics and the Gauss-Bonnet theorem.
Measure-theoretic foundations of probability, up to the strong law and central limit theorem.
Stochastic process models applied to queues, insurance, epidemics and networks.
Theory of statistical inference: likelihood asymptotics, Bayesian methods, decision theory and resampling.
Mathematics of option pricing using martingales, Brownian motion and optimal stopping.
Statistical learning theory and the analysis of common machine-learning algorithms.
Asymptotic expansions of integrals and of solutions to differential equations.
Qualitative behaviour of flows and maps, including bifurcations and chaos.
Exactly solvable nonlinear systems and soliton solutions of dispersive PDEs.
Operator formulation of quantum mechanics, angular momentum, many-particle systems and perturbation theory.
Quantum scattering and solid-state physics, from phonons and band structure to semiconductors.
Statistical mechanics of thermal systems, quantum gases and phase transitions.
Relativistic field theory of electromagnetism, radiation and fields in materials.
Einstein's theory of gravity built on differential geometry, applied to Schwarzschild spacetime and black holes.
Viscous flow at low and high Reynolds number based on the Navier-Stokes equations.
Linear and nonlinear wave motion in fluids and solids, dispersion and ray theory.
Numerical linear algebra and numerical methods for PDEs.
Algebraic number theory applied to Diophantine equations and reciprocity.
Complex analysis on surfaces: the Riemann sphere, elliptic functions and analytic continuation.
Assessed computing projects worth up to 150 marks, with work handed in near the start of Easter Term; over 30 projects are offered.
Fortnightly lab demonstrations in the Fluids Laboratory that support the fluid dynamics courses.
An extended expository essay on a research-level topic chosen from a list of more than 100 titles, submitted early in Easter Term before the exams.

cambridge-med.rules: Part IA and IB courses are all compulsory for medical students. All 2nd MB exams (including all four Preparing for Patients strands) must be passed, and an honours result achieved in Part II, before entering the Clinical School; only two attempts at 2nd MB exams are allowed (resits in September). In Part II, students choose one subject: NST Part II Biological and Biomedical Sciences (one Major of four papers, one Minor and a dissertation of up to 6,000 words), an NST Part II single subject (entry to some is limited), or another Tripos with approval from their Director of Studies. Graduate (affiliated) students skip the Part II year.
cambridge-med.teaching: Years 1-3 are the preclinical stage: the Medical Sciences Tripos (MedST) Part IA (Year 1) and Part IB (Year 2), then a compulsory Part II year in a chosen subject that earns the BA; Years 4-6 are the clinical stage at the School of Clinical Medicine (Core, Specialist and Applied Clinical Practice). Preclinical teaching is a traditional, lecture-led science course with practicals (including full-body cadaveric dissection), seminars and small-group College supervisions, typically 20-25 contact hours a week across three eight-week terms (Michaelmas, Lent, Easter). Preclinical courses are examined mostly in June by MCQ/SBA, practical and essay papers that count for both the Tripos and the professional 2nd MB; SECHI and Preparing for Patients are coursework, and FEBP and Head and Neck Anatomy are examined at the end of Lent. The clinical years run year-round in 4-8 week placement blocks at Addenbrooke's, seven partner hospitals and GP practices across the East of England, with review and integration weeks, weekly near-peer clinical supervisions, and assessment through Final MB Parts I, II and III (written papers, OSCEs, portfolios), the Prescribing Safety Assessment and the Medical Licensing Assessment.

profile.body: Cambridge keeps a traditional split between preclinical science and clinical training rather than using PBL or an integrated case-based model. In Years 1-2 you follow a heavily timetabled programme of lectures and practicals, typically 20-25 hours a week: dissection and prosections in the Human Anatomy Centre, histology classes three afternoons a week, experimental physiology, biochemistry lab work with discussion sessions and two short PBL exercises in MIMS. Alongside this, your College arranges small-group supervisions where you work through essays and problems. In the clinical years teaching moves to the bedside, outpatient clinics and GP surgeries; placements generally have no lectures and expect self-directed learning, supported by small-group seminars, simulated patients, weekly near-peer supervisions with trained junior doctors and Review and Integration weeks that bring the year group back together.

Patient contact in the preclinical years comes through Preparing for Patients, which runs across all three years. In Year 1 (PfP A) you visit general practices to practise interviewing and learn about consent and confidentiality; in Year 2 (PfP B) you meet patients in hospital; over the summer before Year 3 (PfP C) you visit community agencies; and through Year 3 (PfP D) you follow one pregnant woman and her family at home. Full-time clinical placements start in Year 4: a two-week introductory course, then rotations at Addenbrooke's and seven partner hospitals (including Bedford, Ipswich, King's Lynn, Peterborough, Hinchingbrooke, Stevenage and Bury St Edmunds), plus GP practices and community and mental health trusts across the East of England.

Preclinical courses are examined mainly in June by MCQ or SBA papers, practical or data-handling papers and essay papers. Most papers count both for the Tripos (your degree class) and the professional 2nd MB, which must be passed to continue. FEBP is a 45-minute MCQ and SECHI is two 3,000-word essays; both are 2nd MB only. You get two attempts at each 2nd MB exam, with resits in September, and you need an honours result in Part II. In the clinical school, Year 4 ends with Final MB Part I (written test, case portfolio and OSCE) and Year 5 with Final MB Part II (two written papers and an OSCE weighted towards paediatrics and O&G). Year 6 has Final MB Part III written papers and the Medical Licensing Assessment in January, clinical exams in late April, and the national Prescribing Safety Assessment.

Standard-entry students take six years. Years 1 and 2 are MedST Part IA and IB, covering anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, pathology, pharmacology, neuroscience and reproduction, plus a clinical strand. Year 3 is a compulsory, funded intercalated Part II year that leads to a BA (Hons), and every student takes it before clinical school. You can only move on to the Clinical School after passing every 2nd MB exam, including all four Preparing for Patients strands, and gaining honours in Part II. Year 4 (Core Clinical Practice) builds history-taking, examination and reasoning. Year 5 (Specialist Clinical Practice) rotates through four lifespan-themed 8-week blocks, and Year 6 (Applied Clinical Practice) combines an elective, four senior blocks and an apprenticeship before Foundation training. Affiliated (graduate) students skip the Part II year.

There are no options in Years 1-2. The big choice is the Year 3 Part II subject, made in Year 2 with your Director of Studies after a Part II Subject Fair in April. Most medics take NST Part II Biological and Biomedical Sciences (a Major subject, a Minor subject and a dissertation of up to 6,000 words) or a single-subject NST Part II such as Pathology, Pharmacology, PDN or History and Philosophy of Science, where some places are limited. With approval you can instead take another Tripos, such as Management Studies, Philosophy, HSPS, Archaeology/Anthropology or Geography. In the clinical years you choose student-selected components and research blocks (the Faculty's 2026 Open Day slides mention four research blocks across the course) and plan your own elective.

Cambridge is one of very few UK schools that still teaches anatomy through full-body dissection, and its preclinical years are an unusually deep science course examined as a Tripos, so you graduate with a BA as well as the MB BChir. The guaranteed intercalated Part II lets you specialise in almost any subject, from Pathology to Management Studies or Philosophy, and the College supervision system gives weekly small-group teaching throughout. Clinical training is centred on Addenbrooke's and the Cambridge Biomedical Campus with a regional hospital network, and there are routes into an MB/PhD and a separate graduate course. The prospectus cites Medicine as ranked first in the UK by the Complete University Guide 2026.

imperial-aero.name: Aeronautical Engineering MEng
imperial-aero.applies: 2026-27 programme specifications (H401 and H410) and 2026/27 module descriptors; course page shown is for 2027 entry
imperial-aero.rules: Years 1 and 2: all core (60 ECTS each). Year 3: all core modules, one I-Explore module and two 5-ECTS electives (60-62.5 ECTS). Year 4 (H401): Individual Project (35 ECTS) plus five 5-ECTS electives; electives taken in Year 3 cannot be repeated, and availability depends on the timetable. Year 4 (H410): 60 ECTS abroad, including a research project of at least 30 ECTS plus technical modules of equivalent level. Progression requires passing all 60 ECTS with a year average of at least 40%; at most 15 ECTS can be compensated across the programme. Classification weights: Year 1 7.5%, Year 2 20%, Year 3 36.25%, Year 4 36.25%.
imperial-aero.teaching: Imperial's four-year Aeronautical Engineering MEng is applied for under UCAS code H401; H410 is the 'with an Integrated Year Abroad' variant, which students transfer into at the end of Year 3 so that Year 4 is spent at a partner university. Teaching is mainly large-class lectures with pre-reading and guided problem-solving sessions, plus tutorials and labs and design projects in groups of 3-6, and the department provides every student with an iPad. Assessment moves from about 71% written exams in Year 1 to about 42% in Years 3-4, with the rest lab, project and design coursework and practical assessments (presentations, oral exams). The year runs over Autumn, Spring and Summer terms; Years 1-2 are all core, Year 3 adds two electives and a 20-25 person Group Design Project, and Year 4 is a 35-ECTS Individual Project plus five electives.

profile.body: Core material is delivered mainly in large-class sessions, from traditional lectures to more active formats: you study material before class, then practise in guided problem-solving sessions. The department gives every student an iPad for notes, e-reading, in-class questions and interactive notes. In Years 1 and 2 about 15% of your time is lectures and workshops (about 215 hours) and about 7% is small-class tutorials or labs (about 105 hours); you are expected to do 3-4 hours of independent study per contact hour. Labs and design projects run in groups of 3-6 and become more open-ended over time. Engineering drawing and programming (MATLAB, Python, then C++) are taught through guided tutorials, and report writing and presenting through small-group coaching.

Summative assessment is about 71% written exams, 20% coursework and 9% practical in Year 1, then 64/28/8 in Year 2 and roughly 42/37/21 in Year 3; H401's Year 4 is about 42% exams, 35% coursework and 23% practical. Typical core modules combine a closed-book exam (often 80%) with a lab practical and report, while computing modules use mastery tests and projects, and design modules are all coursework with peer assessment of individual contributions. The Year 4 Individual Project is assessed by thesis (60%), interim and final oral exams and supervisor assessment. Years are weighted 7.5%, 20%, 36.25% and 36.25%.

Years 1 and 2 are entirely core: aerodynamics, structures, mathematics, mechanics, materials, thermodynamics, computing, mechatronics, propulsion, flight dynamics and engineering practice. Year 3 brings Aerodynamics 3, Structures 3, Control Systems and Aerospace Vehicle Design, plus a large Group Design Project and two electives. Year 4 on the standard route is an Individual Project (often with a research group or a company) plus five electives. You apply to H401, then can choose an integrated year abroad (H410, Year 4 at a partner such as MIT, NUS, RWTH Aachen or ISAE-SUPAERO), a five-year year-abroad route, or a five-year route with a 9-12 month industry placement. Progression needs all 60 ECTS passed with at least a 40% average.

You choose two electives in Year 3 and five in Year 4 from a shared pool of about 30 Level 7 modules, and a module taken in Year 3 cannot be repeated in Year 4. Options cover advanced aerodynamics and CFD, structures and finite elements, propulsion, spacecraft engineering (orbital mechanics, spacecraft systems, structures and propulsion), control, machine learning, design optimisation, vertical flight, UAV systems and environmental impact, plus interdepartmental exchange modules and, in Year 4, a business or Horizons module. Some combinations are not possible because of timetabling, and a few modules are not running in 2026-27. On the integrated year abroad route, Year 4 modules are chosen from the host university's programme.

Practical aerospace work is built in: Year 2 includes a flight-testing course at Cranfield University's National Flying Laboratory Centre, and Flight Dynamics and Control uses the department's flight simulator. In Year 3, students design an aircraft in small teams (including structural testing) and then join a Group Design Project team of about 20-25 that produces a clean-sheet vehicle design. The course page highlights facilities such as the Aerial Robotics Laboratory and a Flight Simulation Suite. The degree is accredited by the Royal Aeronautical Society and IMechE towards Chartered Engineer status, with an ACGI awarded, and it offers integrated study abroad at partners including MIT and NUS.

imperial-chem.name: Chemical Engineering MEng
imperial-chem.applies: Programme specifications for 2026-27 entry (H801 standard; H802 Year Abroad, July 2026); course page shows 2027 entry
imperial-chem.rules: Years 1-2: nine compulsory modules each, 60 ECTS, no options. Year 3: all core/compulsory modules (including I-Explore, 5 ECTS) plus ONE Level 6 elective. Year 4: Research Project (10 ECTS) and Final Year Design Project (20 ECTS) plus SIX Level 7 electives (5 ECTS each). Electives may be withdrawn for low numbers or staff availability. You must pass the HAZOP component of Safety and Loss Prevention for IChemE accreditation. Progression needs all 60 ECTS passed and a 40% year average; at most 15 ECTS can be compensated across the programme. Classification weights: Y1 7.5%, Y2 20%, Y3 36.25%, Y4 36.25%. The Year Abroad (H802) replaces Year 3 and is entered by transfer from H801.
imperial-chem.teaching: Teaching uses lectures and guest lectures, tutorials, a laboratory sequence (Foundation Lab in Year 1, Knowledge Lab in Year 2, Discovery Lab in Year 3) with pilot-plant training, and team design projects every year. About 25% of Years 1-3 is timetabled contact (around 380 hours a year), with the rest independent study. Assessment is mainly exams early on (70% in Year 1) and moves to 50% exams and 45% coursework by Year 4. The year runs over Autumn, Spring and Summer terms. Year 4 consists of a research project in Autumn and a team plant design project in Spring, plus six electives.

profile.body: Teaching combines lectures (including guest lectures from industry), tutorials, lab and project work, presentations and an online learning environment. Practical work follows a clear sequence: a Foundation Laboratory in Year 1, a Knowledge Laboratory in Year 2 and a Discovery Laboratory in Year 3 with open-ended investigative experiments, alongside training on a pilot plant. Team-based design projects run through every year. In Years 1-3 about a quarter of the roughly 1,500-hour study year is timetabled contact (about 380 hours). In Year 4 lectures and tutorials drop to about 10% (around 150 hours) and team work on the final design project takes about 15% (around 250 hours). Workshops on careers, teamwork, ethics and report writing are also built in.

Assessment uses exams, in-class tests, coursework, lab experiments, individual and group reports, project work and presentations. The typical split moves from 70% exam, 20% coursework and 10% practical in Year 1, to 62.5/30/7.5 in Year 2, 55/40/5 in Year 3 and 50/45/5 in Year 4. The 'Mastery' modules in Years 1-3 assess whether you can apply core chemical engineering as a whole rather than topic by topic. Your classification weights Year 1 at 7.5%, Year 2 at 20%, and Years 3 and 4 at 36.25% each. Passing the HAZOP element of Safety and Loss Prevention is a requirement for accreditation.

Years 1 and 2 are fully prescribed: transfer processes, thermodynamics, separations, reaction engineering, process control, chemistry and maths, plus a practice module and a Mastery module each year. Year 3 adds process design, safety, environmental engineering, particle engineering and optimisation, plus I-Explore and one elective. Year 4 is Master's level: an Autumn research project, a Spring team plant design project and six electives. To progress you must pass all 60 ECTS each year with a 40% average. Selected students can transfer to the H802 Year Abroad route and spend Year 3 at a partner university. This needs upper-second performance in Years 1-2, language proficiency and an interview.

There are no options until Year 3, when you choose one Level 6 elective. The choices are Advanced Fluid Mechanics, Nuclear Chemical Engineering, Process Heat Transfer, Sustainable Energy Technologies, Biochemical Sensors or Entrepreneurship in Chemical Engineering. In Year 4 you choose six Level 7 electives across Autumn and Spring, from areas such as process systems and optimisation, bioprocess and biochemical engineering, colloids, membranes, carbon capture, oil and gas, and machine learning. Several Year 4 modules are flagged as not running in 2026/27, and any elective can be withdrawn for low numbers. Year Abroad students take Level 7 versions of any Year 3 essentials they missed, such as Safety and Loss Prevention, in place of some electives.

Imperial organises the core around a 'Mastery' concept, a holistic, systems-based approach assessed through dedicated Mastery modules in Years 1-3. Students train on an in-house Carbon Capture Pilot Plant, which the course page describes as state-of-the-art. Design projects run in every year and build up to a Master's-level plant design project, and environmental impact and safety run through the whole course. The degree is accredited by IChemE and fully meets CEng requirements, and graduates also receive the ACGI. The Year Abroad partners include MIT, Carnegie Mellon, EPFL, RWTH Aachen and the Universities of Queensland and Sydney.

imperial-civil.name: Civil Engineering MEng
imperial-civil.applies: Programme specifications for 2026-27 entry (H201 standard; H202 Year Abroad, revised July 2026); course page shows 2027 entry
imperial-civil.rules: All modules are core in Years 1 and 2 (60 ECTS each). Year 3: eight core modules plus compulsory I-Explore (pass/fail, 5 ECTS), and one elective from Group A (Spring) and one from Group B (Autumn). Year 4: Individual Research Project (35 ECTS) plus five Group C electives (5 ECTS each), subject to the timetable; the department syllabus page adds 'no more than one from each stream'. Prestressed Concrete requires Year 3 Concrete Structures. Progression needs a 40% year average; at most 15 ECTS can be compensated across the programme. Classification weights: Y1 7.5%, Y2 20%, Y3 36.25%, Y4 36.25%. H202 (Year Abroad) students spend all of Year 4 abroad and need at least 67% across Years 1-2.
imperial-civil.teaching: Teaching combines whole-class lectures with small-group exercises, tutorials supported by graduate and undergraduate teaching assistants (often one GTA per 8-10 students), labs in groups of 4-8, group design projects co-taught by industry practitioners, site visits and residential field trips. Contact time falls from about 579 timetabled hours in Year 1 to 185 in Year 4 as independent study grows. Assessment moves from 68% exams in Year 1 to about two-thirds coursework in Year 4, which is dominated by a 35-ECTS research project. The year has three terms (Autumn, Spring, Summer); the department calls the years Parts I-IV.

profile.body: Lectures go to the whole class and include questions and small-group exercises. Tutorials are run with graduate and undergraduate teaching assistants (in some modules one GTA per group of 8-10), and labs use research facilities in groups of four to eight. Group design projects are a major thread: the Civil Engineering Design modules in Years 1-3 are co-taught by consultants from industry, with regular client-style presentations. Timetabled hours are about 579 in Year 1, 524 in Year 2, 343 in Year 3 and 185 in Year 4, out of roughly 1,500 hours of study a year. Year 1 timetables deliberately leave large blocks of time for individual and group study, and every student has a personal tutor.

Assessment mixes written exams, coursework, lab reports, computer exercises, design projects, presentations, reflective writing and a dissertation-style research project. The indicative coursework/exam split is 32/68 in Year 1, 51/49 in Year 2, 37/63 in Year 3 and about 66/33 in Year 4. Major coursework and projects are blind double-marked, and feedback is promised within three weeks. Late work is capped at a bare pass if up to 24 hours late, and in-class deadlines such as design projects are zero-tolerance. Your classification weights Year 1 at 7.5%, Year 2 at 20%, and Years 3 and 4 at 36.25% each.

Years 1 and 2 (Parts I and II) are entirely core, building the fundamentals of structures, fluids, soils, materials, maths, computing and design, with a surveying field course in Year 1 and the Geology field trip and Constructionarium in Year 2. Year 3 is mostly core with two Level 7 electives and an I-Explore module, and each subject sequence (for example Structural Mechanics 1-3 and Fluid Mechanics 1-3) runs across the years. Year 4 is the specialist year: a 35-ECTS individual research project plus five electives. You need a 40% average each year to progress. On the H202 Year Abroad route you spend Year 4 at a partner university instead, but that needs 67% across Years 1-2 and language proficiency.

Choices start in Year 3, when you pick one Spring elective from Group A (Nonlinear Structural Analysis, Theory of Shells, Coastal Engineering or Highway Engineering) and one Autumn elective from Group B (Concrete Structures, Timber and Masonry, or Traffic Engineering). These are taught at Master's level. In Year 4 you choose five Autumn electives from Group C, spanning structures, geotechnics, water, transport and environmental engineering, subject to the timetable. The department says you can take no more than one per stream. Some modules have prerequisites; for example Prestressed Concrete needs Year 3 Concrete Structures. The lists are indicative and modules may be suspended.

The degree is accredited by five professional bodies (ICE, IStructE, IHE, CIHT and the Permanent Way Institution), and graduates also receive the ACGI. Practical fieldwork is built into the core: a six-day surveying camp in Year 1, a geology field course and the Constructionarium in Year 2, where teams build scaled-down versions of real structures. Design teaching is shared with practising industry consultants, and the curriculum maps onto the department's research sections in structures, geotechnics, environmental, transport and fluids engineering. The department cites first place in the UK for civil engineering in The Guardian and The Times 2026 guides.

imperial-eee.name: Electrical and Electronic Engineering MEng
imperial-eee.applies: Programme specification for 2026-27 entry (revised Jan 2026); department module catalogue snapshot of the September 2026 curriculum; course page shows 2027 entry
imperial-eee.rules: All modules are 5 ECTS unless stated; 60 ECTS per year in Years 1-2. Year 3: compulsory I-Explore (5 or 7.5 ECTS), four Group A (Autumn) options, three Group B (Spring) options, and one Group P (Summer) choice of Group Consultancy Project or Industrial Placement (20 ECTS). Year 4: Individual Project (30 ECTS), one version of the professional portfolio (ELEC70146, 10 ECTS, or ELEC70145 industrial experience, 30 ECTS), and six 5-ECTS electives from Groups A and B, which may include IDX modules from other engineering departments. Electives can be cancelled for low numbers or staff availability. Progression needs a 40% year average; entry to Year 4 needs 50% weighted average over Years 1-3; Year 4 pass mark is 50%. Classification weights: Y1 7.5%, Y2 20%, Y3 36.25%, Y4 36.25%.
imperial-eee.teaching: Teaching mixes lectures, team-based learning, flipped classes, problem classes, small tutorials of three or four students, and lots of lab work done in pairs, plus a group design project every year in teams of six to eight. Years 1 and 2 are entirely core and exam-heavy (roughly 65-70% exams), while Years 3 and 4 shift to about 43% coursework. The year runs over three terms (Autumn, Spring, Summer); many exams sit at the start of the following term or in Summer. Year 3 ends with either a six-month industrial placement or a three-month industry-led group consultancy project, and Year 4 centres on a 30-ECTS individual research project. Years are called Year 1-4 (FHEQ Levels 4-7).

profile.body: In Years 1 and 2 a typical 5-ECTS module has around 20 hours of lectures, about 10 hours of team-based learning and around 20 hours of lab, and you're expected to do two to three hours of self-study per contact hour. Labs are done in pairs, tutorials are in groups of three or four, and the year-long Electronics Design Projects are done in teams of six to eight working to a client brief. Teaching also uses flipped classrooms, workshops, recorded videos and software and hardware labs. By Years 3 and 4 a module is closer to 20 hours of lectures plus about 100 hours of independent work, so the balance moves strongly towards self-study. Each ECTS credit represents about 25 hours of work.

Assessment combines written exams, online tests, coursework reports, group work, hardware and software demonstrations and oral presentations. The specification gives an approximate split of 65% exam / 15% coursework / 20% practical in Year 1, about 70% exam in Year 2, and roughly 54% exam / 43% coursework in Years 3 and 4. Module descriptors show exams often fall at the start of the next term (e.g. Mathematics 1A is examined at the start of Spring) or in Summer, usually with a mid-term test worth 10-20%. Your final classification weights Year 1 at 7.5%, Year 2 at 20%, and Years 3 and 4 at 36.25% each. The final-year Individual Project is marked on an interim report, final report and presentation.

Years 1 and 2 are entirely core: maths, circuits, digital electronics, programming, electromagnetism, signals, power, communications and control, with a design project each year. Year 3 opens up to options split by term, plus an I-Explore module and a Summer-term industrial element: either a six-month placement (April-September) or a three-month group consultancy project. Year 4 is Master's level, built around a 30-ECTS Individual Project and six electives. You must average 40% each year to progress and at least 50% across Years 1-3 to stay on the MEng; otherwise exit awards such as a BEng are possible. A separate Year Abroad route (H601) swaps Year 4 for study at a partner university.

Options start in Year 3: you pick four Autumn modules from Group A and three Spring modules from Group B, then choose between the Group Consultancy Project and the Industrial Placement for Summer. In Year 4 you choose six 5-ECTS electives from a list of around 50 across Autumn (Group A) and Spring (Group B), covering areas such as communications, control, power systems, machine learning, imaging and integrated circuits. Through the Inter-Departmental Exchange (IDX) scheme, some electives can come from other engineering departments. A handful of modules are flagged as not running in 2026/27, and the department warns that low-enrolment electives can be cancelled.

The course is accredited by the IET and meets the academic requirement for Chartered Engineer registration; graduates also receive the ACGI. A design-and-build group project runs through each of the first two years, a Year 3 industrial placement or industry-led consultancy project is built into the structure, and a professional competencies portfolio is built up over all four years and completed in Year 4. The final-year elective list is unusually wide (over 40 modules), electives can be taken from other departments through IDX, and final-year projects often sit inside research groups. A Year Abroad route offers partners including ETH Zurich, KTH, NUS and MIT.

imperial-efds.name: Economics, Finance and Data Science BSc
imperial-efds.applies: Module names from the 2026-entry course page (October 2026 start, UCAS L1N3); codes, credits and terms from the 2024-25 programme specification (the latest one found)
imperial-efds.rules: Each year is 60 ECTS (1 ECTS = 25 hours). Years 1 and 2 are entirely compulsory. In Year 3 students take the final project modules, Essential Skills 3, one I-Explore module (5 or 7.5 ECTS) chosen from another Imperial department, and five electives of 5 ECTS each (the 2026 course page says five; the 2024-25 specification said six), which can be focused on Economics, Finance or Data Science or mixed. Which electives run depends on staff availability, and some combinations may clash in the timetable. Students must pass all modules at each level (first attempt, resit or compensation) with a year average of at least 40% to progress. Degree classification is weighted 7.5% Year 1, 35% Year 2 and 57.5% Year 3 (First 70%, 2:1 60%, 2:2 50%, Third 40%).
imperial-efds.teaching: Imperial's Economics, Finance and Data Science BSc is run by Imperial College Business School and teaches through lectures, small-group tutorials and computing labs, with programming taught from the start. About 400 of the roughly 1,500 study hours each year are timetabled, around a quarter. Years 1 and 2 are fully compulsory across all three disciplines. Year 3 adds a final group project, an I-Explore module from another department and five electives. Most modules are weighted mainly towards unseen exams, with group and individual coursework alongside. The final degree is weighted 7.5%, 35% and 57.5% across the three years.

profile.body: Teaching combines lectures, tutorials and computing labs with group projects, independent learning and a virtual learning environment that holds recordings, slides and problem sets. The programme specification describes tutorials as small groups where you discuss and apply what you have learned, and mentions in-class polling, self-diagnostic quizzes, classroom games and flipped teaching. Each year is 60 ECTS, or about 1,500 hours of study, of which roughly 25% (about 400 hours) is scheduled teaching and 75% is independent study. Tutorial sizes are not published. The intake labelled 'Class of 2029' was 198 students, 55% of them women, from 32 nationalities. Teaching is based at South Kensington, and the Business School also lists White City as a campus.

Assessment mixes individual and group coursework with unseen exams. The specification says most modules are weighted mainly towards exams, while some are wholly or largely coursework. Coursework includes problem sets, project reports, and oral and poster presentations, and exams include in-class or online tests as well as final unseen papers. The Business School also mentions simulations and computing practicals. Imperial aims to return coursework feedback within two weeks and provisional exam marks 25 days after the exam period, confirmed by the Board of Examiners. To progress, you must pass every module at that level, at first attempt, at resit or by compensation, with a year average of at least 40%. Exam dates are not published on the course pages.

Years 1 and 2 are entirely compulsory. Year 1 covers mathematical foundations, probability and statistics, introductory data science, micro- and macroeconomics, data structures and algorithms, accounting, and Big Issues in Economics and Finance. Year 2 moves on to econometrics, machine learning, corporate finance and capital markets, operations research, and databases and cloud computing. Each of the first two years includes an Essential Skills module. Year 3 brings a two-part final group project (Questions and Methods, then Report), Essential Skills 3, an I-Explore module and electives. The final degree is weighted 7.5% Year 1, 35% Year 2 and 57.5% Year 3, with a First at 70%, a 2:1 at 60%, a 2:2 at 50% and a Third at 40%.

Choice comes only in Year 3. You take five electives, which you can concentrate in economics, finance or data science or mix across them. Examples include Industrial Organisation, Health Economics, Advanced Macroeconomics, Derivatives and Structured Products, Financial Engineering and Stochastic Calculus, Mergers, Acquisitions and Private Equity, and Advanced Machine Learning. Which electives run depends on staff availability, and Imperial warns that some combinations may be impossible because of timetable clashes. You also choose one I-Explore module (5 or 7.5 ECTS) from another Imperial department, which counts fully towards your degree.

The degree combines economics, finance and data science in a single Business School programme, drawing on all five of the School's departments. Machine learning and databases and cloud computing are compulsory, and coding starts in Year 1. A sequence of Essential Skills modules covers collaboration, creative problem solving, emotional intelligence and LEADS (leadership, ethics, awareness, diversity and societal impact). The final year is built around a group research project. The School holds EQUIS and AACSB accreditation, and the course page adds AMBA. Careers support includes one-to-one advice during the degree and for three years after graduation, plus employer fairs. No year abroad or placement year is described.

imperial-maths.name: Mathematics BSc
imperial-maths.applies: 2026-27 programme specification and department module guides (2026 entry); course page shown is for 2027 entry
imperial-maths.rules: Year 1: all eight modules (60 ECTS) are core or compulsory. Year 2: four core modules, one I-Explore module (Group A) and four 5-ECTS electives from Group B (60 or 62.5 ECTS). Year 3: 60-62.5 ECTS (eight 7.5-ECTS modules, or seven plus two 5-ECTS modules), with at least 52.5 ECTS from Group A (Level 6 maths), at most one Group C module (Horizons/BPES), and Group B Year 2 electives allowed if not already taken. Each module can only be taken once. No more than two modules per term may have 50%+ term-time assessment. Other-department or Level 7 modules need the Director of Undergraduate Studies' permission. Progression requires passing all 60 ECTS (resit or compensation allowed within limits) with a year average of at least 40%. Classification weights: Year 1 7.5%, Year 2 35%, Year 3 57.5%.
imperial-maths.teaching: The three-year BSc (G100) is taught through lectures (a 5 ECTS module typically has about 20), problems classes run by lecturers and graduate teaching assistants, and, in Year 1, weekly tutorials of about six students with a personal tutor plus a peer tutorial with an older student. Assessment is mostly by written exams held in May/June: exams are typically 70% of a lecture module in Year 1, 80% in Year 2 and 90% in Year 3, with the rest from coursework, tests and projects. The year runs over Autumn, Spring and Summer terms; there are short research projects in the Summer term of Years 1 (individual) and 2 (group), and an optional research project in Year 3. Imperial also runs a four-year MSci Mathematics (G103) that shares the same first two years, and students can move between the BSc and MSci on academic grounds; the BSc is a separate UCAS course rather than an exit route from the MSci.

profile.body: Teaching mixes lectures, problems classes, tutorials, computing labs, group work and a lot of self-study; Imperial expects support to be heaviest early on and to taper as you become independent. A standard 5 ECTS module has roughly 20 lectures, and core Year 1 and 2 modules are taken by the whole cohort, while Year 3 electives are often much smaller. In the Autumn and Spring of Year 1 you have a weekly tutorial in a group of five or six, usually led by your personal tutor, plus a small peer tutorial with a higher-year or MSc student; attendance is recorded. Most Year 1 and 2 modules also have problems classes with graduate teaching assistants, where you work through prepared problem sheets. Scheduled teaching is about 22% of your time in Year 1, 20% in Year 2 and 16% in Year 3.

Most modules combine in-term coursework or tests with a final written exam, and the exam share rises each year: typically 70% of a lecture module in Year 1, 80% in Year 2 and 90% in Year 3. Computational or data-heavy modules may have more coursework or be assessed entirely by project. Main exams are held in May/June, with resits in August/September; Year 1 also has in-term tests, including some in the first week of the Spring term. Projects are assessed through posters, oral presentations and group reports. The final classification weights the years 7.5% (Year 1), 35% (Year 2) and 57.5% (Year 3), with a First at 70% or above.

Year 1 is a common grounding in analysis, linear algebra, calculus, probability and computing, ending with a short individual research project in the Summer term. Year 2 continues core analysis, linear algebra/numerical analysis and differential equations, adds electives and a compulsory I-Explore module from outside maths, and ends with a group research project. Year 3 is entirely elective, with an optional research project. To progress you must pass all 60 ECTS of the year (by first attempt, resit or limited compensation) with a year average of at least 40%. The BSc and four-year MSci (G103) share Years 1-2, so you can switch on academic grounds using a degree change form before 31 March; MSci students need about 60% in Year 2 to continue.

In Year 2 you take one I-Explore module and choose four 5-ECTS electives from eight Group B modules (Groups and Rings, Lebesgue Measure and Integration, Probability for Statistics, Applied PDEs, Principles of Programming, Statistical Modelling, Classical Mechanics, and Network Science when it runs). Some of these are prerequisites for Year 3 modules, so it pays to plan ahead. In Year 3 you choose 60-62.5 ECTS, at least 52.5 ECTS of it from more than 60 Level 6 maths modules across applied maths, pure maths, statistics and finance, and you can add at most one Horizons or business (BPES) module. The list is indicative: some modules are not running in 2026-27, and low-uptake modules may be cancelled.

Imperial's maths degree front-loads research skills: every student does an individual research project at the end of Year 1 and a group research project at the end of Year 2, before an optional Year 3 project. Computing is built in from the start (Python and R in Year 1, LaTeX taught through the project), and the final-year menu is unusually broad, with options linked to department research such as Formalising Mathematics in the Lean proof assistant, mathematical finance and data science. The College-wide I-Explore module means you study something outside mathematics for credit. Year 1 counts for only 7.5% of the degree, so it works as a consolidation year.
