imperial-mech.name: Mechanical Engineering MEng
imperial-mech.applies: 2026-27 programme specification (2026 entry) and 2026/27 departmental module descriptors
imperial-mech.rules: Years 1 and 2: all modules core (60 ECTS each). Year 3: core PES3 (10) and DMT (20), a compulsory I-Explore module (Group F, 5), both modules of at least one of Groups A, B or C, and three further modules from Groups A-E, with no more than two from Group E (BPES). Year 4: core Individual Project (25), exactly one 10-ECTS Group A module, and five 5-ECTS modules from Groups B and C with at most two from C (IDX). A Level 7 'B' version cannot be taken if its Level 6 'A' version was taken. Up to 15 ECTS may be compensated across the whole programme (Engineering Council rule). Classification weights: Year 1 7.5%, Year 2 20%, Year 3 36.25%, Year 4 36.25%.
imperial-mech.teaching: This four-year integrated MEng is taught through lectures (many recorded, with demonstrations), tutorials in groups of about 16, team-based design learning, flipped laboratory classes and workshop practice. Years 1 and 2 are a fixed core, with about 20% of time scheduled; Years 3 and 4 shift to projects and electives, with a year-long Design, Make and Test team project in Year 3 and an Individual Project in Year 4. Assessment moves from about 75% exams in Years 1-2 to about 50-55% exams in Years 3-4, with the rest coursework and practicals; most core lecture modules are 95% end-of-year exam plus a 5% progress test. The year runs over Autumn, Spring and Summer terms. Imperial's programme code is H301, while H300 is the code of the BEng (Hons) exit award; applicants join the MEng and may later transfer to year-abroad, year-in-industry or nuclear engineering variants.

profile.body: Scheduled teaching includes lectures (many recorded, with live demonstrations), tutorials in groups of about 16, team-based learning for design work, lab experiments, practicals and guest lectures. Practical and lab modules use flipped learning: you prepare with online material, then apply it in small-group sessions. In Years 1 and 2 about 20% of your roughly 1,500 study hours a year (around 300 hours) is scheduled, with the rest independent study. In Years 3 and 4 scheduled time drops to about 60 hours, and the rest is split roughly evenly between independent study and project work. Design and Manufacture runs through Years 1 and 2 with CAD and departmental workshop practice, and the Professional Engineering Skills modules carry the lab programme and report writing.

On a typical pathway, assessment is about 75% exams, 20% coursework and 5% practical in Years 1 and 2, moving to about 55% exams in Year 3 and 50% in Year 4 as projects take over. Most core science modules (stress analysis, fluids, thermodynamics, materials, mechatronics) are 95% one 1.5-hour exam and 5% progress test, while Mathematics and Computing combines a 3-hour exam with programming coursework or tests. Design modules and the Year 3 DMT and Year 4 Individual Project are assessed entirely on reports, reviews, logbooks, presentations and exhibitions. Coursework feedback comes within two weeks. The degree weights the years 7.5%, 20%, 36.25% and 36.25%.

Years 1 and 2 are a fixed core in maths and computing, mechanics and dynamics, stress analysis, materials, fluids, thermodynamics, heat transfer, mechatronics, and design and manufacture. Year 3 combines a business-and-research Professional Engineering Skills module (including a Literature Research Project) with the year-long Design, Make and Test team project and electives. Year 4 centres on a 25-ECTS Individual Project, usually in an academic's research group. Everyone applies to the core MEng; you can later transfer to Mechanical Engineering with a Year Abroad, with a Year in Industry, with Nuclear Engineering, or combinations of these. A BEng (Hons) is available only as an exit award, and only 15 ECTS can be compensated across the whole degree.

Choice begins in Year 3. Alongside the core modules and a compulsory I-Explore module, you take both modules from at least one of three themed pairs (Stress Analysis 3A with Fracture Mechanics A; Thermodynamics 3A with Fluid Mechanics 3A; Mechatronics 3A with Machine Dynamics and Vibrations A), plus three more from Groups A-D or the business Group E (at most two business modules). In Year 4 you pick one 10-ECTS design-technology module (such as Aircraft Engine Technology or Future Clean Transport Technology) and five 5-ECTS electives, up to two of which can be interdepartmental exchange modules. Many Year 3 modules have a Level 7 'B' version for Year 4, but you cannot take both versions.

Design and making run through the whole degree: CAD and workshop manufacturing in Year 1, a group design-make-test project and a hackathon-style individual project in Year 2, and the 20-ECTS Design, Make and Test project in Year 3, where teams of about four build and test a product and show it at the DMT Exhibition. Some DMT projects are subtasks of team projects such as Imperial Racing Green. The degree is accredited by the IMechE towards Chartered Engineer status, graduates also receive the City and Guilds Associateship (ACGI), and electives include specialist nuclear, tribology, motorsport and robotics modules.

imperial-med.name: Medicine MBBS/BSc (A100)
imperial-med.applies: Programme specification for the 2026-27 entry cohort (dated September 2026); the live course page describes 2027 entry with the same module list; BSc Management pathway taken from the 2025-26 iBSc specification (2026-27 version not found)
imperial-med.rules: 370 ECTS in total: Year 1 60, Year 2 65, Year 3 60, Year 4 60, Year 5 65, Year 6 60 (1 ECTS = about 25 hours of study). Phases 1 and 3 are all core apart from the compulsory I-Explore module in Year 2; every module must be passed and I-Explore must be attended and completed. In Year 4 students are allocated (by preference) to one BSc pathway. For the 14 Medical Sciences specialisms this means one Group A 'Topics' module (Autumn, 25 ECTS), one Group B 'Group and Independent Analyses' module (Spring, 10 ECTS) and one Group C 'Research Project' (Summer, 25 ECTS) in the same specialism; the Humanities, Philosophy and Law Group B and C modules require the HPL Topics module. The Biomedical Engineering pathway (iBSc A144) is 40 ECTS of compulsory/core modules plus four 5-ECTS electives with no more than one from Group B; the Management pathway (iBSc A127) is ten compulsory modules. A minimum 40% in each Year 4 module is needed; the BSc is classified on Year 4 alone (First 70%, 2:1 60%, 2:2 50%, Third 40%). The MBBS is unclassified; the PSA must be passed in Year 6 and the AKT may be attempted at most four times; maximum registration is eight years.
imperial-med.teaching: Imperial's six-year MBBS/BSc is split into Phase 1 (Years 1-3, called Phase 1a, 1b and 1c), Phase 2 (the compulsory Year 4 BSc) and Phase 3 (Years 5-6, Phase 3a and 3b). Phase 1 uses a flipped-classroom model (online preparation before interactive sessions) with large- and small-group teaching, team-based learning, scientific and clinical practicals, case-based learning and simulation, with patient contact from the first term and extended hospital and GP placements in Year 3 (three 8-week placements, each followed by campus teaching). Phase 2 is a research-focused year of a 12-week taught block, a self-directed group block and a 14-week supervised research project, assessed entirely by coursework such as reviews, presentations, data tasks and a project report. Phase 3 is placement-based across hospital and community specialties with structured teaching, a specialty choice placement, a Pre-Foundation Assistantship and an elective. Assessment is programmatic: written papers (SBA, VSAQ, SAQ), spot tests, workplace-based assessments, a Clinical Practical Assessment in Year 2 and an OSCE in Year 3, then PACES, the national MLA Applied Knowledge Test and Clinical and Professional Skills Assessment, and the Prescribing Safety Assessment in Phase 3. Years 1, 2 and 4 follow Autumn, Spring and Summer terms (in 2026-27 Years 1-2 run 26 Sep-11 Dec, 2 Jan-19 Mar and 24 Apr-25 Jun), while Years 3, 5 and 6 have no term dates and run continuously.

profile.body: Phase 1 runs on a flipped-classroom model: you prepare online, then come in for interactive large- and small-group sessions, team-based and case-based learning, lab and clinical skills classes and simulation. A Year 1 intake of roughly 360 is split into four cohorts of about 90 and small groups of five or six, with communication skills practised in twos and threes. The Lifestyle Medicine and Prevention strand delivers over 90% of its lecture content online and consolidates it in clinician-led tutorials of 12-30 students. Teaching uses South Kensington and Charing Cross, where there is an anatomy dissecting room. Year 4 is research training inside your BSc pathway, and Phase 3 is placement-based learning in hospitals and the community, backed by structured teaching and simulation, with some out-of-hours work expected.

You meet patients from the first term. Year 1 has eight GP days in a London practice (October to March), with patient conversations, clinics and a community survey project, plus a summer hospital placement. Year 2 adds five GP days on history-taking and health coaching. Year 3 is three roughly 8-week placements: hospital Medicine and Surgery, and the Medicine in the Community Apprenticeship, where you run your own parallel GP clinics and a Community Action Project; each is followed by about two weeks on campus. Year 5 includes a 7-week core paediatrics rotation, a 3-week GP placement and a 3-week Specialty Choice Placement. Year 6 has a 4-week GP Senior Assistantship outside London, specialty attachments across Imperial's hospital campuses, a Pre-Foundation Assistantship and an elective.

Imperial uses programmatic assessment, building a picture from many data points rather than a single exam. In Years 1-2 that means in-class single best answer and very short answer papers, spot tests, self-marked short answer questions, group work such as CSI case assessments and the LMAP podcast, workplace-based assessments from Year 1, and a Clinical Practical Assessment in Year 2. Year 3 ends in a summative OSCE. The BSc year is all coursework (review articles, abstracts, presentations, posters and a research report) and alone decides your BSc class. Phase 3 combines placement WBAs, written knowledge tests, PACES, both parts of the UK Medical Licensing Assessment (AKT and CPSA) and the Prescribing Safety Assessment. The MBBS is pass/fail; most assessments allow two attempts and the AKT up to four.

The six years fall into three phases. Phase 1 (Years 1-3, called 1a, 1b and 1c) builds science, clinical skills and professionalism through systems-based teaching, then moves into extended placements in Year 3. Phase 2 (Year 4) is a compulsory intercalated BSc, so every student graduates with an MBBS and a BSc; the programme specification also allows intercalating at another UK university. Phase 3 (Years 5-6, called 3a and 3b) is clinical, following patient care from birth to end of life and finishing with preparation for Foundation posts. You must pass every module to progress; maximum registration is eight years. Students who leave may be able to transfer to a BSc in Medical Sciences, and the course page says exceptional students can add a PhD.

Phases 1 and 3 are almost entirely core. Your first real choice is the Year 2 I-Explore module (5 ECTS), picked from a college-wide catalogue outside medicine; Year 1 LMAP groups also choose one lifestyle theme for their podcast, and Year 2 Clinical Research and Innovation lets you pick a research experience. For the Year 4 BSc you rank 16 pathways and are allocated by preference; on the Medical Sciences pathways you then take a Topics module, a Group and Independent Analyses module and a Research Project in that one specialism, while Biomedical Engineering adds four electives and Management is fixed. In Year 5 you pick a Specialty Choice Placement, and in Year 6 you organise your own elective. Non-credit Imperial Horizons modules are optional in Years 1 and 4.

Every student takes a research-focused BSc, and the 16 pathways include unusual options such as Remote Medicine (with an Extreme Environments Lab for cold and hypoxia work), Surgical Design, Technology and Innovation, Biomedical Engineering alongside bioengineering students, Management with the Business School, and Humanities, Philosophy and Law. Lifestyle medicine and prevention is a core two-year strand, including an optional study in which students track their own activity data and later analyse it. GP contact begins in Year 1, and Year 3 students run their own supervised GP clinics. Graduates also receive the Associateship of the Imperial College School of Medicine (AICSM), and the faculty reports ranking first in the UK for assessment and feedback in the 2026 National Student Survey.

lse-econ.name: BSc in Economics
lse-econ.applies: Programme regulations for students starting in 2026/27 (LSE Calendar 2026-27) and 2026/27 course guides
lse-econ.rules: Year 1: LSE100 (0.5, choose A/B/C); Paper 1 EC1P1 + EC1A1; Paper 2 ST109 + EC1C1; Paper 3 either MA108 + EC1B1 or MA100; Paper 4: if MA108 taken, 1.0 unit from the Year 1 Outside Options List; if MA100 taken, EC1B1 plus a 0.5-unit Autumn Term course from that list. Year 2: EC2A1, EC2B1, EC2C1 compulsory; Paper 8: 1.0 unit from FM214, FM215, EH238 (suspended) or the Years 2 & 3 Outside Options List. Year 3: Papers 9–10: 2.0 units from the Economics Selection List; Paper 11: 1.0 unit from the Economics Selection List or the Additional Section List; Paper 12: 1.0 unit from the listed AC/EH/GY/IR/MA courses, the Economics Selection List, the Additional Section List or (exceptionally, with Departmental Tutor approval) an outside course. Some combinations are mutually exclusive; some first-year courses cannot be taken in later years. Credits are LSE units (1.0 full, 0.5 half).
lse-econ.teaching: BSc Economics is taught through lectures by academic staff and weekly classes of around 20, mostly led by graduate teaching assistants, where problem sets are worked through; first-year quantitative courses add online Q&A sessions and support labs. LSE's programme page suggests about 12 hours of lectures and classes a week and roughly six hours of independent study per course. Assessment is mostly exams in the Spring (May-June) and sometimes January exam periods, with a growing share of continuous assessment: first-year economics courses are 85% exam and 15% coursework, and second-year micro and macro are 70/30. The degree class combines Years 2 and 3 with a First Year Average, and there is no compulsory dissertation.

profile.body: Lectures are given by academic staff, often to large audiences on core courses, and are paired with weekly classes where you go through problem sets. Classes are usually led by graduate teaching assistants (many of them PhD students) and LSE puts them at around 20 students; in 2025/26 EC1A1 Microeconomics I averaged 18 per class and EC2A1 Microeconomics II averaged 20. Core courses add support labs and online discussion forums, and EC1A1 runs online interactive Q&A sessions. Each student has an academic mentor, seen at least once a term, and staff hold office hours. Teaching runs 9am-6pm on weekdays, normally with no undergraduate teaching after noon on Wednesdays.

Exams carry most of the weight. They fall mainly in the Spring exam period (May-June), with some in January. First-year economics courses are typically 85% exam and 15% continuous assessment: EC1A1, for example, is a two-hour exam plus coursework. In Year 2, Microeconomics II and Macroeconomics II are 70% exam (three hours) and 30% continuous assessment, and Econometrics II includes an individual empirical project. Every course also sets unmarked formative work such as problem sets, mock exams and, in EC1A1, a short video presentation on a policy theme, with feedback normally within two weeks. LSE says the current curriculum is designed to widen assessment to include policy briefs and empirical projects.

Your degree class rests on 18 marks under LSE's three-year BA/BSc scheme: the eight Year 2 and Year 3 papers (full units counted twice) make 16, and a First Year Average, taken from your best six of nine first-year marks and counted twice, makes the other two. LSE100 can feed that average if it is among your best six. A First needs ten first-class marks, or eight or nine plus an aggregate of 1180. To move into Year 2 you must pass at least three of the four first-year units, and into Year 3 at least seven of eight. First-year papers allow three attempts and later papers two; a passed resit is capped at 40. Year 1 builds the toolkit (economic reasoning, micro, macro, maths, statistics and econometrics), Year 2 deepens the three cores, and Year 3 is almost entirely options.

Year 1 has a choice of maths route: MA108 with Macroeconomics I and a full outside unit, or the full-unit MA100 with Macroeconomics I and a half-unit Autumn Term outside course. In Year 2, alongside the three cores, you pick one unit from Principles of Finance (FM214, FM215) or the School's outside options list. Year 3 gives you two units from the Economics Selection List, a third from that list or an additional section list, and a fourth from selected accounting, economic history, geography, IR and maths courses or, exceptionally, another department with Departmental Tutor approval. Some first-year courses are closed to later years and some combinations are mutually exclusive.

LSE's programme page describes roughly 12 hours a week of lectures and classes, with about six hours of independent study recommended per course on top. A core course usually means two lectures and one class a week, and you are expected to have attempted that week's problem set and reading before the class. Teaching sits between 9am and 6pm on weekdays, and undergraduate teaching is not normally timetabled after noon on Wednesdays. Week 6 of each teaching term is a reading week with no lectures or classes.

BSc Economics students take core courses designed specifically for them (EC1A1, EC2A1 and so on) rather than the versions taught to joint-honours students, within a curriculum built around maths, econometrics and policy relevance. All first-years also take LSE100, a half-unit interdisciplinary course: in LSE100B students meet in 90-minute seminars in alternate weeks (average class 25) and are assessed 50% on a 1,000-word critical evaluation and 50% on a group project. The department's open-day material describes a route to transfer to BSc Econometrics and Mathematical Economics at the end of Year 2, which involves a quantitative thesis. The 2025-entry programme page says students can apply for a year abroad with an LSE exchange partner.

lse-ir.name: BSc International Relations
lse-ir.applies: Students starting in 2026/27 (LSE Calendar 2026/27 programme regulations, 2026 entry cohort; course guides for 2026/27). The public prospectus page now advertises 2027 entry.
lse-ir.rules: 12 units over three years plus LSE100 (0.5 unit, choose one of LSE100A/B/C). Year 1: IR100 and IR101 compulsory; Paper 3 = HY113 or HY116; Paper 4 = 1 unit of an approved outside course (strongly recommended: EH101, GV101, HY113, HY116, PH103, SO100), a course from the Undergraduate Outside Options List (Year 1), or an approved language course; IR102 unassessed skills course. Year 2: Papers 5-7 = 3 units from IR200, IR202, IR203, IR205, IR206; Paper 8 = a further course from that list, an approved outside course (recommended GV264, HY206, HY235, LL279, LL280) or an approved 1-unit language course. Year 3: Papers 9-11 = 3 units from the IR options list (including IR398 Dissertation); Paper 12 = 1 unit from IR200-IR206 not already taken, LL342, the Selection List of Papers Approved by the Department, the Papers 9-11 options, or an approved intermediate/advanced/proficiency language course. HY118, MG104, MG105, SO100 and SO110 can be taken in Year 1 only. Passing a language course every year in one language at rising levels earns an optional language specialism on the certificate, e.g. 'BSc in International Relations (with French)'. Places on some options are limited.
lse-ir.teaching: In Years 1 and 2 each course pairs lectures, which give a broad overview, with smaller classes usually led by graduate teaching assistants; Year 3 is made up of specialist options. LSE quotes about 10 hours of formal teaching a week (not counting LSE100) and around eight hours of guided independent study. Assessment varies by course, typically combining an exam in the January or Spring exam period with essays or participation marks, and third-years can write a 10,000-word dissertation (IR398). The degree class combines Years 2 and 3 with a First Year Average, and passing a language course in the same language every year earns a language specialism in the degree title.

profile.body: In Years 1 and 2, lectures set out the big picture and smaller classes, usually run by graduate teaching assistants, work through the material in more depth. IR100 had an average class size of 13 in 2025/26 and IR200 about 17. Year 3 moves to specialised options, many of them seminar-based half units. LSE puts formal teaching at around 10 hours a week, excluding LSE100. First-years also take IR102 Thinking Globally, a non-credit skills course, and every student meets an academic mentor regularly.

Each course sets its own assessment, but most combine an exam with coursework or participation. IR100 is a three-hour e-exam worth 80% and a 1,500-word essay due in January worth 20%, preceded by a formative essay and a mock exam under exam conditions. IR200 is 80% e-exam and 20% class participation, with two formative essays and a class presentation. Exams fall in the January or Spring exam periods, and the Spring Term is largely revision and exams. Options can also use policy memos and presentations, and the IR398 dissertation is marked entirely on the written piece.

Your degree class rests on 18 marks under LSE's three-year BA/BSc scheme: the eight Year 2 and Year 3 papers (full units counted twice) make 16, and a First Year Average, taken from your best six of nine first-year marks and counted twice, makes the other two. LSE100 can feed that average if it is among your best six. A First needs ten first-class marks, or eight or nine plus an aggregate of 1180. To move into Year 2 you must pass at least three of the four first-year units, and into Year 3 at least seven of eight. First-year papers allow three attempts and later papers two; a passed resit is capped at 40. Year 1 introduces IR theory and contemporary issues alongside international history, Year 2 is built from the department's core courses, and Year 3 is specialist options.

Year 1 has IR100 and IR101 compulsory, one of two international history courses (HY113 or HY116) and one outside option; the department recommends courses such as GV101, EH101, PH103 or SO100, or a language. Year 2 takes three of the five IR core courses (IR200, IR202, IR203, IR205, IR206) plus a fourth core course, an approved outside course or a language. Year 3 is three units from the IR options list, which includes the IR398 dissertation, and a fourth from IR or approved outside courses or languages. IR398 (up to 10,000 words) needs a supervisor confirmed before it starts and offers up to six short supervisor meetings. Some options are capped.

LSE describes about 10 hours of formal teaching a week, not counting LSE100, made up of lectures and classes in Years 1 and 2. It recommends around eight hours of guided independent study a week alongside this. The teaching day runs from 9am to 6pm on weekdays, with undergraduate teaching not normally scheduled after noon on Wednesdays, and Week 6 of each term is a reading week.

LSE's Department of International Relations dates from 1927, is one of the largest of its kind, and helped found the student-run journal Millennium. The degree offers an optional language specialism: pass a language course in every year, in French, Spanish, German, Mandarin or Russian at rising levels, and the language is added to the degree title, for example 'with French'. The programme leans on international history in Year 1 and lets you draw on law, government and history courses later. All first-years also take LSE100, an interdisciplinary half unit taught in 90-minute seminars in alternate weeks.

lse-law.name: LLB in Laws (Bachelor of Laws)
lse-law.applies: Programme regulations for students starting in 2026/27 (LSE Calendar 2026-27) and 2026/27 course guides
lse-law.rules: Year 1: four compulsory full-unit papers (LL142, LL143, LL106, LL108) plus non-credit LL141 and LL100. Year 2: LL276 Property (1.0); 0.5 unit from List A and 0.5 unit from List B; 2.0 units from Lists A, B, C or the Undergraduate Outside Options List. Year 3: 4.0 units from Lists A, B, C, D or the Outside Options List (courses not already taken). No more than 1.0 unit from the Outside Options List across Years 2 and 3. LL399 is Year 3 only and cannot be combined with LL398. Places on some options are capped and subject to timetabling and prerequisites; some combinations are mutually exclusive. Credits are LSE course units (1.0 = full unit, 0.5 = half unit). The Undergraduate Outside Options List (hundreds of courses from other departments) is not enumerated here.
lse-law.teaching: The LLB is taught mainly through lectures and small classes, with some options run as seminars that open with a short lecture and move into discussion; LSE quotes 12-15 hours of formal teaching a week. Year 1 opens with two non-credit intensive courses (Introduction to Legal Systems and Legal Studies Skills) before four full-unit core subjects run through the Autumn and Winter Terms. Nearly every law course is assessed by a single unseen exam in the Spring exam period, with formative essays during the year that do not count. Under the Law School's own classification scheme, Year 1 must be passed but only Year 2 and Year 3 marks decide the degree class. Third-years can choose a half-unit or full-unit dissertation.

profile.body: Most courses pair lectures with small classes, and some options are seminars that begin with a short lecture and turn into group discussion. LSE's programme page puts formal teaching at 12-15 hours a week. As an example of scale, the first-year course LL142 had 212 students in 2025/26 but an average class of 14, with 16 hours of lectures and 9 of classes in the Autumn Term and 20 and 10 in the Winter Term. Every student has an academic mentor they meet regularly, academic staff offer one-to-one advice and feedback sessions, and a first-year programme supports legal writing. Teaching runs in the Autumn and Winter Terms, each with a reading week in Week 6.

Assessment is overwhelmingly exam-based. Almost every law course is decided by one unseen exam in the Spring exam period: about 150 minutes for half units and 180-210 minutes for full units (LL142, for instance, is a 180-minute exam with 15 minutes' reading time, worth 100%). During the year you write formative essays, LL142 sets one in each teaching term, which earn feedback but no marks. The main exception is the optional third-year dissertation, which is marked entirely on the written piece.

The LLB uses its own classification scheme for students starting from 2024/25. Year 1 does not count towards the class, but you must pass all four first-year courses; failing one unit lets you progress while resitting it, and failing two or more units, or scoring below 30 in one, means failing the year. The class then rests on 16 marks from Years 2 and 3 (full units counted twice). A First needs eight first-class marks, or six plus an aggregate close to 1080. Year 2 progression allows limited compensation for near-miss fails, and a passed resit is capped at 40. A first-class mark from a non-law course is capped at 73 in the aggregate.

Year 1 is fixed. In Year 2 you take Property (LL276) plus half a unit each from Lists A and B, and two more units from Lists A, B, C or the School's outside options. Year 3 is four units of free choice from Lists A-D or outside options, with no more than one unit from outside the Law School across Years 2 and 3. Some options are capped and depend on timetabling and prerequisites. Dissertations are a third-year option: LL398 (half unit, 6,000-8,000 words) or LL399 (full unit, 12,000-15,000 words), each needing a full-time Law School supervisor, your mentor's approval and generally upper-second-level marks. Both run on three workshops and four supervisor meetings that you arrange yourself.

LSE describes a teaching week of 12-15 hours of formal teaching, made up of lectures and small classes (with seminars on some options), across the Autumn and Winter Terms. Around this you are expected to do substantial reading and research on your own; the Learning Lab runs workshops on research, essay writing and managing workload. Weeks start differently in Year 1, which opens with intensive non-credit courses on the legal system and legal study skills before the four core subjects begin.

LSE teaches law from a social science angle, looking at how law affects society, politics, economics and business, and the School points to its role in pioneering fields such as banking, tax, company and labour law. The programme page says the degree covers the knowledge and skills needed to go on to the first stage of the Solicitors Qualifying Exam, and graduates are normally eligible to be considered for Bar training. Like all LSE undergraduates, law students take the half-unit LSE100, though under the LLB scheme its mark does not count. Mooting, the Law Society and Inns of Court events are extracurricular, and the campus is close to London's legal district.

lse-maths-econ.name: BSc Mathematics and Economics
lse-maths-econ.applies: Programme regulations for students starting in 2026/27 (LSE Calendar 2026/27, programme code UBMAEC); course guides 2026/27; prospectus page is for 2027 entry
lse-maths-econ.rules: 12 papers worth 1.0 unit each (half-unit courses pair up) plus LSE100 (0.5 unit) in Year 1. Year 1 is fully prescribed. Year 2: Paper 7 is either FM214+FM215 or EC2C3, plus one of EC2C4/MA208/MA209/MA210/MA211/MA213/MA214; Paper 8 is MA203 plus one of MA208-MA211. Year 3: Paper 9 = 1.0 unit of third-year economics; Paper 10 = two maths half units (the first may be a second-year MA208-MA214 course, the second must be a third-year MA course); Paper 11 = EC2C3 plus a half unit if FM214/215 was taken in Year 2, otherwise one of FM214, FM215, FM321, FM322, ST206, ST216, ST313, any Paper 9 course, or another MA3/EC3 course with Departmental Tutor approval; Paper 12 = 1.0 unit from MA318 and the Paper 9-11 and Undergraduate Outside Options lists. Places on some options are limited and some courses are mutually exclusive. Classified under the School's Three-year Classification Scheme for BA/BSc degrees.
lse-maths-econ.teaching: Each course typically has two lectures and one class a week, so a normal week means about eight lectures and four classes across four courses; classes have roughly 15 students and go through exercises prepared in advance, and computer workshops use Python. Lectures are given by academic staff, with classes taken by teaching fellows and graduate teaching assistants. The year runs across the Autumn and Winter Terms (teaching weeks with a reading week in Week 6) and a Spring Term used mainly for revision and exams. Most core courses are assessed by a final written exam in the January or Spring exam period, often with about 10% continuous assessment. Students refer to Year 1, 2 and 3, and the degree is made up of 12 papers plus LSE100.

profile.body: LSE describes a typical week as two lectures and one class for each course, which adds up to around eight lectures and four classes across four courses. Classes have about 15 students and are built around problem sets you prepare beforehand, then discuss together. Every course includes classes, seminars or computer workshops, and the workshops do practical data work, mainly in Python. Teaching comes from faculty, visiting staff, LSE teaching fellows and graduate teaching assistants, some of them PhD students. Core courses publish their contact time: MA100 has 30 lecture hours and 10 class hours in each of the Autumn and Winter Terms, and ST102 adds computer workshops to its weekly lectures and classes. Every student has an academic mentor, and the Learning Lab runs study-skills sessions.

Most courses end in an unseen written exam in either the January exam period (for Autumn Term courses) or the Spring exam period. First- and second-year economics courses such as EC1A3, EC1B3, EC2A3 and EC2B3 are 90% exam and 10% continuous assessment. MA102 and MA104 use the same 90/10 split. MA100 is split between a one-hour January exam (25%) and a three-hour Spring exam (75%). ST102 has two two-hour exams worth 50% each, one in January and one in Spring. Formative problem sets are set every week but don't count towards marks. The degree is classified under LSE's Three-year Classification Scheme for BA/BSc degrees, and LSE100 counts towards the First Year Average. Third-year options can include projects or a dissertation (MA334).

This is a three-year degree of 12 papers plus LSE100, with time split equally between mathematics and economics. Year 1 is completely fixed: micro and macroeconomics, Mathematical Methods, Elementary Statistical Theory, and the proof-based pair MA102 and MA104, plus your LSE100 theme. Year 2 continues the core with intermediate micro and macro, further calculus and linear algebra, and Real Analysis. You then choose between finance (FM214/FM215) and econometrics (EC2C3), plus a second-year maths half unit. Year 3 is mostly options: a unit of advanced economics, two maths half units (at least one at third-year level), and two further papers. No economics background is needed to start.

Choice opens up in Year 2. Under Paper 7 you take either Principles of Finance I and II, or Econometrics I, together with a half unit such as Econometrics II, Optimisation Theory, Differential Equations, Discrete Mathematics, Algebra and Number Theory, Operations Research Techniques or Algorithms and Data Structures. Paper 8 pairs Real Analysis with one of MA208-MA211. In Year 3, Paper 9 is a full unit of third-year economics from about a dozen options (EC337 is suspended in 2026/27). Paper 10 is third-year maths, including game theory, complex analysis, PDEs, measure-theoretic probability, financial mathematics, machine-learning optimisation and a dissertation. Papers 11 and 12 can go to finance, statistics, more economics or maths, or outside options with approval. Some options have limited places or prerequisites.

The degree is run by the Department of Mathematics and taught jointly with LSE's Department of Economics. LSE pitches it at mathematically or scientifically minded students and says no previous economics study is needed. The maths has a distinctly LSE flavour: discrete mathematics, game theory, operations research, algorithms and optimisation all sit next to analysis and algebra, and third-year options include the mathematics of networks, cryptocurrencies and the blockchain, and optimisation for machine learning. Every student also takes LSE100, the School's interdisciplinary course on a big question (climate, AI or fairness). LSE says recent graduates have gone into corporate finance, accountancy, management and banking, and many go on to postgraduate study in maths or economics.

m.d: A full-year introduction to probability and statistical inference that assumes no previous statistics, taught through lectures, classes and computer workshops. Two two-hour exams (January and Spring) are worth 50% each.
An introduction to rigorous mathematical reasoning and proof, leading into the basics of real analysis. Assessed by a Spring exam (90%) and weekly continuous assessment (10%).

w: Greatest common divisor, Euclid's algorithm and Bézout

m.d: Intermediate microeconomics moving from demand and supply to general equilibrium, welfare and market failure. January exam (90%) plus continuous assessment (10%).
Intermediate macroeconomics on money, inflation, business cycles and stabilisation policy, including open-economy issues. Spring exam (90%) plus continuous assessment (10%).
w: International trade in goods and assets

m.d: Second-year calculus going beyond first-year methods into rigorous integration theory and transforms. Assessed entirely by a 90-minute January exam.

lse-maths-stats.name: BSc Mathematics, Statistics and Business
lse-maths-stats.applies: Programme regulations for students starting in 2026/27 (LSE Calendar 2026/27, programme code UBMSB); course guides 2026/27; prospectus page is for 2027 entry
lse-maths-stats.rules: 12 papers of 1.0 unit each plus LSE100 (0.5) in Year 1. Year 1: ST102, MA100, EC1A3 compulsory; Paper 3 adds EC1B3 or FM101; Paper 4 is 1.0 unit from AC102, AC103, EC1B3, FM101, MA102, MA104, ST101A/W, ST111. Year 2: MA221+MA222 and ST206+ST211 compulsory; Paper 7 is 1.0 unit from List 1 (if MA102 was taken in Year 1) or List 2 (if not, which includes MA102/MA104); Paper 8 is 1.0 unit from AC205, AC206, EC2A3, EC2B3, EC2C3, EC2C4, FM214, FM215. Year 3: Paper 9 from the Paper 9 options list; Paper 10 from the Paper 10 or 9 lists; Paper 11 from the Paper 9, 10 or 11 lists; Paper 12 from those lists or the Undergraduate Outside Options List. The degree page describes three pathways from Year 2: Applied Statistics, Financial Statistics (with economics, finance and accounting), and Mathematics and Research. Places on some options are limited. Classified under the School's Three-year Classification Scheme.
lse-maths-stats.teaching: Students attend lectures plus related classes, seminars or workshops, totalling around 10-15 contact hours a week, and are expected to do at least 25-30 hours of independent study. Lectures are given by academic staff, while classes are led by PhD students and academics; each student has an academic mentor. Teaching happens in the Autumn and Winter Terms (with a reading week in Week 6), and the Spring Term is used mainly for revision and exams. Assessment is mostly by written exams in the January and Spring exam periods, with projects in some third-year statistics courses (for example an applied statistics project). The degree has 12 papers over Years 1-3 plus LSE100, and from Year 2 students follow one of three pathways.

profile.body: LSE says students on this degree have lectures plus related classes, seminars or workshops adding up to about 10-15 hours a week, with at least 25-30 hours of independent study on top, so roughly 40 hours in total. Academic staff give the lectures, and classes are led by PhD students and academics. The standard teaching day runs 9am-6pm, Monday to Friday. Course guides show the pattern: ST102 has 20 lecture hours, 15 class hours and about 10 computer-workshop hours in each of the Autumn and Winter Terms, and MA100 has 30 lecture hours and 10 class hours per term. Every student has an academic mentor, and the Learning Lab offers workshops and one-to-one sessions.

Most courses are examined in the January exam period (Autumn Term courses) or the Spring exam period. In Year 1, ST102 has two two-hour exams worth 50% each, and MA100 is split 25% January and 75% Spring. Economics half units are typically 90% exam and 10% continuous assessment. Some third-year statistics courses use more coursework: ST308 Bayesian Inference is 80% exam and 20% project, ST301 Actuarial Mathematics (Life) is 70/30, ST330 includes a 10% project, and ST312 Applied Statistics Project is assessed by a project (90%) and a presentation (10%). The degree is classified under LSE's Three-year Classification Scheme for BA/BSc degrees.

Three years of 12 papers plus LSE100. Year 1 gives a shared base in statistics (ST102), maths (MA100) and microeconomics, plus a choice between macroeconomics and finance and a unit of options from accounting, finance, proof-based maths, programming for data science and business analytics. Year 2 makes further calculus, linear algebra, probability and applied regression compulsory, and leaves two papers of options in maths/statistics and in accounting/economics/finance. LSE describes three pathways that begin in Year 2: Applied Statistics, Financial Statistics (including economics, finance and accounting), and Mathematics and Research. Year 3 is entirely option-based. LSE also mentions placement opportunities and notes that many students do internships in actuarial and financial firms.

Choices start in Year 1, with EC1B3 or FM101 under Paper 3 and a full unit under Paper 4 from accounting, finance, macroeconomics, MA102/MA104, programming for data science or business analytics. Your Paper 4 choice shapes Year 2. If you took MA102, Paper 7 draws on List 1, which includes Real Analysis and Differential Equations. If you didn't, you take List 2, which brings in MA102 and MA104. Both lists include discrete maths, operations research, algorithms, surveys and experiments, databases, statistical inference, financial maths and survival models. Paper 8 offers accounting, intermediate micro/macro, econometrics and principles of finance. In Year 3, Papers 9-11 come from department options lists, and Paper 12 can also use LSE's outside options. Some courses have limited places or prerequisites.

The degree is run by LSE's long-established Department of Statistics, whose research, submitted jointly with Mathematics to REF 2021, was rated world-leading or internationally excellent. Its stand-out feature is how flexible it is, with three pathways from Year 2 that lean towards applied statistics, financial statistics or maths and research. It also has strong actuarial links: LSE says several courses give exemptions from Institute of Actuaries professional exams, and third-year options such as Actuarial Mathematics (Life), Stochastic Processes and Stochastic and Actuarial Methods in Finance reflect this. LSE emphasises practical projects. Graduates mostly go into financial and professional services, insurance, data and information roles, and accounting and auditing.

lse-pe.name: BSc in Politics and Economics
lse-pe.applies: Programme regulations for students starting in 2026/27 (LSE Calendar 2026-27) and 2026/27 course guides
lse-pe.rules: Year 1: LSE100 (0.5, choose A/B/C); GV100; GV101; EC1A3 + EC1B3; MA107 + ST107. Year 2: Papers 5–6: one unit each from Government List A; Papers 7–8: EC2A3, EC2B3, EC2C3, EC2C4 (all compulsory). Year 3: Paper 9: 1 unit from Government List B; Paper 10: 1 unit from the Economics List; Paper 11: 1 unit from Government List A, Government List B, the Economics List or the Undergraduate Outside Options List; Paper 12: GV390 Government Dissertation Option or 1 unit from the Economics List, Government List B or the Outside Options List. Outside options need tutor approval and prerequisites; some combinations are mutually exclusive; GV346 cannot follow GV267. Credits are LSE units (1.0 full, 0.5 half).
lse-pe.teaching: Run by the Department of Government, the degree splits its time equally between politics and economics. LSE describes four one-hour lectures and four hours of classes a week in the Autumn and Winter Terms, with classes capped at 15 and led by teaching fellows, plus around 30 hours of independent study. Government courses usually mix exams with essays and quizzes (GV100 is half exam, half essay), while economics and quantitative courses rely mainly on exams in January or the Spring exam period with some continuous assessment. Third-years can write a 10,000-word Government dissertation (GV390), and the degree class combines Years 2 and 3 with a First Year Average.

profile.body: Each course has weekly lectures, given by full-time staff, and classes led by teaching fellows (recent doctoral graduates or PhD students). LSE says classes have at most 15 students and focus on presenting and critiquing arguments; in 2025/26 GV100 averaged 13 per class and GV101 averaged 15. The programme page describes four one-hour lectures and four hours of classes a week in the Autumn and Winter Terms, varying by course, and estimates about four hours of independent study per contact hour. You meet an academic mentor regularly, and the Learning Lab offers workshops and one-to-one help with essays and research.

The two halves of the degree are assessed differently. Government courses usually combine exams with coursework: GV100 Introduction to Political Theory is a 90-minute exam (50%) and a 2,000-word essay (50%), and GV101 Introduction to Political Science is a two-hour exam (40%), a 1,500-word essay (40%) and a multiple-choice quiz (20%). Economics and quantitative courses are mainly exams, in January or the Spring exam period, with a small share of continuous assessment. Formative work such as weekly quizzes, problem sets and practice essays gives feedback without counting. Most options are seminar-taught and assessed by a mix of exam and coursework.

Your degree class rests on 18 marks under LSE's three-year BA/BSc scheme: the eight Year 2 and Year 3 papers (full units counted twice) make 16, and a First Year Average, taken from your best six of nine first-year marks and counted twice, makes the other two. LSE100 can feed that average if it is among your best six. A First needs ten first-class marks, or eight or nine plus an aggregate of 1180. To move into Year 2 you must pass at least three of the four first-year units, and into Year 3 at least seven of eight. First-year papers allow three attempts and later papers two; a passed resit is capped at 40. Year 1 is almost entirely compulsory, Year 2 adds intermediate economics and two Government options, and Year 3 is mostly choice.

Year 1 is fixed: GV100, GV101, Microeconomics I and Macroeconomics I, maths and statistics half units, and LSE100. In Year 2 you choose two units from Government List A and take four compulsory economics half units (EC2A3, EC2B3, EC2C3, EC2C4). Year 3 requires one unit from Government List B and one from the Economics List, a free paper from either side or the School's outside options, and a final paper that can be the GV390 dissertation. GV390 (10,000 words, due Spring Term Week 3) runs in empirical and political theory streams; you need a Government supervisor and an approval form in by Week 2 of the Autumn Term. Outside options need approval, and some options are capped.

In the Autumn and Winter Terms LSE describes four one-hour lectures and four hours of small-group classes a week, though the mix varies by course. On top of that it expects around 30 hours of independent study, roughly four hours for every contact hour. The standard teaching day runs from 9am to 6pm on weekdays, and undergraduate teaching is not normally scheduled after noon on Wednesdays. Week 6 of each term is a reading week.

The degree gives equal weight to political theory, comparative politics and political science on one side and micro, macro and quantitative methods on the other, and is based in a Government department of about 850 students and more than 40 faculty, a short walk from Westminster. The dissertation is optional rather than required, so you can finish on taught options if you prefer. All first-years take LSE100, an interdisciplinary half unit on themes such as climate, AI or fairness; in LSE100B students meet in 90-minute seminars in alternate weeks and are assessed half on a short critical evaluation and half on a group project.

lse-pir.name: BSc Politics and International Relations
lse-pir.applies: Students starting in 2026/27 (LSE Calendar 2026/27 programme regulations, 2026 entry cohort; course guides for 2026/27). The public prospectus page now advertises 2027 entry.
lse-pir.rules: 12 units over three years plus LSE100 (0.5 unit, choose one of LSE100A/B/C). Year 1: GV100, GV101, IR100 compulsory, plus 1 unit for Paper 4 (one full-unit course from the list, or EC1A3+EC1B3, or EC1A5+EC1B5); IR102 optional and non-assessed. Year 2: Papers 5 and 6 = 1 unit each from Government List A; Papers 7 and 8 = 1 unit each from IR200, IR202, IR203, IR205, IR206 (not repeating). Year 3: Paper 9 = 1 unit from Government List B; Paper 10 = 1 unit from the International Relations Options List; Paper 11 = 1 unit from the IR Options List, Government List A, Government List B or the Undergraduate Outside Options List (Years 2 & 3); Paper 12 = 1 unit from GV390, IR398, the IR Options List, Government List B or the Outside Options List. Restrictions: GV319 Year 3 only; GV390 available to non-PPE students only under Paper 12; GV346 cannot be taken after GV267. Half-unit options are combined to make up a full Paper. Places on some options are limited and depend on timetabling and prerequisites.
lse-pir.teaching: Teaching is shared equally between the Department of Government and the Department of International Relations. Lectures are given by full-time staff and classes, capped at 15, are led by teaching fellows; LSE describes four one-hour lectures and four hours of classes a week in the Autumn and Winter Terms, plus about 30 hours of independent study. Assessment varies by course, mixing exams in the January or Spring exam periods with essays, quizzes and participation marks. Third-years may write a 10,000-word dissertation in either Government (GV390) or IR (IR398), and the degree class combines Years 2 and 3 with a First Year Average.

profile.body: Courses combine lectures by full-time academic staff with small classes, at most 15 students, run by teaching fellows who hold or are completing PhDs. Class averages in 2025/26 bear this out: 13 in GV100 and IR100, 15 in GV101. LSE describes four one-hour lectures and four hours of classes a week in the Autumn and Winter Terms, varying by course, with around four hours of independent study per contact hour. Third-year options are usually smaller seminars. You meet an academic mentor regularly, and the optional, non-assessed IR102 helps first-years with IR study skills.

Assessment differs from course to course but typically mixes an exam with coursework. IR100 is a three-hour e-exam (80%) and a 1,500-word essay due in January (20%), with a formative essay and an in-class mock exam beforehand. GV100 is a 90-minute exam and a 2,000-word essay weighted equally; GV101 is 40% exam, 40% essay and 20% multiple-choice quiz. Second-year IR core courses such as IR200 are 80% exam and 20% participation. Exams fall in the January or Spring exam periods. The optional dissertation is marked entirely on the written piece.

Your degree class rests on 18 marks under LSE's three-year BA/BSc scheme: the eight Year 2 and Year 3 papers (full units counted twice) make 16, and a First Year Average, taken from your best six of nine first-year marks and counted twice, makes the other two. LSE100 can feed that average if it is among your best six. A First needs ten first-class marks, or eight or nine plus an aggregate of 1180. To move into Year 2 you must pass at least three of the four first-year units, and into Year 3 at least seven of eight. First-year papers allow three attempts and later papers two; a passed resit is capped at 40. Year 1 lays foundations in both disciplines, Year 2 is a set of intermediate core courses, and Year 3 is mostly specialist options.

Year 1 has GV100, GV101 and IR100 compulsory, plus one more unit from a list (or paired micro and macro economics half units). Year 2 takes two units from Government List A and two from the IR core courses IR200, IR202, IR203, IR205 and IR206. Year 3 takes one unit from Government List B, one from the IR options list, one free paper and a final paper that can be a dissertation: GV390 or IR398, but not both. IR398 (up to 10,000 words) needs a confirmed supervisor before it starts, with roughly two 30-minute supervisor meetings a term and submission early in the Spring Term. Half-unit options are paired to fill a paper, and some are capped.

LSE describes four one-hour lectures and four hours of classes a week in the Autumn and Winter Terms, though the mix varies by course. Expect around 30 hours of independent study on top, about four hours per contact hour. Teaching runs from 9am to 6pm on weekdays, and undergraduate teaching is not normally scheduled after noon on Wednesdays. Week 6 of each term is a reading week, and the Spring Term is mainly revision and exams.

This is a genuine half-and-half degree across two large departments: Government (about 850 students and over 40 faculty) and International Relations, founded in 1927 and one of the largest of its kind. Students can choose their dissertation from either side, and in Year 3 can also draw on the School's outside options. The programme page notes that a language, literature or linguistics option may be possible. All first-years also take LSE100, an interdisciplinary half unit on climate, AI or fairness taught in 90-minute seminars in alternate weeks (LSE100B averaged 25 per class).

lse-ppe.name: BSc Philosophy, Politics and Economics
lse-ppe.applies: Students starting in 2026/27 (LSE Calendar 2026/27 programme regulations for BSc in Philosophy, Politics and Economics, 2026 entry cohort; course guides for 2026/27). The public prospectus page now advertises 2027 entry.
lse-ppe.rules: 16 units over four years plus LSE100 (0.5 unit, choose one of LSE100A/B/C). Year 1: Paper 1 is either ST107 plus MA107 or MA108, or MA100; GV101, PH103, EC1A3 and EC1B3 compulsory. Year 2: Paper 5 depends on the Paper 1 route (ST107 route: GV249 or EC2C3+EC2C4; MA100 route: ST102 compulsory); GV100, EC241+PH111 and EC2A3+EC2B3 compulsory. Year 3: Paper 9 = 1 unit from Government List A or B; Paper 10 = PH344 plus 0.5 unit from a set philosophy list; Paper 11 = 1 unit from the Economics Options List; Paper 12 = 1 unit from the Philosophy, Economics or Government List A/B options (ST107 route) or EC2C3+EC2C4 (MA100/ST102 route). Year 4: PH341 and GV343+GV344 compulsory; Paper 15 = 1 unit from Philosophy, Economics or Government List B options; Paper 16 = the same lists or 1 unit from the Undergraduate Outside Options List (Years 2 & 3). GV390 is available to PPE students as a Government List B option; GV319 Year 3 only; GV346 not after GV267. A separate 'with a Year Abroad' version of the programme exists.
lse-ppe.teaching: LSE's PPE is a four-year BSc, run by the Department of Philosophy, Logic and Scientific Method, in which philosophy, politics and economics all carry equal weight for the first three years. Every course has weekly lectures and smaller classes, staff hold weekly drop-in office hours, and each student has an academic mentor. Assessment mixes January and Spring exams, especially in economics, maths and statistics, with essays, group projects, presentations and an oral exam. Year 4 is built around an interdisciplinary applications course (PH341), a team capstone project for an external client and an individual research project, and Years 2-4 count towards the degree class alongside a First Year Average.

profile.body: Each course runs weekly lectures and smaller classes, taught by a mix of faculty, LSE teaching fellows, visiting staff and graduate teaching assistants (usually PhD students). The programme page does not give total contact hours and points to course guides instead. Staff hold weekly office hours that any student can drop into, and each student meets an academic mentor regularly. The final-year PH341 shows the later style: in each teaching term, 15 hours of large seminars setting out ideas from all three disciplines, with Q&A and guest speakers, plus 15 hours of smaller classes.

Economics, maths and statistics courses rely mainly on January and Spring exams with some problem-set continuous assessment, while politics and philosophy add essays. Year 4 is assessed very differently. PH341 is 15% participation, 15% peer review, 35% a 2,000-word essay and 35% an oral exam. The GV343 Capstone is 80% a team report of 8,000 words and 20% a team presentation, both in Week 11 of the Autumn Term. The GV344 Research Project is 80% an individual report of up to 5,000 words and 20% a short video presentation, both due in Week 1 of the Spring Term.

PPE uses LSE's four-year classification scheme. Your class rests on 26 marks: all twelve Year 2-4 papers (full units counted twice) make 24, and a First Year Average from your best six of nine first-year marks, counted twice, makes the other two. LSE100 can count in that average if it is among your best six. A First needs 14 first-class marks, or 12-13 plus an aggregate of 1700. To progress you must pass three of four units by the end of Year 1, seven of eight by Year 2 and eleven of twelve by Year 3. First-year papers allow three attempts and later ones two. A separate 'with a Year Abroad' version lets students spend Year 3 abroad.

The first choice comes in Year 1: statistics plus a lighter maths course (ST107 with MA107 or MA108), or the full-unit MA100, which leads to ST102 in Year 2. Year 2 is otherwise compulsory: GV100, EC241 with PH111, and intermediate micro and macro. In Year 3 you choose one Government unit, a philosophy half unit alongside PH344, an economics option, and a fourth paper whose list depends on your maths route. In Year 4, PH341, the Capstone and the Research Project are compulsory, leaving two option units, one of which can come from the School's outside options. PPE students may take the GV390 dissertation as a Government List B option.

Unlike most PPE degrees, LSE's keeps all three subjects going for three years and adds a fourth year of interdisciplinary work. The Capstone puts students in teams on a real policy problem for a client, which might be a government body, company, international organisation, think tank or NGO, with workshops and a mid-term course-correction session. The Research Project asks for an interdisciplinary question of your own; the best work appears in the online journal Studies in Philosophy, Politics and Economics and at an annual showcase. The host department was founded by Karl Popper in 1946. All first-years also take LSE100.

oxford-em.name: Economics and Management BA
oxford-em.applies: Course Information Sheet for 2026 entry; BA Economics and Management Student Handbook 2025-26 (Economics Department/Said Business School); Honour School regulations change notice (Gazette, July 2024)
oxford-em.rules: Prelims: three compulsory papers (Introductory Economics, General Management, Financial Management); all must be passed (one resit in September). FHS: eight papers, or seven plus a thesis (up to 15,000 words) replacing one option; at least two Management papers (Schedule A) and at least two Economics papers (Schedule B), the rest from either. At least one Economics paper must be Microeconomics, Macroeconomics, Quantitative Economics or History of the World Economy. Microeconomics, Macroeconomics, Quantitative Economics and History of the World Economy must be taken in Year 2; other Economics papers only in Year 3 and have prerequisites. Accounting and Global Business History must be taken in Year 2. Taking more than two FHS papers in one term needs tutor permission. Some options are capped; availability varies by year.
oxford-em.teaching: Economics and Management is taught jointly by the Department of Economics and Said Business School. Teaching combines lectures, college tutorials of two to four students and classes of usually up to about 20, or up to 40 on popular papers. A typical week has up to six lectures and two or three tutorials or classes, and preparing for each can take up to two and a half days. Colleges set unassessed mock exams (collections) in Week 0 of each term, and Year 1 ends with Prelims: three three-hour exams in Week 9 of Trinity that you must pass but that do not count. Finals are eight papers, or seven plus a thesis, mostly three-hour exams in Trinity of Year 3, and the class rests on the average mark, with a recent First boundary of 68.5.

profile.body: Tutorials usually have two to four students and a tutor, and Management tutorials last an hour. Classes usually have no more than about 20 students, though popular papers can reach 40, and most classes last 90 minutes. Tutorials and classes are compulsory, and lectures are strongly encouraged. Management lectures run for two hours and are mostly held at Said Business School. Each second- and third-year Economics paper generally has 16 to 24 hours of lectures and 6 to 8 tutorials or classes. First-year Introductory Economics has around 16 tutorials or classes, normally arranged by colleges. Tutors set problem sets, reading and essays each week. Most teaching is by subject tutors, with some by doctoral students. The university expects about 40 hours of academic work a week.

Collections, college mock exams in Week 0 of each term, are usually compulsory but do not count. Prelims are three three-hour exams in Week 9 of Trinity of Year 1. The result is Pass, Fail or Distinction, with Distinctions going to students with a high total across all three papers. You must pass all three to continue, a failed paper can be resat once in September, and Prelims do not count towards your class. There are no university exams in Year 2. Most Finals papers are three-hour exams in Trinity of Year 3. Global Business History, Climate Leadership and the thesis are assessed in other ways, and Environmental Economics and Climate Change pairs coursework with a shorter exam. The class is based on the average of your marks, and in recent years the First boundary has been 68.5. A First also needs at least two marks above 70 and none below 50. There are no vivas.

Year 1 has three compulsory papers. Introductory Economics covers micro, macro and quantitative methods. General Management is an introduction to firms and the main areas of management, set in the history of big business. Financial Management is the third. Years 2 and 3 make up the Final Honour School of eight papers. Microeconomics, Macroeconomics, Quantitative Economics and History of the World Economy must be taken in Year 2, as must Accounting and Global Business History. Most other Economics options can only be taken in Year 3 and have prerequisites; Econometrics, for example, needs Quantitative Economics. Management options can be fitted into either year. Trinity of Year 3 is mainly for revision and exams. A thesis title is submitted from Trinity of Year 2, approved by Week 5 of Michaelmas of Year 3, and handed in at noon on Thursday of Week 0 of Trinity of Year 3.

Finals need at least two Management papers and at least two Economics papers, and the rest can come from either list. At least one Economics paper must be Microeconomics, Macroeconomics, Quantitative Economics or History of the World Economy. Example options include Strategic Management, Marketing, Organisational Behaviour and Analysis, Technology and Operations Management, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, Finance, Accounting, Game Theory, Econometrics, Money and Banking and Development Economics. Some options are capped and availability changes from year to year. You choose the next year's options during Years 1 and 2. Taking more than two Finals papers in one term is not advised and needs your college tutor's permission. A thesis of up to 15,000 words in Economics or Management can replace one option, with six one-hour supervision tutorials and feedback on drafts.

The university describes a typical week as up to six lectures and normally two or three tutorials or classes, with private study filling the rest. Preparing for each tutorial or class, through reading, essays or problem sets, can take up to two and a half days. Management weeks usually mean two-hour lectures and 90-minute classes at Said Business School. Economics weeks involve problem sets and tutorials arranged by your college. In all, the university expects about 40 hours of academic work a week during term.

The degree is run jointly by Said Business School and the Department of Economics. The department stresses that it is an academic social science degree, not business studies. You get college tutorials in both subjects and much of the Management teaching inside the Business School. A-level Maths is required, but Economics or Business is not. History runs through both sides, with History of the World Economy, Global Business History and a first-year management paper set in the history of big business. Recent options cover AI in Management and Climate Leadership. The university says most graduates go into finance or consulting, and the department runs the Oxford Intesa Sanpaolo Prize, which includes an internship.

oxford-eng.name: Engineering Science (MEng)
oxford-eng.applies: 2025-26 handbooks and syllabuses (latest published); course pages for current entry
oxford-eng.rules: Prelims: P1-P4 (one exam unit each) plus P5 coursework (0.5 EU). Part A: A1-A4 (1 EU each) plus A5 practicals (0.5 EU) = 4.5 EU; Part B: B1 (0.5), B2 (1), B3 (1), B4 (0.5) plus five B options at 0.5 EU each = 5.5 EU (EEM pathway: B2E1, B2E2, B3E and four options). Parts A+B total 10 EU. Part C: six C options (0.5 EU each, 3 EU) plus the 4YP (3 EU) = 6 EU; EEM route takes four C options plus Entrepreneurship and Innovation (1 EU). Progression to Part C requires at least second-class standard across Parts A and B at first attempt; otherwise students may leave with a BA.
oxford-eng.teaching: Teaching runs over three eight-week terms (Michaelmas, Hilary, Trinity). In the first two years students typically have around ten lectures a week, two college tutorials or classes and up to five hours of lab work, with a problem sheet for every four lectures. The first year is the Preliminary Examination (Prelims) and years two to four form the Final Honour School, examined as Parts A, B and C. Assessment is mainly by written exams in Trinity Term each year, plus continuously assessed lab work, a third-year group design project and a fourth-year individual project worth half the final year. The first two years are common to all students; specialisation through options begins in the third year.

profile.body: Lectures are given by the department, while first-year tutorials are arranged by your college, usually in very small groups. In years one and two expect about ten lectures a week, two tutorials or classes, and up to five hours of practical work. Each block of four lectures comes with a sheet of around ten problems, and one sheet can take about ten hours to prepare. Labs are run centrally and normally last five hours, with preparation due beforehand. In the third year teaching includes up to ten lectures, two tutorials, group design work and a weekly lab; B-option tutorials are intercollegiate. In the fourth year there are no labs, and some options are taught in larger lecturer-led classes of up to 50.

Each year ends with three-hour or 1.5-hour written exams in Trinity Term. In Prelims, four exam papers count for one unit each and coursework for half a unit; the coursework cannot be retaken, but failed exam papers can be resat in September. Finals are measured in examination units: 4.5 in Part A and 5.5 in Part B, making 10 across the two, and 6 in Part C. Coursework carries real weight: the third-year group design project is worth one unit, and the fourth-year project is worth three units, half of the final year. Exact classification conventions are published to students on Canvas.

Year one (Prelims) and year two (Part A) cover a common core every engineer is expected to know: mathematics, electrical and information engineering, structures and mechanics, and energy, along with design-build-test projects and labs. In year three (Part B) you specialise through options in one of eight branches, from biomedical to thermofluids, and complete a team design project. Year four (Part C) combines six advanced options with a major individual project. To enter Part C you need at least second-class standard in Parts A and B combined, at first attempt; otherwise you can graduate with a BA. Up to five students a year can spend their third year on exchange at Princeton.

Options start at the end of the second year with coursework modules: one CAD-based design module plus two chosen from a list circulated near the end of Hilary Term. In Part B you take five half-unit option papers from around sixteen offered across the disciplines (biomedical, civil, chemical, control, electrical, information and mechanical). In Part C you choose six from about thirty options, and the list changes each year. Students on the Engineering, Entrepreneurship and Management (EEM) pathway take fewer technical options in exchange for business papers, and may replace the fourth-year project with a 24-week industrial placement. A department document on Canvas maps options to discipline pathways and chartership requirements.

Oxford teaches a single, unified Engineering Science degree rather than separate branch degrees. Everyone studies the full breadth of engineering for two years before specialising, so students can change their intended field late. Small-group college tutorials sit alongside departmental labs and hands-on design-build-test projects such as a rocket lander, a bridge and a music box. The MEng is accredited by several professional institutions (IChemE, IET, InstMC, IMechE, JBM and RAeS) as the first step towards Chartered Engineer status, and the fourth-year project takes up about half of the final year, often as original research.

oxford-hp.name: History and Politics BA
oxford-hp.applies: Admissions course page (2026 entry); History and Politics Prelims Handbook (Michaelmas 2024 cohort) and FHS Second-Year Handbook; History Faculty paper pages (marked illustrative and subject to change)
oxford-hp.rules: Prelims: (1) one History period (British Isles 1-6 or European & World 1-4); (2) Introduction to the Theory of Politics or Theories of the State; (3) one of Quantification in History, Approaches to History, Historiography: Tacitus to Weber, a Foreign Text, or an Optional Subject; (4) Introduction to the Practice of Politics (compulsory), plus Political Analysis (essay). FHS: seven papers in one of four combinations - (1) HO, two Politics cores, Special Subject (2 papers), Politics option, History thesis; (2) two HO, two Politics cores, Special Subject (2 papers), Politics thesis/supervised dissertation; (3) two HO, two Politics cores, Further Subject, Politics option, Politics thesis/dissertation; (4) HO, two Politics cores, Further Subject, two Politics options, History thesis. Politics cores: two of 201, 202, 203, 214, 220. A History thesis replaces an outline paper; a Politics thesis replaces a Politics option. Cannot take both a Further and a Special Subject. Students with no pre-19th-century period at Prelims must take one in Finals; FHS outline papers cannot repeat their Prelims equivalent. Clashes: 202 with BIF7; 215 with Scholastic and Humanist Political Thought or The Science of Society; 216 with Political Theory and Social Science. Capped Further/Special Subjects are balloted.
oxford-hp.teaching: History and Politics combines faculty lectures with college tutorials of two to four students, usually an hour long and built around a weekly essay. Faculty classes of up to about 20 are added in Years 2 and 3. Year 1 ends with Prelims: four three-hour papers at the end of Trinity, each worth 25%, plus a Political Analysis essay, and must be passed but do not count towards the degree. Finals are seven equally weighted units. Most are three-hour exams in Trinity of Year 3, plus a pre-submitted thesis that every student must write, and in some combinations a 6,000-word Special Subject extended essay. A First normally needs an average of at least 68.5, at least two marks of 70 or more and no mark below 50.

profile.body: In Year 1 you can expect around five lectures a week, plus tutorials of two to four students that usually last an hour. Each paper gets about seven tutorials, with an essay for each. Prelims Optional Subjects add faculty classes of eight to twelve students, and Quantification in History runs eight two-hour classes. In Years 2 and 3, faculty classes have no more than about 20 students. A History outline paper typically gets 16 lectures and 8 tutorials. Further Subjects run 12 sessions in Hilary of Year 2, usually 6 tutorials and 6 classes of eight to twelve. Special Subjects run 6 tutorials and 8 classes in Michaelmas of Year 3. Politics core papers have 16 lectures and 7 or 8 tutorials. Politics options have 8 to 16 lectures and 8 tutorials in one term. Some teaching is by doctoral students.

Prelims are four three-hour written papers at the end of Trinity of Year 1, each worth a quarter; a pass needs 40+ on every paper and a Distinction needs an average of 67, two marks of 70+ and none below 60. Failed papers can be resat in September, capped at a pass. Political Analysis is assessed by a tutorial essay of up to 2,000 words. Finals are seven equal units, mostly three-hour, three-essay exams in Trinity of Year 3. A Special Subject counts as two units: a passage-commentary (gobbets) exam and an extended essay of up to 6,000 words, due in Week 0 of Hilary in Year 3. A First needs an average of 68.5, two marks of 70+ and none below 50; a second route allows an average of 67.5 with half your marks at 70 or more. A 2:1 needs an average of 59, two marks of 60+ and none below 40.

Year 1 has four elements. You take one History period, from British Isles or European and World history. You take either Introduction to the Theory of Politics or Theories of the State. You take one methods, documents or optional paper. You also take Introduction to the Practice of Politics and the Political Analysis course. Prelims do not count towards the degree. In Year 2, History outline papers are usually taught in Michaelmas or Trinity, Further Subjects in Hilary, and you take two of the five Politics core papers. In Year 3, Special Subjects run in Michaelmas. A History thesis of 12,000 words is due at noon on Friday of Week 8 of Hilary. Finals papers are sat in Trinity, so the whole degree class rests on Years 2 and 3.

Finals must follow one of four set combinations. Each includes History outline papers and two Politics cores. It then adds either a Further Subject or a two-part Special Subject (never both), Politics options, and a thesis in History or Politics. A History thesis takes the place of an outline paper, and a Politics thesis takes the place of a Politics option. If you did not study a period before the 19th century at Prelims, you must take one in Finals, and you cannot repeat a period studied at Prelims. Some History and Politics pairings are barred because they overlap. Capped Further and Special Subjects, like capped Prelims Optional Subjects, are allocated by random ballot. You list backup choices, at least one of which should be a subject unlikely to fill. Colleges may restrict some choices.

The university describes Year 1 as around five lectures a week, regular meetings with tutors, independent research, at least one essay a week, and training in quantitative methods. Tutorials normally last an hour, with one to three other students. In Years 2 and 3, faculty classes come on top of tutorials and the timetable becomes more flexible. The university says students are very much in charge of their own timetable, choosing from a wide range of lectures. The Politics department says most students have one to three tutorials a week, each preceded by an essay.

The degree is run jointly by the History Faculty and the Department of Politics and International Relations, and it gives both subjects roughly equal weight. Every student writes a thesis based on independent research, in History or Politics. In History, the Special Subject asks you to work closely from primary sources, assessed through a passage-commentary exam and an extended essay. The rule on studying a period before the 19th century guarantees some chronological range. First-year quantitative political analysis also gives students data skills, alongside essay-based tutorials and Oxford's large History library collections.
