oxford-law.name: Law (Jurisprudence) BA - BA in Jurisprudence (Course I)
oxford-law.applies: Faculty of Law pages describing the 2026/27 academic year (options availability marked for 2026/27)
oxford-law.rules: Mods: three papers (A Roman Introduction to Private Law, Constitutional Law, Criminal Law) plus Stage 1 of the Legal Research and Mooting Skills Programme, all compulsory. FHS: seven compulsory subjects (Administrative Law, Contract, European Union Law, Jurisprudence, Land Law, Tort, Trusts) plus Stage 2 of the Legal Research and Mooting Skills Programme, and 2 optional courses taken in the final year. Land Law and Trusts must both be offered. A Dissertation may replace one standard FHS option (proposal of up to 500 words due in Trinity Term before the course starts, subject to supervisor agreement). Personal Property cannot be combined with Commercial Law. The Jessup Moot PIL option is only for students already picked for the Faculty's Philip C. Jessup moot team. Employment Law, Human Rights Law and International Trade are not running in 2026/27; Advanced Criminal Law availability for 2026/27 is to be confirmed.
oxford-law.teaching: Oxford Law is not modular. It runs on compulsory college tutorials, where one law tutor meets two or three students, usually every week, and most subjects get seven or eight tutorials with about an essay and a half to write each week. Faculty lectures form a wide menu that is optional and picked with your tutor's advice. Law Moderations (three papers) come at the end of the second term of Year 1 and must be passed. The Final Honour School then runs from Trinity of Year 1 to the end of Year 3. Year 2 has no public exams, and the degree class rests on Finals plus a Jurisprudence mini-option essay written over the summer after Year 2. Tutors set unassessed practice exams (collections) at the start of each term.

profile.body: The core of the degree is the college tutorial: one law tutor with usually two or three students. Most examinable subjects have seven or eight tutorials, either weekly across one term or fortnightly across two, and you write an essay for most of them, averaging around an essay and a half a week. Tutorials are compulsory. The Faculty puts on a wide range of lectures, but attendance is optional and your tutor helps you choose. Some tutors add preparatory classes, and some options use seminars or classes instead; Advanced Constitutional and Administrative Law, for example, has 12 classes. Jurisprudence has six tutorials on core topics followed by mini-option classes. First years also complete the compulsory Legal Research and Mooting Skills Programme, backed by online units on finding cases, legislation and articles in print and on Lexis and Westlaw. The Faculty expects about 45 hours of work a week in term, plus vacation reading.

Law Mods come at the end of Hilary Term of Year 1 and must be passed. They are three unseen written papers of two or three hours, each asking three or four questions. Tutors' start-of-term practice exams (collections) do not count. Finals cover nine papers: seven compulsory subjects and two options. In 2025 most were three-hour exams sat in person on the Inspera platform and were closed-book again, with some materials supplied. Jurisprudence was two hours: answer two questions out of ten. A few options, including History of English Law, Feminist Perspectives in Law, Comparative Law and Advanced Criminal Law, were assessed by essays written over a working week. The Jurisprudence mini-option essay is the only work done outside the exam room that counts. The degree class is set entirely by Finals. In 2025, 20.8% of BA Jurisprudence candidates got a First and 75.3% got a 2:1.

In Michaelmas and Hilary of Year 1 you study for Mods: A Roman Introduction to Private Law, Constitutional Law and Criminal Law, plus Stage 1 of the mooting skills programme. Teaching for the Final Honour School starts in Trinity of Year 1. The seven compulsory FHS subjects are Administrative Law, Contract, EU Law, Jurisprudence, Land Law, Tort and Trusts, and colleges decide the order. Year 2 has no public exams. You take Jurisprudence tutorials, sign up for a mini-option around Week 8 of Hilary, and write the assessed essay over the summer. Your two options come in the final year, followed by Finals. The four-year Law with Law Studies in Europe adds law and language classes in Years 1 and 2 and a third year at Paris (Pantheon-Assas), Bonn or Munich, Siena, Pompeu Fabra in Barcelona, or Leiden. You must pass that year, but it does not count towards the class.

You take two optional subjects, both in the final year, from a list of more than twenty, including Company, Commercial, Family, Public International, Environmental, Medical Law and Ethics, Taxation, Competition and Criminology. For 2026/27, Advanced Constitutional and Administrative Law is new. Employment Law, Human Rights Law and International Trade are not running, and Advanced Criminal Law is to be confirmed. Some combinations are barred: Personal Property cannot be taken with Commercial Law, and the Jessup Moot option is only for students already chosen for the Faculty's Jessup team. A dissertation can replace one option. You submit a proposal of no more than 500 words in the Trinity Term before the course begins, after getting a likely supervisor to agree in principle. Dissertation material cannot be reused in other exam answers. Separately, you choose a Jurisprudence mini-option in Year 2 from a list the teaching group publishes in Hilary.

The Faculty says the course is designed for about 45 hours of work a week during term. A typical week centres on preparing for and attending tutorials: research in the library from the original law reports and statutes, then writing an essay. Over a term this averages about an essay and a half a week. Around that you pick lectures with your tutor's guidance, and some weeks there are preparatory classes. Vacations are also needed for reading, consolidation and revision. Colleges set their own limits on paid work during term.

The Faculty presents the tutorial as particularly intensive training in the art of argument. You read statutes and cases in their original reported form rather than relying mainly on textbooks. The course is not modular, and almost all assessment is crammed into Mods and Finals, so Year 2 is free of public exams. Unusually for a UK law degree, the first year includes Roman law, studied through translated texts by Gaius and Justinian, and Jurisprudence is compulsory, with part of it assessed by an essay. Legal research and mooting skills run as a compulsory programme across both Mods and the FHS. The Law with Law Studies in Europe route offers a full year at a partner university in France, Germany, Italy, Spain or the Netherlands.

m.n: A Roman Introduction to Private Law
m.d: Uses translated primary texts from Gaius and Justinian's Institutes to introduce how Roman jurists thought about private law and how that shaped modern systems. Latin is not needed.
w: Sources of law and scheme of the Institutes

m.d: Covers the structure and core principles of the UK constitution, including how EU law has affected it and how the Human Rights Act 1998 works. Taught by tutorial; every syllabus topic can be examined.
w: Separation of powers and role of courts
Devolution to Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland
Supremacy of EU law and state liability
Human Rights Act 1998: structure and effect

m.d: Studies the general principles of criminal liability and a set of major offences through statute and case law, tested by essays and problem questions.
w: Actus reus, mens rea and causation

m.n: Legal Research and Mooting Skills Programme (Stage 1)

w: Subject research process and search techniques

m.d: Examines how courts control executive decisions and rules, the remedies open to challengers, and when public bodies are liable in contract and tort. A foundation subject for professional qualification.
w: Grounds of judicial review: substance and procedure
Public authority liability in contract and tort

m.d: Covers how contracts are made, their terms, vitiating factors, privity, breach, frustration and remedies, with some restitution as it bears on contract. The exam can also include tort material.
w: Terms, exclusion clauses and unfair terms
Remedies: damages, agreed sum, specific performance

m.d: Studies the EU's institutions and law-making powers, the core doctrines of EU law, and the free movement of persons, services and goods. Taught in college tutorials.
w: Review of legality of EU acts
Free movement of workers and self-employed

m.d: Philosophy of law: what legal systems are, how legal reasoning works and why legal institutions matter. Six core tutorials are examined by a two-hour final paper, and a class-taught mini-option is assessed by an unsupervised summer essay.
w: Six core tutorials in philosophy of law
Mini-option on philosophy of a legal area

m.d: Focuses on interests in land that bind third parties, such as freeholds, leases, easements and mortgages, and when purchasers take subject to them. Must be offered together with Trusts.
w: Interests in land binding third parties
Purchasers and the land transfer context

m.n: Legal Research and Mooting Skills Programme (Stage 2)
m.d: The second stage of the Faculty's legal research and mooting skills training, listed as a compulsory FHS element. Details are published to students on Canvas rather than publicly.
Centres on compensation for personal injury and property damage, and also covers protection of reputation, liberty, property and commercial interests. Taught by tutorials plus Faculty lectures.
Studies how express trusts and trusts imposed by law arise and operate, and the wider legal control of fiduciaries. Must be offered together with Land Law.
w: Trusts imposed by law, e.g. shared homes
How different trusts arise and operate

m.d: A new option taught in 12 classes across three themes on the UK constitution in its international setting, parliamentary law-making and the administrative state.
w: Empire, allegiance, dualism and international law
Statutory interpretation and principle of legality

m.d: Explores specialist criminal law themes beyond the Mods course, from the tort/crime boundary to terrorism and hate crime. Running in 2026/27 is not yet confirmed.
Looks at how civil disputes are resolved, from fair trial rights and court procedure to mediation and arbitration, and the theory behind procedural justice.
w: Right to a fair trial and access to court
Civil Procedure Rules and overriding objective
Procedural justice and the rule of law

m.d: Applies personal property and contract law to commercial dealings, including sale of goods, agency and security interests. Cannot be combined with Personal Property.
Introduces the conceptual framework of company law and the policy questions in regulating companies, working from cases and the Companies Act 2006.
An introduction to comparative private law in Europe, setting English law beside French and German law and examining comparative method.
w: Contract in English, French, German law
Tort in English, French, German law
Property in English, French, German law

m.d: Covers European competition rules and the economics behind them, taught through lectures and problem-solving tutorials.

m.n: Copyright, Trade Marks and Allied Rights
m.d: Examines why and how the law protects valuable intangibles such as creative works and brands, through seminars and tutorials.
A seminar-based option in four thematic blocks, each with a tutorial, surveying criminological theory and how criminal justice works at home and globally.

m.g: FHS options (choose 2) - replaces one standard option
m.d: An independent research dissertation taken instead of one standard option, supported by cohort research seminars and a Faculty supervisor. Entry depends on an approved proposal.
w: Research seminars on questions and structure

m.d: Thematic study of the law of work, from hiring and firing to collective labour rights, normally taught by seminars and four tutorials. Not offered in 2026/27.
Studies UK environmental law in its administrative, EU and socio-political context, with seminars, tutorials and guest speakers.
w: Links to administrative and EU law

m.d: Covers the substantive law of adult relationships and children, using social science and policy material to see how the family justice system works in practice.
A seminar course led by specialist convenors applying feminist legal theory to a range of legal fields. No prerequisite.
Traces the origins of English law and courts and the growth of core private law subjects from roughly the 13th to 19th centuries, using translated sources.
w: Origins of English law and courts

m.d: Examines human rights theory and specific rights under UK law and the ECHR, plus reform and procedure. Not offered in 2026/27.
w: Reform of UK human rights law

m.d: Covers the legal side of cross-border sales: buyer-seller relations, sea carriage and payment by letters of credit. Not offered in 2026/27.
Compares the laws of China, Japan, India and Singapore in social context through seven cross-cutting themes.
Explores how law should respond to new technologies, balancing benefits, harms and uncertainty. Assessed by a submitted piece of work.
w: Law supporting technological advance and access

m.d: Studies media freedom and the legal limits on publishing and newsgathering, plus how press, broadcast and online media are regulated.
w: Meaning and justification of media freedom

m.d: Interactive lectures with guest practitioners on legal and ethical issues in healthcare, from consent to end of life.
Part A asks what morality is and why be moral; Part B covers central ideas in political philosophy.
w: Objectivity of morality and reasons to be moral

m.d: A critical look at the concepts underpinning property in things other than land, including conversion and gifts. Cannot be combined with Commercial Law.
Lectures and tutorials on the foundations of international law, with feminist and TWAIL perspectives. A Jessup Moot PIL variant is open only to the Faculty's Jessup team members.
w: Nature and sources of international law

m.d: Close reading of translated Digest texts on Roman wrongs, then how civil liability developed later. Assessed by exam; no Latin needed.
Examines who should inherit, how wills work and fail, how estates pass on death, and the tax consequences.
A non-computational study of what makes a good tax system, the main UK direct taxes, and responses to avoidance.
w: Aims of a good tax system

oxford-maths.name: Mathematics (BA or MMath)
oxford-maths.applies: 2026-27 academic year course pages and 2026-27 entry handbook (BA 3 years / MMath 4 years)
oxford-maths.rules: Prelims: five compulsory papers (Mathematics I-V) plus two Computational Mathematics projects counting as half a paper. Part A: offer 9 papers: 3 core (A0, A1, A2 = Metric Spaces + Complex Analysis), 5 long options and 1 short-option paper (three short options recommended); a 10th long-option paper is allowed. Part B: the equivalent of eight 16-hour units, with double-unit extended essays or structured projects allowed in place of some units. Part C: 8 to 10 units, two of which are the compulsory dissertation. A Part B average of at least 59.5 is required to continue to Part C. BA classification = 40% Part A + 60% Part B; MMath shows a separate Part C classification.
oxford-maths.teaching: Teaching runs over three eight-week terms (Michaelmas, Hilary, Trinity), with lectures from the Mathematical Institute and small-group tutorials organised by colleges. In the first two years students have about ten lectures and two or three tutorials or classes a week; in Parts B and C, lectured units are supported by intercollegiate classes of roughly 5 to 12 students. Year 1 is the Preliminary Examination (Prelims), and the Second Public Examination follows as Parts A, B and C at the end of years 2, 3 and 4. Assessment is almost entirely by written exams in Trinity Term, plus Computational Mathematics projects in the first year, optional extended essays and projects in Part B, and a compulsory dissertation in Part C. The BA is awarded after Part B (Part A 40%, Part B 60%); the MMath adds Part C, which is classified separately.

profile.body: Lectures, usually an hour long and recorded or livestreamed, take about ten hours a week. In Prelims and Part A your college runs tutorials, typically two a week of about an hour with one to three other students, built around problem sheets set by the lecturers. In the first year there is a sheet for every two lectures; from the second year, one for every four. In Parts B and C, each 16-lecture unit is backed by four 1.5-hour intercollegiate classes of around 5 to 12 students (larger for popular options), led by a class tutor with a teaching assistant who marks submitted work. Tutors expect about 40 hours of study a week in term.

University exams take place in Trinity Term: roughly Week 9 for Prelims, Weeks 8 and 9 for Part A, and Weeks 6 to 8 for Part B. College 'collections' at the start of each term check progress but don't count. Prelims has five papers lasting 2 to 3 hours each, plus Computational Mathematics projects worth half a paper; you need at least 40 on every paper to pass, and a distinction needs an average of 70. The BA class is based on Part A (40%) and Part B (60%). MMath students receive a second, separate classification for Part C, which includes a compulsory dissertation.

The first year builds a common foundation in algebra, analysis, calculus, probability and statistics, geometry and dynamics. In the second year (Part A) you take compulsory core courses in linear algebra, differential equations, metric spaces and complex analysis alongside your first options. Years three and four (Parts B and C) are made up entirely of options, and Part C is taught at master's level alongside the MSc in Mathematical Sciences. You decide in the third year whether to continue to the MMath, and you need a Part B average of 59.5 or above to do so. After year three you can also apply to switch to the MMathPhys in mathematical and theoretical physics.

In Part A you offer nine papers: the three core papers, five long options (16 lectures each) and one short-option paper (three 8-lecture short options are recommended). You may add a tenth long option after talking to your tutors. Probability and Statistics are taught by the Department of Statistics. In Part B you choose the equivalent of eight units from about 38 courses. Double-unit extended essays or structured projects can replace lectured units, and history of mathematics and Statistics options are available. In Part C you take eight to ten units from about 50 courses, two of which are the dissertation. Mathematics & Statistics is a separate joint degree you can switch to at the end of your fourth term.

Oxford combines Mathematical Institute lectures with college tutorials in groups of two to four, so you work through problem sheets in close discussion with a tutor for your first two years. The range of options in the final two years is unusually wide, from logic and number theory to mathematical biology, finance and deep learning, plus history of mathematics and Computer Science options. Part C is taught alongside the master's programme. Mathematics and Mathematics & Statistics share one admissions route, so you don't commit to either until the end of your fourth term (the first term of the second year), and the MMathPhys transfer offers a route into theoretical physics.

oxford-med.name: Medicine (BM BCh), UCAS A100 - six-year course including a BA in Medical Sciences
oxford-med.applies: 2026 entry course page and course information sheet; 2025-26 First BM Part I and Part II syllabuses; First BM regulations for students starting from Michaelmas 2023; FHS theme rule for cohorts from Michaelmas 2022; Second BM (clinical) regulations for students entering Year 4 from 2023-24; current Medical Sciences Division clinical pages; 2025-26 exam timetables
oxford-med.rules: All First BM courses are compulsory; Part I must be passed before Part II (exceptional cases aside), and a unit may normally be taken at most twice. Distinctions and merits need all units passed at the first sitting. In the Final Honour School each advanced option is split into three themes; students cover eight themes in total across their chosen options, plus a submitted essay and an experimental research project on a topic they propose. Entry to the Oxford clinical school (Years 4-6) is by application during the final pre-clinical year; students who started in 2021 or later cannot transfer to a London clinical school. Clinical assessments must be passed to progress, with one resit per failed part. Year 4 includes a chosen four-week Special Study Theme; Year 6 includes 12 weeks of student-selected Clinical Options and Special Study Modules (2-4 weeks each) and a 10-week elective approved by the Director of Clinical Studies.
oxford-med.teaching: The pre-clinical stage (Years 1-3) runs in three eight-week terms (Michaelmas, Hilary, Trinity) and is split into First BM Part I (Terms 1-3), First BM Part II (Terms 4-5) and the Final Honour School in Medical Sciences (Terms 6-9), which leads to a BA. In First BM about half the time is university lectures, seminars and practicals at the Medical Sciences Teaching Centre (lectures up to 200, classes 10-50), with college tutorials, typically two a week in pairs, and small-group GP sessions in Learning with Patients. Each First BM science subject is examined by a computer-based Core MCQ paper and an essay paper, with take-home assignments for Medical Sociology and Psychology; the BA year keeps lecturing to a minimum and is assessed by computer-based finals, a submitted essay and an oral presentation of an experimental research project. The clinical stage (Years 4-6, entered by applying in the final pre-clinical year) runs for 40, 48 and 48 weeks in Oxford hospitals, GP practices and partner district general hospitals, with Applied Knowledge Tests and OSCEs at the end of Years 4, 5 and 6, the last two forming the GMC Medical Licensing Assessment.

profile.body: Oxford keeps a traditional split between a science-heavy pre-clinical stage and a hospital-based clinical stage, rather than PBL. In Years 1-2 about half your time is university lectures (up to around 200 students), seminars and practical classes at the Medical Sciences Teaching Centre, including anatomy from prosected specimens. Alongside these, your college gives tutorials, usually two a week with one or two partners, each needing written work such as an essay; the syllabus leaves 'Extension' material for you to pursue with tutors. Patient contact starts in Year 1 with Learning with Patients: small groups of 3-7 visiting a college GP tutor (five 3-hour afternoons in Year 1, four in Year 2). The BA year has minimal lectures and centres on research literature, tutorials and a lab project. Years 4-6 are taught by NHS clinicians in Oxford hospitals, GP practices and district general hospitals, with small bedside groups.

First BM Part I (end of Year 1) and Part II (early Trinity of Year 2) set two computer-based papers per science subject: Part A, multiple choice on the Core syllabus, and Part B, essays drawing on Core and Extension material. Medical Sociology and Psychology for Medicine are take-home assignments, Part II adds a Synoptic Questions paper, and Learning with Patients, practicals and statistics are certified by attendance. The BA is classified on three computer-based finals papers in late May of Year 3 (Critical Reading, Data Analysis and Experimental Design; Specialist Themes; Advanced Synoptic Questions), a submitted essay and an oral presentation of your research project. Clinically, each year ends with an Applied Knowledge Test and an OSCE: Laboratory Medicine and Medicine/Surgery in Year 4, an Integrated Summative Assessment in Year 5 and General Clinical Studies in Year 6. The Year 5 and 6 clinical exams form the MLA's CPSA, and the MLA AKT is sat in Year 6.

The six years fall into two stages. Years 1-3 are pre-clinical: First BM Part I (Terms 1-3) covers the structure and function of the healthy body; Part II (Terms 4-5) moves to neuroscience, pathology, psychology and applied physiology; then the Final Honour School (Terms 6-9, from Trinity of Year 2) leads to a BA Honours in Medical Sciences, so every student graduates with a science degree without a separate intercalated year. You must pass Part I before Part II. During the final pre-clinical year you apply to the Oxford clinical school; students starting from 2021 can no longer transfer to London. Year 4 (40 weeks) builds core clinical skills through laboratory medicine, medicine, surgery and a special study theme; Year 5 (48 weeks) rotates through six specialties; Year 6 (48 weeks) consolidates medicine and surgery, then covers options, a 10-week elective, an assistantship and preparation for Foundation Year 1.

Choice is concentrated in Year 3 and the clinical years. In the Final Honour School you choose advanced options from a list of twelve, such as Systems, Cellular, Translational or Cognitive and Behavioural Neuroscience, Cardiovascular Science, Pharmacology and Signalling, Molecular Pathology, Cancer, and Infection and Immunity. Each option is divided into three themes, published by Week 0 of Trinity Term in Year 2, and you must cover eight themes in total. Options may not all run every year. You also propose your own experimental research project in a lab across the Medical Sciences Division and write a submitted essay. Clinically, you pick one four-week Special Study Theme in Year 4 (areas include ethics, philosophy, management and global health), then 12 weeks of Clinical Options and Special Study Modules in Year 6, which you can design yourself, plus a 10-week elective anywhere in the UK or abroad.

Oxford stresses the basic science and research behind medicine more than most UK schools. It keeps a distinct three-year pre-clinical course in which every A100 student completes an Honours BA in Medical Sciences and an experimental research project, rather than integrating clinical teaching from day one. Teaching relies on the college tutorial system, often in pairs with academics and clinicians, and the medical school is relatively small. Patient contact in the early years comes through GP-based Learning with Patients rather than hospital placements. The clinical school is based around Oxford University Hospitals, a regional referral centre, with district general hospital placements in Reading, Swindon, Northampton, Buckinghamshire and Milton Keynes, and the clinical course emphasises self-directed learning, critical appraisal and evidence-based medicine.

oxford-ppe.name: Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) BA
oxford-ppe.applies: Admissions course page and Course Information Sheet for 2026 entry; PPE Prelims Handbook 2025-26; Honour School of PPE regulations (Gazette change notice, July 2024, incl. paper 140 from MT 2025); Philosophy Faculty Finals course descriptions and Economics Department PPE page as live in 2025-26
oxford-ppe.rules: Prelims: three compulsory papers (Introduction to Philosophy; Introduction to the Theory and Practice of Politics; Introductory Economics), at least one question from each section/area. FHS: eight papers. Tripartite (A): one of 101/102/115/116, plus 103 Ethics, any two of Politics cores 201/202/203/214/220, at least two Economics papers, and two free choices. Philosophy & Politics (B): one of 101/102/115/116, 103, two Politics cores, four further papers with at least one Philosophy and one Politics (not thesis) and at most one Economics paper from 300/301/302/311. Politics & Economics (C): two Politics cores, at least three Economics papers, three further with at least one Politics (not thesis) and at most one Philosophy paper. Philosophy & Economics (D): one of 101/102/115/116, 103, at least three Economics, three further with at least one Philosophy and at most one Politics paper (from 201, 202, 214, 215, 216, 217, 220, 229). Economics papers 300, 301, 302 and 311 must be taken in the first FHS year; other Economics options only in the second, and most need 300/301/302 as prerequisites. Bipartite Economics students must take at least one of Micro/Macro/Quantitative Economics; tripartite at least one of those or 311. Only one thesis across 199/298/299/399 (max 15,000 words). 114 and 203 cannot both be taken; 110 and 111 are mutually exclusive; 140 cannot be combined with 106/124. Paper 106 is closed to students starting FHS from MT 2025 (replaced by 140). Option availability varies by year and some are capped.
oxford-ppe.teaching: PPE is taught mainly through college tutorials of two to four students with a tutor, usually lasting an hour, plus some classes of about six to ten and faculty lectures. A typical week has six to eight lectures and two tutorials, or one tutorial and one class, with an essay or problem set for each. Year 1 covers all three subjects and ends with Prelims: three papers, normally in Week 9 of Trinity, which you must pass but which do not count towards the degree. In Years 2 and 3 you either keep all three subjects or drop one, and sit eight papers in Finals at the end of Year 3. One of the eight can be a thesis. Colleges set practice exams (collections) before the start of each term.

profile.body: The university says all three subjects are taught mainly through tutorials rather than classes. A tutorial typically has two to four students and a tutor and lasts an hour. Classes, where a paper uses them, usually have about six to ten students, although one computer-based Politics training course can take up to 24. Most teaching is by subject specialists, with some by doctoral students. As a rough pattern, a Finals option has 8 to 16 lectures and 8 tutorials. Economics options are recommended 16 lectures and 8 tutorials, and technical material may be taught in classes. The Politics core papers have 7 or 8 tutorials each. In first-year Philosophy, tutors may run 8 tutorials and 4 classes, 6 and 6, or another mix. The handbook says a tutorial essay should take at least three days, and you should not normally be set more than twelve essays a term. Expect about 40 hours of academic work a week.

Prelims, the first university exams, are three written papers taken normally in Week 9 of Trinity Term of Year 1: Introduction to Philosophy, Introduction to the Theory and Practice of Politics, and Introductory Economics. You must pass them to continue, but they do not count towards your class. Political Analysis is compulsory in Year 1 but not examined in Prelims. College collections (practice exams) before each term do not count. Finals are eight papers at the end of Year 3, normally held between Weeks 5 and 7 of Trinity. They are mostly timed written exams, with some coursework. One paper may be a thesis of up to 15,000 words, due by noon on the Thursday before Trinity Full Term of the final year. There are no university exams in Year 2. You enter for Finals yourself in Michaelmas of Year 3, and your class is decided by Finals alone.

Year 1 is the same for everyone. Philosophy covers formal logic, moral philosophy through Mill's Utilitarianism, and general philosophy. Politics covers political theory and the practice of politics, plus the unexamined Political Analysis course. Economics covers micro, macro and mathematical and statistical techniques. After Prelims you choose whether to stay tripartite (all three subjects) or go bipartite (any two). Students who continue with Philosophy take Ethics plus one of a set of core theoretical papers. Those continuing with Politics take two of five core papers. Those continuing with Economics take at least one of Microeconomics, Macroeconomics or Quantitative Economics, and tripartite students can count History of the World Economy instead. These Economics papers have to be taken in the first year of Finals. Most other Economics options come in the final year and build on them as prerequisites.

You sit eight papers in Finals, and each route has its own rules. Tripartite students need Philosophy cores including Ethics, two Politics cores, at least two Economics papers and two free choices. Bipartite routes set minimums in the two subjects you keep, and some allow one paper from the subject you dropped. Some pairings are barred. Options are not all taught every year and some are capped, so check the exam regulations with your college tutors. Economics options are settled at an options fair in Hilary. Politics supervised dissertation topics are circulated by Week 4 of Hilary in the penultimate year. You may offer only one thesis or supervised dissertation. The handbook advises choosing by interest, as long as your tutors think you are suited, and not reading too much into Prelims marks.

Both the university and the PPE handbook describe a term-time week of up to eight lectures, usually six to eight, plus two tutorials, or one tutorial and one class. Most of the rest of the week goes on private study, mainly reading for and writing tutorial essays or working through problem sets. Each essay should take at least three days. Lectures typically last an hour. Over a full year the university expects about 40 hours a week of academic work, and vacations are for consolidating reading, especially set texts. The handbook stresses that students are responsible for their own academic progress.

The university presents flexibility as the main draw of the course. Everyone studies all three subjects in Year 1, then you can keep all three or focus on two. Within Politics, options let you specialise in fields such as sociology or international relations. The university says more than 200 scholars teach across the three subjects. The college tutorial, where two to four students defend an essay or problem set in front of a specialist, remains the main way of teaching all three. Prelims are pass-or-fail hurdles that do not count, so the whole class rests on the eight Finals papers at the end of Year 3.

m.d: First-year philosophy paper with three parts: formal logic, moral philosophy through Mill's Utilitarianism, and general philosophy. Candidates must answer at least one question from each part.

m.n: Introduction to the Theory and Practice of Politics

w: Theory: Locke, Rousseau, Tocqueville, Marx and Engels, Mill
Theory: rights, democracy, civil society, power
Theory: liberty, paternalism and free speech
Practice: regime types and measuring democracy

qmul-econ.name: Economics BSc (Econ) (Hons)
qmul-econ.applies: 2026 entry (start September 2026), QMUL undergraduate course page; semester timings and most codes taken from an older (2017-19 entry) SEF programme specification for a sister degree
qmul-econ.rules: Year 1: the listed first-year modules plus Personal and Career Development Plan 1 (the course page does not mark them compulsory/optional; a student account says 8 modules plus a careers module). Year 2: seven compulsory modules (incl. Personal and Career Development Plan 2) plus two options chosen from any level 5 School of Economics and Finance module. Year 3: Personal and Career Development Plan 3 is compulsory; choose at least four level 6 economics modules (60 credits); up to two modules (30 credits) may come from any other Queen Mary programme subject to availability, and one module (15 credits) may be at level 5. Options listed are examples only and vary from year to year. Variants: with Year in Industry (L109), with Year Abroad (L10Y), with Integrated Foundation Year (L10F) and combinations.
qmul-econ.teaching: Queen Mary's BSc Economics (L100) is taught over two semesters a year, with exam periods in January and May. Each module has about three hours of contact a week, mostly a lecture led by academic staff plus a smaller class or tutorial. Students are expected to do two to three hours of independent study for every hour in class. Assessment combines coursework (presentations, assignments, report writing, in-class tests and project work) with exams. Years 1 and 2 are mostly compulsory core economics, and the final year is largely made up of options. Variants add a year abroad or a year in industry in Year 3, and the degree class is weighted 10%, 30% and 60% across the three years.

profile.body: Each module has roughly three hours of contact a week, mostly lectures from academic staff alongside smaller classes. A first-year student interviewed by Queen Mary describes a two-hour lecture and a one-hour tutorial per module, with four modules in each semester. On top of contact time, students are expected to do two to three hours of independent study for every hour in class. Support classes cover the mathematical modules and the second-semester statistics module. Some first-year teaching is deliberately different: Economics and Finance in Action takes place entirely outside the classroom, through weekly tasks in an IT lab and workshops. Every student has an academic adviser. Teaching uses the Graduate Centre, which has a trading lab with 25 Bloomberg terminals.

Assessment mixes coursework and exams, and the exam periods fall in January and May. Coursework can take the form of presentations, assignments, essay-style reports, in-class tests, and research and project work. Some modules break assessment into many smaller pieces. For example, the first-year World Economy module uses weekly online quizzes worth 1% each, a written assignment applying models to real policy cases, and a group country poster presented at the end of the first semester. The course page gives no overall exam-to-coursework percentages. Under Queen Mary's degree algorithm, the years count 10%, 30% and 60%, all 360 credits count, and there is a 1.5% borderline zone. You get two attempts per module, and resit marks are capped at the pass mark.

Year 1 builds the foundations through nine modules. These cover micro- and macroeconomics, mathematical and statistical methods, principles of economics, the world economy, finance and applied work, plus the first Personal and Career Development Plan module. Year 2 is mostly compulsory: Econometrics 1 and 2, Games and Strategies, Macroeconomics 2 and 3, Microeconomics 2 and Personal and Career Development Plan 2, plus two electives. Year 3 is largely chosen by you, with only Personal and Career Development Plan 3 fixed. A dissertation is not compulsory, although an Economics Project is listed among the options. If you take the year abroad or year in industry variant, the placement becomes Year 3 and your final-year modules move to Year 4.

In Year 2 you choose two electives from any level 5 module in the School of Economics and Finance. Examples include International Finance, International Trade, Economics of Social Issues, Empirical Methods in Applied Economics, Managerial Strategy and Introduction to Banking. In Year 3 you take at least four level 6 economics modules (60 credits). Up to two modules (30 credits) can come from other Queen Mary programmes, subject to availability, and one 15-credit module can be at level 5. Level 6 examples include Applied Econometrics, Behavioural, Development, Environmental, Health, Labour and Public Economics, Advanced Microeconomics, Macroeconomic Policy, Political Economy, Economics of Inequality and the Economics Project. The lists change from year to year.

Career development is built into the degree through a Personal and Career Development Plan module in every year. Students can also join the Finance Trading Programme and the qNomics consultancy scheme, where they work on real projects. Data and software resources include Bloomberg, Macrobond, WRDS, Stata, MATLAB and ArcGIS. The School highlights its location near the City and Canary Wharf, and recent graduates have joined employers such as EY, PwC, Deloitte, Barclays and HMRC. The final year offers unusual freedom, with up to 30 credits from outside economics. The four-year variants add either a year at a partner university in Europe, North America, Asia or Australia, or a year working in industry.

qmul-law.name: Law LLB (Hons)
qmul-law.applies: September 2026 entry (UCAS M100); the 2027-entry page shows the same structure
qmul-law.rules: Year 1: six compulsory modules. Year 2: three compulsory modules (Tort Law, Criminal Law, Equity and Trusts) plus either one full module or two half modules from the Year 2 list. Year 3: compulsory Jurisprudence and Legal Theory (30 credits) plus full and/or half modules adding up to three full modules, chosen from Year 2 modules and modules open only to final-year students. A 30-credit Dissertation may replace a taught module. Only modules on the published lists can be chosen, and the lists are indicative and subject to change. A full module appears to be 30 credits and a half module 15 credits, since the 30-credit dissertation is listed as a full module, but individual pages do not confirm this.
qmul-law.teaching: Queen Mary's LLB Law (M100) is a three-year modular degree. Each module usually pairs a two-hour lecture with a one-hour small-group tutorial, held weekly or fortnightly. First-years have about 12 contact hours a week, plus four to six hours of independent study for every hour in class. Assessment varies by module and can include written exams, oral presentations, midterm essays and coursework. Year 1 and most of Year 2 are compulsory foundation subjects, while the final year adds compulsory Jurisprudence and Legal Theory and an optional 30-credit dissertation. Queen Mary's degree algorithm weights the three years 10%, 30% and 60%.

profile.body: Each module usually has a two-hour lecture and a one-hour small-group tutorial, which runs weekly or fortnightly depending on the module. In first year this adds up to about 12 hours of contact time a week. For every hour in class, Queen Mary expects four to six hours of independent study: reading, preparing for tutorials, projects and revision. The course page does not give tutorial group sizes. Student Support Officers provide pastoral and academic-wellbeing support, and the careers service offers one-to-one appointments with a dedicated careers adviser. All modules are listed as subject to change.

Each module sets its own assessment. Depending on the module, this can mean one or more of written exams, oral presentations, midterm essays and coursework. The compulsory final-year Jurisprudence and Legal Theory module, for example, is a 30-credit module assessed entirely by exam. The course page does not give an overall exam-to-coursework split. Queen Mary's Degree Outcomes Statement sets the classification as a weighted average of all 360 credits: 10% Year 1, 30% Year 2 and 60% Year 3. Students within 1.5% of a boundary go up a class if at least half their final-year credits reach the higher class. You get two attempts at each module, and a resit mark is capped at the pass mark.

Year 1 has six compulsory modules: Public Law, Land Law, Contract Law I (Formation and Vitiation), Contract Law II (Terms, Breach and Remedies), Legal Skills, Methods and Context, and European Union Law. In Year 2 you take Tort Law, Criminal Law, and Equity and Trusts, plus one full module or two half modules of your choice. In Year 3 Jurisprudence and Legal Theory is compulsory, and the rest of the year adds up to three full modules. These can be any Year 2 options or modules open only to finalists, and one can be a dissertation on a legal topic of your choice. Students accepted onto the LLB can also apply for the four-year Law in Practice route, which adds a paid placement of about eight months in Year 3.

Choice starts in Year 2, when you take one full or two half modules. Examples include Advanced Contract Law, Administrative Law, Internet Law, Health Law Problems, UK Human Rights Law, Intellectual Property (Trademark Law), and Public Legal Education and Community Street Law. The final year opens up much more widely. There are full modules such as Commercial, Company, Competition, Family, Media and Medical Negligence Law, International Human Rights Law and Criminology, plus around 35 half modules, from Employment Law to Climate Justice and Fashion Law. Clinical options linked to the Legal Advice Centre include a 30-credit Student Legal Adviser module, open to second- and third-years, in which you handle five client cases over the year. There is also a 15-credit Street Law module. The lists are indicative and change from year to year.

The course page describes the first-year pattern as about 12 contact hours a week, built from two-hour lectures for each module plus one-hour small-group tutorials, which run weekly or fortnightly. On top of this, the School expects four to six hours of independent study per contact hour. That covers reading cases and materials, preparing tutorial answers and working on assessed pieces, so most of the week is self-directed study around a fairly compact timetable.

Practical legal experience is a strong feature. In the award-winning Legal Advice Centre, students work alongside trained solicitors to give free advice to members of the public, and this can be taken for credit. The four-year Law in Practice LLB includes a paid placement of around eight months with a partner legal service provider, such as an international law firm, an in-house legal team, a family practice or a charity. Queen Mary says the LLB helps prepare students for both the SQE and the Bar. The School is close to London's legal district, has links with major firms and offers mentoring schemes. It is ranked 7th in the UK for law in both the QS and THE 2026 subject rankings.

qmul-maths.rules: Each year is 120 credits. Year 1: six compulsory modules (four 15-credit, two 30-credit year-long). Year 2: Semester A has three compulsory modules plus one of Convergence and Continuity / Actuarial Mathematics I; Semester B has Programming in Python II plus three of four options (Differential and Integral Analysis requires Convergence and Continuity); Professional Skills for Mathematicians runs all year (0 credits in the 2025-26 spec). Year 3: choose one pathway (General, Pure, or Statistics and Financial; the Statistics and Financial pathway requires MTH5129) and take four 15-credit modules per semester from that pathway's list. Communicating and Teaching Mathematics needs an application/approval in Semester A. Up to 30 credits of off-diet modules may be taken in any year with School approval (programme spec). A placement year or year abroad (separate programme codes) is taken after Year 2 and pushes Year 3 to Year 4; the two cannot be combined.
qmul-maths.teaching: Teaching at Queen Mary's School of Mathematical Sciences is mainly lectures, backed up by tutorials and exercise classes where students work through problems together, plus computer-lab sessions in programming and some other modules. The course page puts formal teaching at about 16 hours a week, with independent study on top. Most modules are assessed mainly by written exam (usually 60-80% of the mark), with the remainder from coursework, tests, presentations and group tasks; project modules are judged on a report and presentation. The year runs in two teaching semesters, Semester A (autumn) and Semester B (spring), and some modules run across both. Years are simply called Year 1, 2 and 3, and in Year 3 students follow one of three pathways: General, Pure, or Statistics and Financial.

profile.body: Queen Mary's maths teaching is built around formal lectures, with most lower- and middle-level modules adding tutorial or exercise classes where you work through problem sheets with others and can ask questions. Several modules, starting with Programming in Python I in your first semester, also have computer-lab practicals. The course page gives roughly 16 hours of timetabled teaching a week, and you are expected to add substantial independent study: reading notes and textbooks, attempting exercises, and using staff office hours. Project and reading modules switch to guided reading with weekly seminars or supervisions. Every student has a personal academic advisor, and the School runs Peer-Assisted Study Support (PASS) sessions. Teaching is based at Mile End in the School's recently renovated (£18m) building, which has teaching rooms, study space and a social hub.

Written examinations dominate. The course page says most modules take 60-80% of their mark from the exam, with the rest from coursework, in-term tests, oral presentations or group tasks; the programme specification describes continuous assessment (weekly or fortnightly exercises or tests) contributing up to 25% in some modules. As an example, the published description of Convergence and Continuity uses a short mid-term test worth 10% and a two-hour final exam worth 90%. Project modules such as the Third Year Project are assessed by a written report and a presentation, with an oral exam at the examiners' discretion. A final-year project is optional on the BSc but compulsory on the MSci. QMUL's official pages consulted did not state how the three years are weighted for the final degree classification.

Year 1 is entirely compulsory and lays foundations: proof and number systems, analysis with calculus, algebra, vectors and matrices, probability and statistics, and Python programming. Year 2 keeps a compulsory core (linear algebra, differential equations, probability and statistics, more Python and a year-long professional skills strand) but lets you start steering: one choice in Semester A between pure analysis and actuarial mathematics, and three of four options in Semester B. In Year 3 you commit to a pathway, General, Pure, or Statistics and Financial, and build the year from that pathway's list. Variants of the degree add a paid professional placement year (mainly in finance) or a year abroad at partners in North America, Asia or Australia after Year 2, and a four-year MSci and foundation-year route also exist. CertHE and DipHE are the interim exit awards.

Choices begin in Year 2. In Semester A you pick Convergence and Continuity or Actuarial Mathematics I; in Semester B you pick three of Complex Variables, Differential and Integral Analysis, Linear Optimisation and Game Theory, and Statistical Modelling I. Choosing Convergence and Continuity keeps Differential and Integral Analysis (and the purer Year 3 route) open. For Year 3 you choose a pathway and then four modules per semester from it; the Statistics and Financial pathway needs Probability and Statistics II, and Communicating and Teaching Mathematics (a schools-based module) has limited places and requires approval during Semester A. The programme specification allows up to 30 credits of off-diet modules per year with School approval, though School pages note off-pathway choices open only once the timetable is fixed. The School's 2026-27 structure adds new Year 3 modules such as Quantum Computing and History of Mathematics.

The degree is organised around three named final-year pathways, so you can finish with a broad, a pure, or a statistics-and-finance profile without switching programme, and option lists are tied to the School's seven research groups (including algebra and number theory, and statistics with data science). Programming in Python is compulsory in both Year 1 and Year 2, and Year 3 options include machine learning, neural networks and C/C++ numerical computing. There is a strong finance and employability thread: Financial Mathematics I and II and Mathematical Tools for Asset Management in Year 3, a paid placement-year variant focused largely on the financial sector, careers support from the start including Excel and SAS certifications, and recent graduate employers quoted as J.P. Morgan, KPMG, the FCA and the Bank of England. The School also holds an Athena SWAN Bronze award.

qmul-mech.name: Mechanical Engineering BEng (Hons)
qmul-mech.applies: September 2026 entry (QMUL course finder, 2026; module lists identical on the 2027 entry page).
qmul-mech.rules: Each year is 120 credits; the course page does not give credits for individual modules other than EMS690U Integrated Design Project (30 credits). Years 1 and 2 are listed as a fixed set of eight core/specialist modules each. Year 3 has three core modules (EMS690U, EMS602U, EMS604U) plus optional modules chosen from seven, with optional credits balanced across the two semesters. The four-year MEng (H301) adds Year 4 with a compulsory EMS700U Industry/Research Project plus options. Year in industry (H304/H302) or year abroad (H30Y/H31Y) variants exist and cannot be combined.
qmul-mech.teaching: Mechanical Engineering at Queen Mary is taught by the School of Engineering and Materials Science through lectures, laboratory practicals and problem-based learning, with group project work running alongside. The course page gives 14-17 hours of formal teaching a week plus group project time, and expects one to two hours of independent study for every hour in class. Assessment mixes coursework, written reports, projects, presentations and group work with exams in the summer. The year is split into two teaching semesters (Semester A in autumn, Semester B in spring), and the stages are simply Year 1, 2 and 3, with a fourth year for the MEng. Year 3 centres on a 30-credit Integrated Design Project.

profile.body: Teaching combines lectures, hands-on laboratory practicals and problem-based learning, where you tackle engineering problems in groups. The course page quotes 14-17 hours of formal teaching per week plus time spent on group projects, and asks for one to two hours of independent study per contact hour. Practical work starts in Year 1 through two Experimental Design and Practice modules and two Computational and Mathematical Modelling modules, and design is taught from the start in Engineering Design. Facilities named by QMUL include a combustion lab, nanofluids research labs, mechanical testing facilities, two-phase flow and heat transfer labs, and the Makerspace workshop; the School says it has invested £30 million in new and refurbished teaching labs. Guest speakers from companies such as Ford, Jaguar Land Rover, Aston Martin F1 and Rolls-Royce feed into teaching.

QMUL describes a mix of coursework, written reports, projects, presentations, group work and exams, with exams sitting in the summer; it does not publish a percentage split between exams and coursework for this degree. Lab-based and design modules lean on reports and project deliverables, while the analytical modules (fluids, thermodynamics, solid mechanics, control) are where exams feature. In the final BEng year the biggest single piece of work is the 30-credit Integrated Design Project, a group design exercise, and MEng students add an individual Industry/Research Project in Year 4. The official pages consulted did not state how each year counts towards the final degree classification.

Year 1 builds the core: engineering design, materials, fluid mechanics and thermodynamics, computational and mathematical modelling, and experimental practice, plus an Exploring Mechanical Engineering module. Year 2 deepens the specialist subjects: applied fluid and solid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, thermodynamic cycles, instrumentation, control, numerical methods and data science, and sustainable manufacture. Year 3 is built around the Integrated Design Project, simulation tools and fuels and sustainability, plus options. The MEng (H301) adds a Year 4 with a compulsory Industry/Research Project and advanced options. You can also add a paid year in industry (Year 3 or 4 of the BEng) or a year abroad in Year 3, but not both. A foundation-year route (HHX3) feeds into the degree.

Years 1 and 2 have no published option choices; all eight modules in each year are listed as the programme's core and specialist content. Choice arrives in Year 3, where you add options to the three core modules from: Vehicles for the Future, Electrical Systems for Renewable Energies, Heat Exchange and Waste Minimisation, Modelling and Control of Robotic Systems, Sustainability Assessment for Design, Failure of Materials, and Advanced Robotics Systems, keeping optional credits balanced across the two semesters. MEng students pick Year 4 options from a list that includes Computational Fluid Dynamics, Computational Engineering, Engineering Design Optimisation and Decision Making, Renewable Energy Sources, Renewable Fuels, Solar Energy Engineering, Electrochemical Energy Storage Systems, Introduction to Systems Engineering, Machine Learning and AI for Engineering, Modern Robotics, and Environment, Ethics and Economics in Engineering Design.

The degree has a strong sustainability and energy thread running through every year, from Designing for Sustainable Manufacture in Year 2 to Fuels and Sustainability, renewable-energy electrical systems and waste minimisation in Year 3, and renewable fuels, solar and battery modules on the MEng. Robotics is a second clear strand, with two Year 3 robotics options. It is accredited by both the Institution of Mechanical Engineers and the Royal Aeronautical Society: the BEng partially meets the academic requirements for Chartered Engineer registration and the MEng fully meets them, so students aiming for CEng often take the MEng. The course page says the School's courses ranked first in London and third in the UK for Student Voice in the 2026 National Student Survey, and lists 2025-26 placement employers including Airbus, GE, Cummins, Mercedes, GSK and Deloitte.

qmul-med.name: Medicine (5 Year Programme) MBBS
qmul-med.applies: September 2026 entry (UCAS A100). The 2026 course page and the A100 structure page still describe the existing three-phase, systems-based curriculum, so that is the structure shown here. Module names and topics come from Barts' COMPAS curriculum map (undated, but its Year 1-5 lists match the 2024-25 programme specification). An MBBS curriculum redesign was discussed at an April 2026 symposium. No start date, entry cohort or new module names have been published, so it is not shown here (see 'unverified').
qmul-med.rules: Every component is compulsory, and the degree is classified only as pass or fail. The 2024-25 programme specification treats each year as a single core Part made up of five assessment Sections (A continuous assessment, B applied knowledge, C data interpretation, D OSCE, E SSCs; in Year 5, C is the Prescribing Safety Assessment). Each Section must be passed on its own at 50%, with no compensation between them. Merits (next 15%) and distinctions (top 10%) are awarded per Part to students who pass everything at the first attempt. Each Phase 1 year has five systems-based modules and three SSCs. SSCs run in every year and must be passed to progress. The core curriculum is about 80% of the course and student choice about 20%. Students without a previous degree may intercalate (subject to performance, interview and written School permission): an iBSc after Year 2, 3 or 4, a 12-month MSc/MRes/ResM after Year 3 or 4, or a 3-year MB PhD after Year 3.
qmul-med.teaching: Barts and The London School of Medicine and Dentistry runs the MBBS as an integrated, systems-based course in three phases. There is no separate preclinical and clinical split. Phase 1 (Years 1-2) is campus-based: body-system modules are taught through lectures, problem-based and team-based learning, anatomy and physiology practicals, and clinical and communication skills sessions, with a fortnightly GP placement from the first term. Phase 2 (Years 3-4) is spent on hospital and GP rotations in East London and Essex, with regular returns to campus. Phase 3 (Year 5) prepares students for work as an FY1 through acute-care placements, a GP apprenticeship, an elective and a student assistantship. Each year is formally one 120-credit 'Part' assessed in five sections: continuous assessment, applied knowledge, data interpretation, an OSCE, and student-selected components (SSCs). Teaching runs in blocks rather than conventional terms.

profile.body: Barts uses an integrated, systems-based curriculum rather than a traditional preclinical/clinical split. In Years 1-2, each body system (cardiorespiratory, metabolism, locomotor, human development, brain and behaviour) is taught as a block of a few weeks through lectures, problem-based learning cases, team-based learning, anatomy and physiology practicals, and clinical skills lab sessions. Year 1 opens with a 9-week Fundamentals of Medicine block. Year 2 returns to the same systems with the focus on disease, adding Cancer and Human Sciences and Public Health. In Years 3-5, learning is mostly on placement, combined with PBL/CBL, introductory teaching weeks, simulation and campus teaching blocks. Lectures are recorded on the virtual learning environment, and some classroom and mock-ward teaching takes place at a satellite campus in Ilford. Weekly contact hours are not published.

Patient contact starts in the first term. From September of Year 1, groups of eight spend a fortnightly session at a GP surgery with a GP tutor, and this community teaching continues in Year 2 alongside online mental-health teaching with ELFT/NELFT psychiatrists. Year 3 is three 9-week hospital attachments, each with GP sessions and a hospice visit. 'In-firms' at Royal London, Homerton, Newham, Whipps Cross, King George and Queen's are reached by daily commute. 'Out-firms' at Southend, Colchester and Princess Alexandra usually come with hospital accommodation. Year 4 adds 6-week specialty blocks, a mental health Trust placement and GP placements. Year 5 covers emergency medicine, anaesthesia and intensive care, surgery and general medicine, a GP apprenticeship, a self-funded elective in the UK or abroad, and a three-week assistantship shadowing an FY1.

Assessment is programmatic: engagement and in-course work are tracked all year, followed by end-of-year exams. Under the programme specification, each year has five Sections that must each be passed at 50% with no compensation. They are continuous assessment (case write-ups, presentations, logbooks, workplace-based assessments, firm grades), an applied knowledge paper, a data-interpretation paper (computer-based anatomy, histology and image questions in earlier years), an OSCE every year from Year 1, and the SSC portfolio. Written formats include SBAs, EMQs, VSAQs and short answers. Final year adds the Prescribing Safety Assessment. To join the medical register, graduates must also pass both parts of the UK Medical Licensing Assessment: the GMC's Applied Knowledge Test and a school-run Clinical and Professional Skills Assessment. The degree is pass or fail, with merits and distinctions each year.

The course has three phases. Phase 1 (Years 1-2, Stages 1-2) builds normal and then abnormal structure and function system by system, with early GP contact. Phase 2 covers Year 3, which focuses on cardiorespiratory, gastrointestinal/surgical and renal/endocrine medicine, and Year 4, which covers specialties: O&G, child health, psychiatry, neurology, MSK, elderly care, dermatology, ENT, ophthalmology, sexual health. Phase 3 (Year 5) is preparation for practice, ending with the elective and the FY1 assistantship. Progression depends on passing every Section of each year, including the SSCs. Students without a degree can add an intercalated year after Year 2, 3 or 4, or a three-year MB PhD after Year 3. Exit awards are a CertHE after Year 1, a DipHE after Year 2 and a BSc Medical Sciences after Year 3.

Around a fifth of the course is student-selected. Three Student Selected Components run in each Phase 1 year, lasting 2-5 weeks or a whole year, and SSCs continue in Years 3, 4 and 5. Topics range from basic science and clinical specialties to community and public health and ethics and law. Each SSC is graded, goes into a portfolio, and must be passed to progress. The elective is the other big choice: you arrange it yourself and pay for it, and some hosts charge up to GBP 6,000. Intercalation is competitive. Intercalated BSc options are Experimental Pathology, Global Medical Humanities, Global Public Health, Neuroscience, Pharmacology and Innovative Therapeutics, Prehospital Medicine, and Sports and Exercise Medicine. About 17 MSc, MRes and ResM options are available after Year 3 or 4. Selection uses results and an interview (held February-March), and the School must give written permission.

Barts and The London teaches in two historic hospitals, St Bartholomew's in the City and The London Hospital in the East End, and the school stresses the wide range of patients that brings. The health of East London is built into teaching from the Year 1 Fundamentals of Medicine block. The school says it has completely removed the traditional preclinical/clinical divide, and its hospital placements reach into Essex, so some students live on site at out-firm hospitals. It publishes its whole learning-outcome map openly on COMPAS, links teaching to Barts Health through the Barts Life Sciences partnership, has a whole-body simulator in its clinical skills lab, and runs the same curriculum at Queen Mary Malta. Its intercalation catalogue includes less common options such as Prehospital Medicine and Global Medical Humanities.

Students starting in September 2026 begin on the current curriculum described here: the 2026 course page and the A100 structure page are unchanged, with three phases, five systems modules and three SSCs per Phase 1 year, and an 8-week GP apprenticeship. In April 2026, QMUL's Digital Education Studio reported that the MBBS is being 'reimagined'. Proposals include a fully integrated five-year programme organised around longitudinal themes (health equity and inclusion, reflective practice, clinical research and scholarship, digital health and innovation), more sustained patient contact, interprofessional learning from the start, year-by-year 'clinical readiness' outcomes, portfolios from day one and an AI framework. No start date, affected cohort or new module names have been announced. Module names may change for later years of the 2026 cohort, so check QMplus each year.

qmul-pir.name: Politics and International Relations BA (Hons)
qmul-pir.applies: 2026 entry (start September 2026) course page, cross-checked against the 2027 entry page; module codes, credits and semesters from the QMUL Module Directory 2025-26
qmul-pir.rules: Year 1: four compulsory modules plus a choice of Background to British Politics, Global Histories, or 15 credits from another school. Year 2: 45 compulsory credits, either Modern Political Thought I and II (15 + 15) or International Relations Theory (30), plus Introduction to Social Science Methodologies (15); one 15-credit methods module from three; at least 30 credits from the Politics list; at least 30 credits from the International Relations list. Year 3: compulsory Dissertation in Politics/International Relations plus the remaining 75 credits from the option list. Students may take some modules from outside the department each year. All modules are subject to change.
qmul-pir.teaching: Queen Mary's BA Politics and International Relations is run by the Department of Sociology, Politics and International Relations and taught through lectures and small-group seminars. Students have about 8-12 contact hours a week plus around 20 hours of independent study, across two semesters, and some modules span the whole year. Assessment combines coursework and exams, and a few modules are coursework only. Year 2 balances political thought or IR theory, research methods, and Politics and IR options, while Year 3 centres on a compulsory dissertation. A four-year Year Abroad variant (L24Y) spends Year 3 at a partner university, and the degree is classified on a 10:30:60 weighting across the three taught years.

profile.body: Teaching combines formal lectures with small-group seminars. Seminars can involve student presentations, group exercises, role-play and open discussion. Queen Mary gives about 8-12 contact hours a week, and expects a further 20 hours of independent study. The year is split into two semesters, autumn and spring. Some modules last the full year, either as single 30-credit modules or as paired 15-credit halves. Thinking Politically, for example, runs across the year in first year. Seminar group sizes are not published. A dedicated careers consultant offers one-to-one guidance, workshops and webinars. All modules are listed as subject to change.

You are assessed through a combination of coursework and exams, and a few modules are coursework only. Coursework includes essays, portfolios, group presentations, research projects and reflective journals. For example, the first-year Politics in Action module has been assessed by a group presentation worth 20% and a 3,000-word writing portfolio worth 80%. The course page gives no overall exam-to-coursework split. Queen Mary weights the classification 10% Year 1, 30% Year 2 and 60% Year 3, with all 360 credits counting. Students within 1.5% of a boundary go up a class if half their final-year credits reach the higher class. You get two attempts at each module, and resit marks are capped at the pass mark.

Year 1 has four compulsory modules: Thinking Politically, Introduction to International Relations, Political Analysis and Politics in Action. You then add one of Background to British Politics, Global Histories, or 15 credits from another school. Year 2 has 45 compulsory credits. You take either Modern Political Thought I and II or International Relations Theory, plus Introduction to Social Science Methodologies. You also choose one methods module (Qualitative, Quantitative or Unsettling Methods), at least 30 credits of Politics options and at least 30 credits of IR options. In Year 3 the Dissertation in Politics/International Relations is compulsory, and the remaining 75 credits are options. On the Year Abroad route, Year 3 is spent abroad and the final-year modules move to Year 4.

Choice grows each year. In Year 2, Politics options include British Politics, Comparative Politics, US Politics and The UK and the EU. IR options include Global Theory, Gender and Feminisms in World Politics, Foreign Policy Analysis and War in World Politics. In Year 3 you choose 75 credits from modules such as Analysing Public Policy, Environmental Politics, Latin American Politics, Populism: A Global Perspective and US Foreign Policy. There are also two internship modules: Parliamentary Studies (Internship), which the School calls unique, and Civil Society – Internship. Each year you can take some modules from outside the School, for example in English, history, geography or languages. Option lists change from year to year.

The degree uses its London location: the Parliamentary Studies internship module places politics in practice within the curriculum, alongside a civil society internship option. The School hosts the Mile End Institute, a policy hub on contemporary British politics that brings in high-profile speakers. It also hosts the Centre for European Research, a Jean Monnet Centre of Excellence. Staff expertise covers the Americas, Europe, Africa, Russia, South Asia and Southeast Asia. Every student writes a dissertation. The four-year route offers a year at partner universities in Europe, North America, Asia or Australia. Recent graduates have gone to employers including the House of Commons and the Home Office.

ucl-civil.applies: 2026 entry prospectus page (2027-entry page also checked); module catalogue entries for 2026/27; Year 2-3 modules from the 2026 BEng page; Year 4 options are candidate Level 7 CEGE modules (prescribed lists not published)
ucl-civil.rules: 120 credits per year from 15- or 30-credit modules (30 credits = 15 ECTS); 480 credits for the MEng (Hons). Everything is compulsory except the three-module IEP Minor (one module in Year 2, two in Year 3) and four Master's-level optional modules in Year 4 chosen from prescribed lists; the Year 4 Integrated Design project is worth 60 credits (half the year). Separate 'with Year in Industry' (placement between Years 3 and 4, needs departmental approval and a reflective report) and 'with Study Abroad' (Year 3 abroad, usually needs Year 1 results above about 70%) routes exist.
ucl-civil.teaching: Teaching mixes lectures, interactive tutorials, computational workshops, laboratory training, site visits, guest lectures from practising engineers and scenario-based group design projects, within UCL Engineering's Integrated Engineering Programme. UCL quotes 8-12 contact hours a week plus about 25-30 hours of independent study. Assessment is varied: written exams, coursework, lab reports, practical tests, online quizzes, video submissions, group projects, posters and dissertations, with many design modules assessed entirely by group work. Teaching runs over Terms 1 and 2, with Term 3 used for exams and the Year 2 surveying field course in Wales; years are called Year 1-4, with Year 4 at Master's level.

profile.body: UCL lists lectures, interactive tutorials, computational workshops, laboratory training and coursework, plus hands-on group projects using design software, site visits and guest lectures from practising engineers. Typical contact time is 8-12 hours a week, varying by year and options, with around 25-30 hours of self-directed study expected on top. Design teaching is project-led: first-year Civil Engineering Design uses lectures, workshops and a field trip, Design and Professional Skills II is built around a term-long group design project, and the Year 4 Integrated Design capstone meets weekly with industry partners acting as clients. Field courses include the Year 2 surveying and dam-engineering course in Wales and a construction skills field course within the Year 3 design module.

Methods include written exams, coursework, video submissions, practical tests, lab reports, online quizzes, group projects, dissertations and poster presentations. The balance varies by module: core analysis modules such as Structural Mechanics and Structural Analysis and Design are 70% exam, whereas Civil Engineering Design, Design and Professional Skills II and the Year 4 Integrated Design are assessed by group work (plus a viva for Integrated Design). Year 3 includes a 30-credit individual research project assessed by interim and final reports and a presentation. UCL's pages reached did not state how years are weighted in the final degree classification.

Year 1 lays foundations in structures, soils and geology, fluids and materials, transport and design, alongside IEP Engineering Challenges and maths. Year 2 deepens the core (structural design to Eurocodes, concrete, fluids, geotechnics, professional skills) and adds the first minor module and the Wales surveying field course. Year 3 brings advanced core modules, a large sustainable design and construction module, an individual research project and two more minor modules. Year 4 is a Master's-level year centred on the 60-credit Integrated Design project plus four options. Optional variants add a Year in Industry between Years 3 and 4 or a year abroad in Year 3 at a partner in Asia, Europe, North America or Australia.

The only choices before Year 4 are your IEP Minor pathway: three linked modules, one in Year 2 and two in Year 3. You rank first and second choices at the end of Year 1 and confirm at the start of Year 2; some minors have prerequisites or exclusions, and choosing one does not change your degree title. In Year 4 you pick four Master's-level optional modules from prescribed lists. UCL does not publish those lists on the course page; the department's Level 7 catalogue includes options in seismic and structural design, geotechnics, finite elements, flooding, roads and tunnels, materials, project finance and international development.

The course runs within UCL Engineering's Integrated Engineering Programme, so civil engineers work on interdisciplinary Challenges and scenario projects with other engineering students from their first term (although civil students do not currently take How to Change the World). UCL highlights its research strengths in earthquake resilience, transport and structural design, links with ARUP, TfL and Network Rail, and facilities such as PEARL, CAVE and StrEnTHE at Here East. The Year 4 capstone puts half the year's credits into a team design project run with industry partners. The MEng is accredited by the Joint Board of Moderators (ICE, IStructE, IHE, CIHT, PWI) as meeting the academic requirement for Chartered Engineer registration.
