ucl-econ.name: Economics BSc (Econ) (Hons), UCL Department of Economics (UCAS L100)
ucl-econ.applies: 2026 entry (UCL prospectus page for September 2026 start); module details from the UCL Module Catalogue and the Economics department module list for 2026/27
ucl-econ.rules: Three years full time. Each year is 120 credits, made up of modules normally worth 15 or 30 credits (30 UCL credits = 15 ECTS). 360 credits are needed to graduate. Year 1: four compulsory modules (90 credits) plus 30 credits of optional modules, from the listed ECON options or pre-approved modules in other departments, including languages. Year 2: three compulsory modules (90 credits) plus 30 credits of options. Year 3: 120 credits, all optional. The 2026-entry page says at least one Year 3 module must include an assessed research project and that a dissertation is available. The department splits final-year options into Group 1 and Group 2 but does not publish the rule for choosing between the groups. The 2027-entry page instead asks for at least two 30-credit Year 3 modules with a research project component. UCL describes the module lists as indicative and subject to change.
ucl-econ.teaching: UCL Economics teaches through lectures, small-group classes and tutorials, with about 10 to 15 timetabled hours a week and 25 to 30 hours of independent study. Lectures are large: the first-year Economics module had more than 700 students last year. Assessment is mostly end-of-year written exams, with term-time quizzes, essays and group projects alongside. Years 1 and 2 build a compulsory core in economics, mathematics, statistics and econometrics. The final year is entirely optional but must include research-project work, and a 7,500-word dissertation is available.

profile.body: Teaching combines lectures, small-group classes and tutorials, and group discussion, and some assessed work is done with other students. UCL quotes about 10 to 15 timetabled hours per teaching week and advises 25 to 30 hours of independent study. Cohorts are big. Last year the Module Catalogue recorded 724 students on Year 1 Economics (ECON0002), 535 on Mathematics for Economics (ECON0010), 518 on Year 2 Microeconomics (ECON0013) and 438 on Quantitative Economics and Econometrics (ECON0019). Tutorial sizes are not published. The first year draws on CORE Econ materials. The department also runs optional, non-credit Dedicated Academic Support Sessions on independent study and professional skills, and its teaching draws on research from the Centre for Teaching and Learning Economics (CTaLE).

UCL lists written end-of-year assessments, term-time quizzes, essays, and group projects with written or video outputs and presentations. In the core modules, exams carry most of the weight. ECON0002 Economics, ECON0010 Mathematics for Economics and ECON0019 Econometrics are each 80% exam and 20% coursework, and ECON0013 Microeconomics is 100% exam across three assessments. The dissertation (ECON0117) is 80% thesis, 10% portfolio and 10% coursework. Modules are assessed in the year you take them. Under UCL's general rules you progress by passing 120 credits a year. Up to 30 credits with marks between 1.00 and 39.99 can be condoned if you pass at least 90 credits, pass any non-condonable modules and average at least 40%, but dissertations are always non-condonable. Exam dates are not given on the course page.

Each year is 120 credits, and you need 360 to graduate with a BSc (Econ). Year 1 has four compulsory modules worth 90 credits, covering economics, mathematics, statistics and applied economics, plus 30 credits of options. Year 2 has three compulsory modules worth 90 credits, covering microeconomics, macroeconomics and econometrics, plus 30 credits of options. Year 3 is 120 credits, all optional. UCL's default classification scheme for three-year degrees weights the years 1:3:5, counting your best 90 credits in Years 1 and 2 and all 120 credits in Year 3. A First starts at a final weighted mark of 69.50%, or 68.50% if at least half your final-year credits score 70% or more. The department does not say which scheme it uses.

In Year 1 your 30 option credits can come from listed Economics modules or from approved modules in other departments, including languages. Year 2 has another 30 credits of options. In the final year everything is optional, but you must take research-project work. The 2026-entry page says at least one module must include an assessed research project, while its course overview suggests one per term. Final-year options are split into Group 1 and Group 2, but the rule for choosing between them is not published. The optional dissertation (ECON0117, 30 credits) runs across Terms 1 and 2. It is a roughly 7,500-word independent project, empirical or theoretical, supported by fortnightly thesis seminars with work-in-progress presentations and one or more supervisors. Module lists are labelled indicative and change from year to year.

The final-year requirement for assessed research projects means every student does some independent research, and students can present their work at the department's annual undergraduate research conference. The department also runs the Gorman Lectures, links to UCL Policy Lab events, and supports the student-run Economist's Society and its magazine, The Economic Tribune. UCL says roughly 50 to 60% of students on the programme are international. The course page does not mention a study abroad year or a placement year.

m.d: A year-long first course in micro and macroeconomics, built around the CORE approach. It looks at how households, firms and policymakers make decisions in goods, labour and credit markets, and at why markets sometimes work and sometimes fail.
w: Historical and cross-country growth, inequality, stability
Core concepts of micro and macroeconomics
Institutions as the rules of the game
Sources of market success and failure
Households and firms in the aggregate economy

m.d: A first module in empirical economics. Students take economic theory to real data, use basic regression techniques in Stata, and learn to interpret the results both statistically and economically.
w: Statistical and economic interpretation of results

m.d: The probability and statistics that later econometrics relies on, running from probability theory to estimation, hypothesis testing and an introduction to linear regression, with practical work in Stata.
w: Law of large numbers and central limit theorem

m.d: A year-long maths course for single-honours economists. It takes students from A-level standard to the mathematics the rest of the degree needs, then consolidates it at specialist level in the second term.
w: Term 1: bridging A-level to degree maths

m.d: A largely non-technical introduction to the concepts economists use to understand today's global economy. It covers trade and financial globalisation, global value chains and who gains or loses from globalisation.
w: Global value chains; rise of China, India

m.d: Reads classic texts in economic thought and links past ideas to current debates. The aim is to bring back perspectives that modern mainstream theory has largely dropped, and to help students discuss economic issues in public debate.

The core intermediate microeconomics module, giving a thorough, mathematically grounded treatment of microeconomic concepts and methods. The catalogue gives the aims and prerequisites but no topic list.

Core intermediate macroeconomics. Term 1 covers income, unemployment, inflation and interest rates, with the frameworks behind fiscal and monetary policy debates. Term 2 turns to international macroeconomics: the current account and exchange rates.
w: Financial sector and global financial crisis
Intertemporal current account theory, terms of trade

m.d: The core econometrics module, teaching the quantitative methods used to test economic theories and measure magnitudes that matter for policy. The catalogue gives no topic list.

Applies core micro theory and empirical methods to labour markets, from supply and demand through to human capital, discrimination and unemployment. It focuses on what the evidence shows rather than on detailed statistical method.
w: Characteristics and trends of labour markets

m.d: An introduction to modern finance theory: how asset markets work, how asset prices are set and how financial markets share out risk. It ends with derivatives and corporate finance.
w: Portfolio selection and factor pricing models

m.d: Surveys the main questions and controversies in development economics, from why some countries are rich to whether aid and microfinance work. It draws on recent research and randomised trials.
w: Why some countries are rich, others poor
Foreign aid, World Bank and IMF

m.d: Sets out a framework for modern international trade theory and uses it to analyse the main policy issues in world trade. The catalogue gives aims but no topic list.

Introduces the core ideas of environmental and resource economics and applies them to pollution, resource depletion, climate change and biodiversity. It compares regulatory and market-based policy tools.
w: Policy case studies, e.g. climate adaptation

m.d: Looks at how science and technology interact with the economy. It covers modelling technological progress, how research is funded and institutionally organised, and the economic role of science education.
w: Science, technology and the economy: data
Modelling technological progress in growth models
Uncertainty and the economics of science

m.n: Economics of Finance and Financial Markets
m.d: A rigorous treatment of financial markets and asset pricing that combines theory with real-world applications. It stresses how information, expectations and risk shape market outcomes.

Examines gaps in income, education and labour market outcomes by gender, ethnicity and other dimensions, and evaluates policies such as affirmative action. Students finish by carrying out and presenting their own empirical research project.
w: Income, education and labour market disparities
Causes and consequences by gender, ethnicity

m.d: Covers why and how governments intervene in the economy, including tax design, public goods, externalities and social insurance. It uses international case studies, recent research and guest speakers from policy.
w: Case for government intervention; behavioural responses
Case studies and guest policy lectures

m.n: Game Theory and the Economics of Information
m.d: Part one develops non-cooperative and cooperative game theory, including matching. Part two studies asymmetric information (moral hazard, adverse selection and contract design) with applications and empirical evidence.
Teaches advanced econometric tools for evaluating policies and business strategies with large datasets. Students work hands-on in a programming language and finish with empirical projects.

m.n: Industrial Economics, Competition Policy and Regulation
m.d: Models strategic firm behaviour in concentrated markets, then studies how competition authorities and regulators intervene. It applies empirical tools such as demand estimation and merger analysis.

Applies economic theory and evidence to current policy questions, including issues too new for textbooks. It is restricted to final-year single-honours Economics students (with some joint-degree exceptions).
An independent research project supported by fortnightly thesis seminars over two terms, ending in a thesis of about 7,500 words. Projects can be empirical, theoretical or literature-based.
w: Finding and formulating a research question
Refining the question with supervisor input

m.d: Applied consumer theory: how individual choice is modelled and measured, and how that feeds into designing and evaluating policies aimed at individuals. It mixes reading, some empirical work and formal derivations.
Studies what drives long-run economic growth and why income levels differ so widely across countries today.

Traces industrialisation and growth from the late nineteenth century to today, asking what helped or held back different countries. It uses past industrial revolutions to think about the possible effects of AI.
Builds the econometric techniques used to analyse financial markets and macroeconomic data. The catalogue lists only assumed knowledge, not taught topics.
Applies economics to education policy. It weighs the arguments for and against different policies against empirical evidence on the returns to different kinds of human capital investment.

m.n: Economics of Migration and Job Search
m.d: Teaches students to set up and solve dynamic models and apply them to migration, job transitions and wage dispersion, linking the analysis to current debates on migration and labour market policy.
Introduces research that uses psychology to explain behaviour standard models miss. Applications include saving, procrastination, education, labour supply, finance and policy.
Covers five macro topics, drawn from a published list of seven. Each one combines data or historical episodes, the history of economists' thinking on it, and modern computer-aided modelling.

m.n: The Economics of Money and Banking
m.d: Covers money, credit and banking: why banks exist and how they compete, why banking crises happen and how regulation tries to prevent them. It uses models, evidence and policy reports.
w: Why banks exist and how they compete
Causes and consequences of banking crises
Government role and future bank regulation

m.d: Named as a Year 3 option on the 2026-entry prospectus page. It has no linked catalogue page, so no details were confirmed.
Named as a Year 3 option on the 2026-entry prospectus page, with no catalogue link. It may correspond to ECON0103 Public Economics and Tax Policy, but UCL does not confirm this.

m.n: Gender and Ethnicity in the Economy
m.d: Looks at gender and ethnic gaps in the labour market and education: theories and measurement of discrimination, and affirmative action policies. Named on the 2026 prospectus. The code and lecture list come from an undated department syllabus file.
w: Women and minorities in the economics profession
Gender and ethnicity in the labour market
Gender and ethnic gaps in education

ucl-eee.name: Electronic and Electrical Engineering MEng
ucl-eee.applies: 2026 entry prospectus page; module catalogue entries for 2026/27 (module lists are indicative; Year 3 options taken from the 2026 BEng page and Year 4 options from UCL's EEE study-abroad module sample)
ucl-eee.rules: 120 credits per year from modules of 15 or 30 credits (one 30-credit module = 15 ECTS); 480 credits for the MEng (Hons). Years 1 and 2 are almost entirely compulsory, plus one IEP Minor module in Year 2. Year 3: compulsory Project I (30 credits), two IEP Minor modules, and optional modules; Year 4: Master's-level options plus the Project II team project. Entry to MEng Year 3 generally needs at least a 50% average at the end of Year 2. For IET accreditation students must pass all modules (some optional modules may be excepted), with at most two attempts per module.
ucl-eee.teaching: Teaching combines lectures, tutorials and problem classes, laboratories, hands-on workshops and e-learning, framed by UCL Engineering's Integrated Engineering Programme (IEP) of project-based Challenges and week-long Scenarios. Years 1 and 2 include tutorials; in Years 3 and 4 students instead have project supervision with an academic. The prospectus quotes about 18-21 contact hours a week plus a similar amount of independent study. Most modules end in a written exam in the summer term (Term 3), with a share of the mark from labs and coursework; the department describes a typical lecture module as about 80% exam and 20% coursework. The year runs in three terms: Terms 1 and 2 for teaching and Term 3 mainly for exams; years are simply called Year 1-4, with Year 4 taught at Master's level.

profile.body: UCL describes a mix of lectures, laboratories, tutorials, hands-on workshops and e-learning, and says the department was among the first in the UK to adopt scenario-based learning. A typical day pairs lectures with a tutorial or problem class and private study, and some days are given over to a full-day lab; Wednesday afternoons are kept free. Tutorials support Years 1 and 2, and from Year 3 you meet an academic for project supervision instead. The 2026 prospectus quotes roughly 18-21 contact hours in a typical week plus a similar amount of self-directed study (an older department FAQ cites more than 30 timetabled hours in Years 1-2). Several Year 4 options, such as Radar Systems and RF Circuits, are taught as intensive one-week blocks.

Most modules have a written exam in the summer term, with part of the mark from labs and coursework; the department's FAQ gives about 80% exam and 20% coursework as typical for a lecture module, and labs require written reports. Module catalogue entries bear this out: for example Introduction to Electronic Engineering is 70% exam/30% coursework, while Digital Design gives 50% to practical lab work and Design and Professional Practice 2 is entirely coursework. Year 3 includes a 30-credit individual Project I (reports, coursework and a viva/presentation) and Year 4 a 45-credit team Project II. UCL's published pages reached did not state how years are weighted in the final classification.

Years 1 and 2 build core fundamentals (circuits, digital electronics, physics of devices, signals, programming and IEP maths and design) and are shared with the BEng, so you can move between BEng and MEng at the end of Year 2; MEng Year 3 normally requires a 50%+ Year 2 average. Year 2 ends with IEP scenario work and the two-week How to Change the World project. Year 3 centres on an individual project, your minor and optional modules, and Year 4 is a Master's-level year with a large team project. Alternatives include an International Programme spending Year 3 at a partner university (named examples include Columbia, Caltech, CUHK, Melbourne and Tokyo) and a Year in Industry that extends the course to five years.

Every IEP student takes a three-module minor: one module in Year 2 and two in Year 3. You rank first and second choices at the end of Year 1 and confirm at the start of Year 2; some minors have prerequisites, and you cannot take a minor that duplicates your core subject. Pathways named by UCL include data science, entrepreneurship, management, modern languages, intelligent systems/robotics, environmental and crime and security engineering. In Year 2 you can also apply (within UCL, not via UCAS) for specialist MEng routes 'with Communications', 'with Computer Science' or 'with Nanotechnology', which add compulsory Year 3-4 modules, or for the year-abroad International Programme. Years 3 and 4 offer a wide choice of optional modules, including some from other departments such as Management Science.

The degree sits inside UCL Engineering's Integrated Engineering Programme, so EEE students work in interdisciplinary teams with other engineers from their first term (Engineering Challenges), take intensive scenario weeks in Years 1-2, and finish Year 2 with the faculty-wide How to Change the World project tied to the UN Sustainable Development Goals. The compulsory minor lets you add a second field, from finance and entrepreneurship to languages. Teaching is research-led, with Year 4 options drawn from the department's photonics, optical networks, radar and RF research, and the MEng is IET-accredited as meeting the academic requirement for Chartered Engineer registration.

m.d: The opening problem-based module of the Integrated Engineering Programme: two five-week design challenges, first within your own department and then in an interdisciplinary team.

Teamwork, communication and basic project management

Faculty-wide first-year maths taught by flipped learning, pairing core mathematical methods with MATLAB modelling of engineering and sustainability problems.

Quantitative report writing and ethical, societal and environmental issues

Kirchhoff's laws, circuit analysis, Thévenin and Norton equivalents
Capacitance, inductance, impedance and maximum power transfer

Adders and subtractors with 1's and 2's complement

Diodes, LEDs, solar cells and transistors

Light generation in semiconductors; laser principles

Power amplifiers: classes A, B, AB

Python libraries for maths, data science and ML

III-V semiconductors in bulk and at the nanoscale

ucl-law.name: Law LLB (Hons)
ucl-law.applies: 2026/27 (prospectus page for September 2026 entry; UCL Module Catalogue deliveries for 2026/27)
ucl-law.rules: Each year is worth 120 credits, made up of modules normally worth 15 or 30 credits; 360 credits are needed for the LLB (Hons). Years 1 and 2 are entirely compulsory, and progression to the next year requires passing all of that year's examinations. In the final year students choose 120 credits from a list of optional modules; one may be a supervised Research Essay (subject to departmental approval), and up to 30 credits may be taken from outside Laws, subject to availability and approval. UCL describes the option list as indicative and says content and availability may change; some listed modules are marked as not running in 2026/27. Laws examinations are generally held in Term 3 in London.
ucl-law.teaching: UCL's three-year LLB teaches through lectures together with seminars and tutorials built around work prepared in advance, and the Faculty stresses small-group teaching and active discussion. Contact time runs from 6 to 14 hours a week, with 26 to 34 hours of independent study expected. The first two years are entirely compulsory, with four 30-credit foundation subjects each year, and every first- and second-year exam must be passed to move on. The final year is made up wholly of options, which can include a supervised Research Essay. Almost all Laws exams sit in Term 3 and must be taken in person in London.

profile.body: UCL Laws combines lectures with seminars and tutorial groups. Seminars and tutorials are based on work you prepare beforehand, and the Faculty says it puts considerable emphasis on small-group teaching and expects substantial participation and discussion. Tutorial group sizes are not published. Lectures for the compulsory modules are large: the Module Catalogue reports about 246 to 256 students on each Year 1 compulsory module last year. Year 1 starts with a two-week induction of more than 15 hours, including the zero-credit Laws' Connections module on the role of law in social challenges. After that, contact time is 6 to 14 hours a week depending on year and options, and you are expected to do 26 to 34 hours of independent study a week. All teaching is in person, with materials on Moodle.

You must pass written assessments in every module each year, and some modules also use group work or presentations. The core modules lean heavily on exams. In the 2026/27 Module Catalogue, Public Law, Criminal Law and Tort are assessed 100% by exam, and Contract is split 50% exam and 50% coursework. The Research Essay is the main exception, assessed entirely by coursework. Exams for almost all Laws modules are held in Term 3. You must sit them in person in London, the timetable is published in Term 2, and the Faculty says no alternative modes of assessment are available. Modules are assessed in the year you take them. Under UCL's general regulations, a year normally counts as passed when you pass all 120 credits, though limited condonement of marks from 1.00 to 39.99 is possible for up to 30 credits if the year average is at least 40%.

Each year is worth 120 credits, and the LLB (Hons) needs 360. Year 1 covers Public Law, Contract, Property I and Criminal Law, all compulsory. Year 2 covers Tort, Property II, European Union Law, and Jurisprudence and Legal Theory, also all compulsory. UCL says progression to the next year requires passing all of that year's examinations. The final year is entirely optional, with 120 credits chosen from the Faculty's list. UCL's default classification scheme for three-year bachelor's degrees weights the years 1:3:5, using your best 90 credits in each of Years 1 and 2 and all 120 credits in Year 3. A First needs a final weighted mark of at least 69.50%, or 68.50% if at least half your final-year credits score 70% or more. Which scheme Laws applies is not stated on the course pages.

In the final year you pick 120 credits of Laws options, mostly worth 15 or 30 credits. Up to 30 credits may come from outside the Faculty, subject to availability and approval. One option can be the Research Essay (LAWS0028, 30 credits), which needs departmental approval. You submit a research proposal in Term 1, supervisors are usually allocated after Reading Week, most supervision happens in Term 2, you may send up to two 3,000-word drafts for feedback, and the essay is due at the start of Term 3. It cannot repeat an area of law you study in another module. UCL calls the option list indicative, and several modules are marked as not running in 2026/27. The Faculty warns that popular modules can fill up and does not rearrange timetables to fix clashes with modules taken outside Laws.

Practical legal experience is built in through mooting, client interviewing and negotiation competitions, and through pro bono work at the UCL Integrated Legal Advice Clinic, run by the UCL Centre for Access to Justice. International Mooting is available as an option. After Year 2 you can extend the degree by a year and study in the USA, Australia, Hong Kong or Singapore. You can also transfer to the four-year joint LLB/JD, with Years 3 and 4 at Columbia in New York, or to Law with Another Legal System, with Year 3 at UNSW, HKU or NUS. The UCL 200 LLB Opportunity Scholarship offers eligible students up to £15,000 a year towards living costs. It does not cover tuition.

m.d: An introduction to the core doctrines of English contract law across a contract's life, treating exchange as the defining feature. It lays foundations for later subjects such as commercial law and points out tensions within the doctrine.
w: Formation: consideration, promissory estoppel and intention to create legal relations
Judicial control of unfair terms: exemption clauses, UCTA 1977, CRA 2015 and penalties
Vitiating factors: duress, undue influence and unconscionable bargains

m.d: Introduces property law generally with a detailed focus on land law, looking at what makes a right proprietary rather than personal and why that matters. Covers how property rights arise, pass between people and are prioritised when claims compete, with close reading of statute and case law.
w: Land law within English private law
Social and economic functions of land law
Acquiring, transferring and enforcing land rights
Roles of common law, equity and statute
Critical evaluation of land law rules

m.d: A first-year introduction to UK constitutional and administrative law, starting with the institutions of government and constitutional principles. The second part turns to judicial review, the UK-EU constitutional relationship and human rights protection under the Human Rights Act 1998.
w: Separation of powers and rule of law
Human rights under the Human Rights Act 1998

m.d: Introduces the criminal law of England and Wales while building core legal analysis and argument skills. It moves from the structure of liability and basic concepts to specific offences and defences.
w: Structure of criminal law; actus reus, mens rea

m.d: A non-credit induction course in the first weeks of term that introduces the English legal system, legal skills and study methods. Students work in small groups on a case study built around a social issue, reading their first cases and articles and producing a short written piece and presentation.
w: Introduction to the Study of Law lectures
Case study group work (e.g. climate change)
Short written piece and group presentation

m.d: Follows on from Property I to cover the general law of trusts: how trusts are validly created, what beneficiaries can claim against trustees and third parties, and the remedies available. Special categories such as charitable trusts are also examined, combining doctrine with academic commentary.
w: Remedies for breach of fiduciary duty
Proprietary claims after breach of trust
Third-party liability after breach of trust

m.d: A philosophical study of what law is, drawing on several centuries of legal and political theory and UCL's own jurisprudential tradition (Bentham, Austin, Dworkin). Students are pushed to form and defend their own views on law's nature and purpose; assessment is half coursework, half oral.
w: Nature of legal obligations and rights
Freedom and equality in legal systems

m.d: Introduces civil wrongs that give rise to damages, the reasoning behind the main torts and how to apply them to facts. After studying core torts and cross-cutting issues, students pick a specialist area for in-depth study in the second half of Term 2.

Studies EU law in the post-Brexit setting, explaining why it still matters for UK law and for a qualifying law degree. It covers how the EU makes and applies law, the economic freedoms and citizenship, and the EU's continuing regulatory influence on the UK.
w: WTO, customs union and EU trade policy
EU competences, supremacy and direct effect
Fundamental rights in the EU order
EU citizenship and free movement of persons
Level playing field and the Brussels Effect

m.d: Examines UK employment and equality law together with its social, economic and political context. Looks at worker protection, dismissal, collective labour rights and competing ideas of what equality requires.
Looks at how creative and inventive output gains legal protection and how those rights operate. Also explores policy tensions between owners, competitors, consumers and the wider public interest.

Covers UK company law built around the Companies Act 2006 and its interaction with common law and equity. Mixes practical and critical angles on corporate governance, including recent failures and theoretical debates.
Shows how contract, property and equity principles work in commercial settings such as agency and assignment. Considers how the law trades off commercial certainty against flexibility.

ucl-maths.name: Mathematics BSc
ucl-maths.applies: 2026 entry (UCAS G100); module descriptions are the department's 2026-27 syllabus sheets
ucl-maths.rules: 120 credits per year, mostly 15-credit modules (8 a year). Year 1: all eight modules compulsory. Year 2: four compulsory Term 1 modules, then four options in Term 2 plus a group project and presentation. Year 3: options only. To graduate with a BSc you need 360 credits, at least 90 at level 6 or above, and no more than 150 at level 4. Outside options (e.g. economics, management, languages) are possible subject to suitability, availability and these level rules. Progression requires passing all 120 credits with a year mean of at least 40%; up to 30 credits a year (60 overall) can be condoned, but not the compulsory first-year maths modules.
ucl-maths.teaching: Teaching is lecture-led, with roughly 12-16 hours of lectures plus about 4 hours of small-group tutorials a week in Year 1 and the first half of Year 2, falling to about 12 lecture hours in Year 3. Weekly problem sheets, computer labs, module office hours and a first-year Student Mentor scheme support the lectures. Most modules are examined in Term 3 (late April/May) with a small coursework element, and Year 1 modules also carry a January mid-sessional test. UCL runs three terms: Terms 1 and 2 are teaching terms and Term 3 is mainly exams. Years are simply called Year 1, 2 and 3; modules sit at levels 4-7.

profile.body: Most teaching is through lectures, backed up by small-group tutorials and weekly problem sheets. In Year 1 and the first half of Year 2 the department expects about 12-16 hours of lectures and around 4 hours of tutorials a week, so roughly 16-20 contact hours; by Year 3 this drops to about 12 hours of lectures. On top of that you should plan for 15-20 hours of independent study a week. Year 1 includes computer lab sessions, and Mathematical Methods 2 teaches Python programming alongside multivariable calculus. Each module runs office hours for one-to-one help with lecturers or tutors, and first-years are paired with older students through a Student Mentor scheme.

The dominant assessment is the written exam, sat in the main exam period in late April and May, with a small coursework element; typical weightings on the 2026-27 syllabus sheets are 85/15 or 90/10 exam to coursework. Year 1 modules such as Analysis 1 and Algebra 1 also include a mid-sessional test in January worth 10%. A few options break the pattern: Theorem Proving in Lean has no exam, using coursework, tests and a written report. Modules pass at 40% (50% at level 7), and the compulsory first-year maths modules also need 40% on the exam itself. Resits take place in the Late Summer Assessment period in August/September and are capped at the pass mark.

Year 1 is entirely compulsory: two modules each in analysis, algebra and mathematical methods, plus applied mathematics and Newtonian mechanics. Year 2 is split by term: in Term 1 everyone takes complex analysis, further linear algebra, fluid mechanics and Mathematical Methods 3, and in Term 2 you choose options and complete a group project and presentation on a second-year topic. Year 3 is made up of advanced options. To move on each year you must pass 120 credits with an average of at least 40%, though limited condonement is allowed. The first two years are identical to the four-year MSci, and transfers between the BSc and MSci are possible if you meet the criteria. UCL also supports the Year in Industry scheme for students deferring entry.

Options come in two stages. In Term 2 of Year 2 you pick four from about nine second-year modules, such as Probability and Statistics, Algebra 4, Analysis 4, Number Theory, Computational Methods and Electromagnetism and Special Relativity. In Year 3 you build the whole 120 credits from a pool of more than 30 options at level 6 and level 7, covering pure, applied, computational and historical topics. Your choices must meet the level rules: at least 90 credits at level 6 or above across the degree and no more than 150 at level 4. Outside options in subjects like economics, management or a language are allowed if they are suitable and available. The department publishes an interactive catalogue showing prerequisites and follow-on modules, plus a pathways map.

UCL's department is large and research-active, with strengths in geometry, spectral theory, number theory, fluid dynamics, numerical analysis and mathematical modelling, and it reports that three of the six British Fields Medal winners have links to it. That breadth shows in the final-year menu, which runs from Galois theory, algebraic topology and modular forms to geophysical fluid dynamics, biomathematics and financial mathematics. There are also unusual options such as Theorem Proving in Lean, Mathematics for Machine Learning and AI, and History of Mathematics. Programming is part of the compulsory first year, and the Year 2 structure (common core in Term 1, options in Term 2) lets students start specialising early. The course page cites a 6th-in-UK place in the QS 2024 subject rankings.

ucl-mech.name: Mechanical Engineering MEng
ucl-mech.applies: 2026 entry (UCAS H301); module details from the UCL Module Catalogue for 2026/27
ucl-mech.rules: 120 credits a year from 15- or 30-credit modules; 480 credits for the MEng. Years 1-2 are mostly compulsory core plus IEP modules, with the first IEP Minor module in Year 2. Year 3: individual project (30), core modules, two IEP Minor modules and master's-level options. Year 4: 60-credit capstone group project plus master's-level options to make up 120 credits. IEP Minor choices are made at the end of Year 1 and confirmed at the start of Year 2; you cannot take a minor that overlaps your core subject. Year 3 abroad (Go Abroad) or a year in industry between Years 3 and 4 need UCL approval.
ucl-mech.teaching: Teaching combines lectures (some flipped), problem classes and tutorials, laboratories and a lot of project work through UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme (IEP), including week-long Scenarios where normal lectures stop. Typical contact time is 8-14 hours of lectures and 4-6 hours of classes a week in Years 1-2, with 22-40 hours of labs or project work a year. Assessment mixes exams, individual and group coursework, presentations, design scenarios and lab work. Year 3 is built around an individual project and Year 4 around a 60-credit group capstone. UCL's year has three terms, with Term 3 mainly for exams; stages are simply Years 1-4.

profile.body: Mechanical Engineering is taught within UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme, so lectures (some flipped, with material reviewed beforehand) sit alongside problem classes, tutorials, experimental and computer labs and plenty of team projects. In Years 1 and 2 you can expect roughly 8-14 hours of lectures and 4-6 hours of problem classes or tutorials a week, plus 22-40 hours of lab or project work across the year. In Year 3 lectures rise to 11-14 hours a week with about half an hour of project supervision. In Year 4 the capstone takes around 20 hours of project work and an hour of supervision a week. Full-time study is planned as about a 35-hour week, including 15-17 hours of self-study.

Assessment is deliberately mixed: written exams, individual and group coursework, presentations, design scenarios and practical lab work. The balance varies by module. Core analytical modules such as Engineering Dynamics are 70% exam, Design and Professional Skills II is 90% group work, and Advanced Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics is assessed entirely by coursework. Modules are assessed in the year they are taken. The Year 3 individual project is marked on a dissertation, a viva or presentation and other outputs. The Year 4 capstone is assessed largely through group deliverables and practical work. The pages consulted do not give the classification weighting across years.

Year 1 lays foundations in statics, thermofluids, dynamics and materials alongside the IEP modules: Engineering Challenges, Design and Professional Skills I and Mathematical Modelling and Analysis 1. Year 2 moves to intermediate thermofluids, solids and structures, materials failure, control and instrumentation and further maths, and starts your IEP Minor. It ends with How to Change the World, a two-week interdisciplinary project. Year 3 centres on a year-long individual project with advanced dynamics, thermofluids and elasticity, and you can apply to spend it abroad. Year 4 is the master's year, with a 60-credit capstone group design project. The degree is IMechE-accredited, and an approved industry year can be taken between Years 3 and 4.

The first choice is your IEP Minor, a three-module pathway in a subject outside your core (examples include data science, robotics, intelligent systems, environmental engineering and entrepreneurship). You state first and second choices at the end of Year 1 and confirm the pathway at the start of Year 2. You then take one minor module in Year 2 and two in Year 3. You cannot pick a minor that duplicates your core programme. Later, master's-level options in Years 3 and 4 let you specialise in areas such as renewable energy, extreme-environment engineering, medical imaging, turbomachinery, materials and fatigue, electrical machines and propulsion, and ship dynamics. Students who study abroad in Year 3 may not be able to finish their minor modules.

The defining feature is the IEP. You work in interdisciplinary teams with students from other engineering departments through Engineering Challenges in your first term, through Scenario weeks in Years 1 and 2, and through How to Change the World, where teams pitch solutions to UN Sustainable Development Goal problems to external panels. The department highlights MechSpace, a student build space for assessed and extracurricular prototypes, and specialist labs for nanoengineering, materials testing, engine cells and wave tanks. Some activities take place at UCL East in Stratford. The option list also includes marine and naval topics such as ship dynamics and electrical propulsion, and sustainability is built into the curriculum.

ucl-med.name: Medicine MBBS BSc
ucl-med.applies: 2026 entry (programme starting September 2026); module details from the UCL Module Catalogue 2026/27 deliveries. Note: the 2027-entry prospectus page lists a revised Year 1 module set (see Year 1 notes).
ucl-med.rules: Six-year integrated programme: five years of medicine plus a compulsory intercalated BSc (iBSc) in Year 3; UK graduates are exempt from the iBSc and finish in five years. Years 1 and 2 each carry 120 credits and Years 4-6 each carry 180 credits, awarded on end-of-year assessments (the catalogue attaches credits to the Applied Knowledge Test and Clinical and Professional Skills Assessment modules; teaching modules show 0 credits). All MBBS modules in Years 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 are listed as compulsory; choice comes via the Student Selected Components (topic chosen by the student; preferences submitted around Term 1) and the Year 6 clinical elective. Year 3 iBSc: choose one programme; students rank five preferences, oversubscribed programmes are allocated competitively on anonymised personal statements, and allocations are final. Each iBSc is 120 credits of 15- or 30-credit modules, with core modules plus any optional modules approved by the programme tutor/department, and includes a dissertation or research project worth 30 or 45 credits. Passing 120 iBSc credits earns a BSc (Hons) and is required to progress to Year 4; only Year 3 marks count towards iBSc classification. To progress each MBBS year students must pass both the AKT and the CPSA (pass marks are criterion-referenced; OSCEs also require passing 55% of stations) and complete sign-off and the portfolio. The top 20% of each year receive a Certificate of Merit; Distinctions go to the top 10% across Years 1-2 (Medical Sciences), Years 4-5 (Clinical Science) and Year 6 (Clinical Practice). The MBBS must be completed within 9 years (8 for UK graduates exempt from the iBSc).
ucl-med.teaching: UCL teaches medicine as an integrated six-year programme: Years 1-2 (Fundamentals of Clinical Science) are sequential systems-based modules taught through interactive lectures, small groups, practicals, dissection and prosection, computer-assisted learning and simulation, with a weekly half-day of Clinical and Professional Practice (CPP) and patient-pathway visits. Year 3 is a compulsory intercalated BSc, then Years 4-6 are mainly placement-based in NHS Trusts, GP practices and community settings in and around London (Integrated Clinical Care, The Life Cycle and Specialist Practice, Preparation for Practice). Years 1-3 follow UCL's three-term calendar (late September to June), while the clinical years run from September to July with longer terms. Every MBBS year ends with summative assessment in two parts, an Applied Knowledge Test (SBA and VSA questions) and a Clinical and Professional Skills Assessment (an OSCE from Year 2 onward), plus a portfolio and sign-off; the final-year AKT and CPSA form the UK Medical Licensing Assessment.

profile.body: Years 1 and 2 are built from consecutive modules organised around body systems rather than separate subjects such as anatomy or biochemistry; each module integrates the sciences with clinical themes and builds on the last. Teaching mixes interactive lectures, small-group work, practicals, anatomy by dissection, prosection and computer simulation, self-paced online learning and simulation. Running through all six years is Clinical and Professional Practice (CPP), about 20% of the curriculum and its assessment: 16 vertical modules spanning anatomy and imaging, clinical skills, 'doctor as data scientist', pathology and prescribing, plus communication, ethics and law, mental health, patient safety, professionalism and social determinants of health. Timetables run 9am-5pm Monday to Friday with Wednesday afternoons free; UCL quotes about 32 timetabled hours a week (28.5 weeks a year in Years 1-2) and recommends at least 10 hours of private study weekly.

Patient contact starts in Year 1 through community visits and 'patient pathways': Integrated and Community Care (Years 1-2), Cardiometabolic Illness (Year 2), Cancer (Year 4) and Person-centred Care (Year 5), where students follow real patients and services over time. From Year 4 learning is mostly on placement in NHS Trusts, GP practices and community providers in and around London, about 36 placement weeks a year in Years 4 and 5 and 32 in Year 6, 104 weeks in total. Year 4 rotates through three 12-13 week integrated clinical care modules covering acute and general medicine, surgery and the medical specialties; Year 5 covers child and family health, women's and men's health, and older people, psychiatry, oncology and eyes. Year 6 includes a 15-week district general hospital assistantship and a 5-week GP assistantship outside London. Placements can involve on-call and weekend rotas.

Each MBBS year ends with summative exams that decide progression, in two parts. The Applied Knowledge Test is computer-based: in Years 1-2 it mixes single-best-answer and very-short-answer questions (two 2-hour papers), and from Year 4 it is 200 case-based single-best-answer items, with no negative marking. The Clinical and Professional Skills Assessment is an OSCE of 8-12 stations of 12 minutes (from Year 2; in Year 1 the second component is a second written paper). Students must pass both parts and complete a portfolio of coursework, workplace-based assessments and sign-offs. Formative mock exams run in the consolidation weeks of Years 1-2 and in each clinical module. In Year 6 the AKT, sat in February, is the national written part of the GMC's Medical Licensing Assessment, and the final OSCE is the clinical part. Merits and distinctions are awarded on rank, not degree classes.

The six years are named stages: Fundamentals of Clinical Science 1 and 2 (Years 1-2), the Integrated BSc (Year 3), Integrated Clinical Care (Year 4), The Life Cycle and Specialist Practice (Year 5) and Preparation for Practice (Year 6). Intercalation is built in: every student without a UK degree takes a 120-credit iBSc in Year 3, earning a BSc (Hons) classified only on Year 3 marks, which must be awarded before Year 4. Around 90% of iBSc students get a first or upper second. UK graduates skip the iBSc and finish in five years. A small number of students can take the MBPhD, a three-year PhD between Years 4 and 5. Each year must be passed to progress; students who fail a clinical year can defer their resit and repeat the year, and the MBBS must be finished within nine years. For 2027 entry UCL is introducing a revised Year 1 with fewer, larger modules.

Most of the MBBS is compulsory, so choice comes in three places. Student Selected Components in Years 1 and 2 let students study a medical, humanities or social-science topic outside or beyond the core, with options published on Moodle each year. The Year 3 iBSc offers one of the widest ranges in the UK, about 20 programmes from neuroscience, oncology and surgical sciences to global health, medical anthropology and history and philosophy of medicine. Students rank five programmes and write personal statements for their top two by early January of Year 2; oversubscribed programmes are allocated competitively on anonymised statements, allocations are final, and module choices within the programme open in April. Each iBSc is 120 credits of 15- or 30-credit modules plus a 30- or 45-credit project. In Year 6 students choose an eight-week clinical elective in the UK or abroad, with need- and merit-based bursaries.

UCL has taught medicine since 1834 and aims to produce the 'UCL Doctor': scientifically literate and patient-centred. Its compulsory iBSc is unusual in breadth, drawing on faculties across UCL from engineering and maths to anthropology and history. The CPP strand, which makes up a fifth of the course, threads data science, ethics, mental health and social determinants of health through every year, and the patient pathways give structured, longitudinal contact with patients from Year 1. Clinical training uses UCL's central London teaching hospitals and community providers, and the final year is organised around assistantships in which students share the work of a named FY1 doctor. UCL also offers the MBPhD for students aiming at academic medicine. Applicants are selected partly through multiple mini interviews, held December to March.

ucl-pir.name: Politics and International Relations BSc
ucl-pir.applies: Prospectus page for September 2026 entry (a September 2027 entry page also exists); module details from UCL Module Catalogue entries for 2026/27; departmental module list headed for 2025/26
ucl-pir.rules: Award: BSc (Hons) Politics and International Relations on completion of 360 credits (120 per year); UCAS code L251. Modules normally 15 or 30 credits. Year 1: compulsory modules in international relations, comparative politics, public policy and political theory plus skills/data content, together with small-group 'Hot Topic' modules (number to choose not stated by UCL). Year 2: three compulsory modules (including Quantitative Data Analysis and Qualitative Research Methods) plus two electives in Term 1 and three electives in Term 2, from departmental options. Year 3: six modules chosen from intermediate (Level 5) and advanced (Level 6) options, which may include modules from other departments with approval, plus a year-long research project culminating in a dissertation (POLS0086, 30 credits per catalogue). Optional year abroad (subject to Year 1 grades and a Year 2 application) extends the degree to four years, with the abroad year taken as Year 3.
ucl-pir.teaching: UCL's Politics and International Relations BSc is taught mainly through lectures with linked seminars, by staff from the Department of Political Science and the School of Public Policy. Contact time is about 8 to 12 hours a week, with 25 to 30 hours of independent study. Year 1 covers the main subfields of politics alongside small 'Hot Topic' modules. Year 2 adds compulsory quantitative and qualitative methods to a wide choice of electives. Year 3 combines six options with a year-long supervised dissertation. Assessment is varied, ranging from essays, problem sets and policy briefs to exams and the final research project.

profile.body: Teaching is usually by lectures and seminars, and UCL puts weekly contact time at about 8 to 12 hours, covering lectures, seminars, practice-based activities and e-learning. You are expected to do about 25 to 30 hours of independent study a week. Staff come from both the Department of Political Science and the School of Public Policy. Core Year 1 lectures are large: Democracy and Authoritarianism had 200 PIR students last year. The Year 1 Hot Topic modules are deliberately smaller. Climate Change: Politics and Policy, for example, is described as a small class with a weekly one-hour interactive lecture and one-hour seminar, and had 56 students last year. Seminar group sizes are not published.

UCL lists essays, problem sets, exams, presentations, literature reviews, policy briefs, research designs, course portfolios and a final research project. The balance varies a lot by module. Democracy and Authoritarianism is 60% exam and 40% coursework. The Hot Topic module on climate change is 100% coursework across two assessments. Qualitative Research Methods is 100% coursework, and the dissertation is assessed entirely on the written project. Modules are assessed in the year you take them. Under UCL's general regulations you progress by passing 120 credits a year. Up to 30 credits with marks between 1.00 and 39.99 can be condoned if you pass at least 90 credits and average at least 40%. Undergraduate dissertations are always non-condonable. Exam timing is not given on the course pages.

Each year is 120 credits, and the BSc (Hons) needs 360. Year 1 introduces international relations, comparative politics, public policy and political theory, alongside training in writing, oral communication and the use and misuse of data in politics. Year 2 deepens your subject knowledge through departmental electives and includes compulsory Quantitative Data Analysis and Qualitative Research Methods, plus contact with politics and policy practitioners. Year 3 combines six options with a year-long research project leading to a dissertation (POLS0086, 30 credits, about 125 students last year). UCL's default scheme for three-year degrees weights the years 1:3:5, counting your best 90 credits in Years 1 and 2 and all 120 credits in Year 3, with a First from 69.50%. The department does not say which scheme it uses.

In Year 1 you take Hot Topic modules, small-group courses on urgent social and policy problems, alongside the core subfields. UCL does not say how many you choose. In Year 2 you take two electives in Term 1 and three in Term 2 from the department's list. In Year 3 you choose six modules from intermediate (Level 5) and advanced (Level 6) options, which can include modules from other departments with approval. You also pick your own dissertation topic, subject to approval. The department's pages do not describe the selection process, deadlines or caps.

The Hot Topic modules give first-years small-group teaching on live policy problems from their first term. The department's flagship Policy & Practice Seminar Series brings practitioners in to speak, and coursework is deliberately linked to current events. Training in quantitative and qualitative methods is compulsory for everyone. A limited number of study abroad places are available, depending on your Year 1 grades and a successful application in Year 2. If you get one, you transfer to the four-year programme at the end of Year 2 and spend Year 3 abroad. UCL estimates extra costs of £200 to £1,000 a month. No work placements are mentioned.

ucl-ppe.name: Philosophy, Politics and Economics BSc
ucl-ppe.applies: 2026 entry (programme starting September 2026; UCAS code 4V86). Module details taken from the UCL Module Catalogue 2026/27 deliveries. A 2027-entry prospectus page also exists with the same title and 3-year length but shows only an indicative subset of modules.
ucl-ppe.rules: Full-time, 3 academic years; award is BSc (Hons) Philosophy, Politics and Economics. 120 credits per year (360 total), made up of modules normally worth 15 or 30 credits; modules are assessed in the year taken. Year 1 is common to all students: compulsory Philosophy, Politics and Economics modules plus Introduction to Quantitative Research Methods, a Philosophy option, and a choice between Mathematics for Economics (required to take Economics beyond Year 1; Economics route) and Principles of Social Science Research (Philosophy route). After Year 1 students choose a priority subject pairing (Politics and Economics, or Politics and Philosophy) and a research-methods specialism (Social Data Science, or Mixed Methods). Year 2 compulsories: Public Policy (all); Microeconomics and Macroeconomic Theory and Policy (Politics and Economics); Data Analysis (Social Data Science / Q-Step); Qualitative Research Methods (Mixed Methods). Final year: a dissertation in political science, economics or philosophy (depending on discipline) plus six further modules depending on route and stream. The Social Data Science (Q-Step) stream leads to BSc (Hons) Philosophy, Politics and Economics with Social Data Science. Limited study-abroad places (subject to Year 1 performance) transfer the student to a four-year programme. UCL describes module lists as indicative and subject to change.
ucl-ppe.teaching: UCL's PPE is led by Political Science, with Philosophy and Economics teaching, and is built around lectures and small-group seminars. You typically have one lecture and one seminar per module each week, adding up to about 8 to 10 contact hours, with 25 to 30 hours of independent study. Year 1 is a common foundation. From Year 2 you follow one of four routes, combining a subject pairing (Politics and Economics, or Politics and Philosophy) with a methods stream (Social Data Science or Mixed Methods). Every route ends with a compulsory 30-credit dissertation. Assessment mixes coursework, exams, presentations and independent research.

profile.body: Teaching combines lectures with small-group seminars or tutorials, delivered across the Political Science, Philosophy and Economics departments. UCL quotes about 8 to 10 contact hours a week and expects 25 to 30 hours of independent study. Group sizes vary widely. The PPE-only Introduction to Politics had 69 students last year, while Economics (ECON0002), shared with the Economics degree, had 724. Introduction to Quantitative Research Methods (209 students) takes a hands-on approach with tutor-supported seminars. The final-year PPE dissertation module had 41 students. Seminar sizes as such are not published.

UCL lists written coursework, exams, presentations and an independent research project or dissertation, and says graded coursework is meant to build towards the dissertation. Modules are assessed in the year you take them. The splits vary. Introduction to Politics is 75% exam and 25% coursework, Economics is 80% exam and 20% coursework, and the methods modules (Introduction to Quantitative Research Methods, Data Analysis, Qualitative Research Methods) are 100% coursework. The dissertation is assessed entirely on the written project. The programme structure makes Introduction to Politics, Economics, Introduction to Political Philosophy and the dissertation non-condonable, so they must be passed outright. Other modules follow UCL's rule allowing up to 30 credits with marks of 1.00 to 39.99 to be condoned if you average at least 40%. Honours also needs at least 90 credits passed at Level 6.

Each year is 120 credits, out of 360 in total. Year 1 is shared by all students: Introduction to Politics, Economics and Introduction to Political Philosophy, a Term 2 philosophy choice, and Introduction to Quantitative Research Methods. Students on the Economics concentration add Introduction to Mathematics for Economics, and those on the Philosophy concentration add Principles of Social Science Research. In Year 2 everyone takes Public Policy. The Economics routes add Microeconomics and Macroeconomic Theory and Policy, the Social Data Science stream adds Data Analysis, and the Mixed Methods stream adds Qualitative Research Methods. The final year is a 30-credit dissertation plus methods and subject options. UCL's default classification scheme weights the years 1:3:5, though the scheme PPE uses is not stated.

You choose your concentration and methods stream in Year 1. You can move out of the Politics and Economics concentration later, but not into it, so the Year 1 maths choice matters. Philosophy-route students must take at least one Year 2 philosophy module from Group B (Normative Philosophy), and Year 2 allows at most one advanced Level 6 module. In the final year, the Social Data Science stream takes 30 credits of methods, normally Causal Analysis and Measurement in Data Science, with other modules subject to space. Mixed Methods takes 15 credits from a short list and needs at least 30 credits in each discipline, 75 credits in total. The dissertation can be in politics (POLS0102), economics (ECON0117) or philosophy (PHIL0083), depending on your route.

UCL says PPE students are generally expected to attend one lecture and one seminar per module each week, adding up to about 8 to 10 contact hours. Most modules run for a single term, and some run across two. For 2026/27, Term 1 runs from 28 September to 18 December, Term 2 from 11 January to 24 March, and Term 3 from 26 April to 11 June. Students must be available throughout term time for teaching and assessment. Outside class, you are expected to put in about 25 to 30 hours of independent study a week.

UCL's PPE has a strong policy and research-methods focus. Public Policy is compulsory for everyone, and every student takes a methods specialism. The Social Data Science (Q-Step) stream, run with the UCL Social Data Institute, leads to the named award BSc (Hons) Philosophy, Politics and Economics with Social Data Science. Students can attend the Political Science Policy & Practice Seminar Series. A limited number of year-abroad places are available, depending on Year 1 performance and an application. If you get one, you move to the four-year programme, and UCL estimates extra costs of £200 to £1,000 a month.
